root.title: Machine Learning
root.text: A machine learning model is a program you did not write line by line. You supply examples, and an algorithm searches for a rule that fits them and, more importantly, holds up on examples it has never seen. That second part is the whole difficulty, and it is why this pathway is shaped the way it is. Six sections: what learning from data actually means, the classical algorithm families and when each earns its place, how models are trained, how to evaluate them honestly, what you can do without labels, and what breaks once a model is serving real traffic.

children.title: Foundations of Learning
children.text: Before any algorithm makes sense, four questions have to be settled: what it means for a program to learn from examples rather than instructions, what it is actually trying to minimise, why doing well on the data you have does not mean doing well on the data you don't, and what properties your data must have for any of it to work. Those four questions are the four parts of this section. They are not preliminaries you skim past. Almost every failure you will hit later in practice is one of these four ideas being quietly violated somewhere upstream.

children.title: What Learning From Data Means
children.text: A learned system differs from a written one in where its behaviour comes from: you supply examples and a fitting procedure, and the behaviour falls out. Making that concrete takes four things. You need to see the contrast with hand-written rules to know what has actually changed. You need the taxonomy of what kind of feedback the examples carry, because that determines which methods apply at all. You need the vocabulary for how examples are represented. And you need the idea that a learner searches a restricted set of candidate functions, not all possible ones.

children.title: Rules vs. Learned Behaviour
children.text: Hand-written rules encode behaviour you already understand; learning extracts behaviour you can demonstrate but cannot articulate. Anyone can label a thousand photos as cat or not-cat in an afternoon, and nobody can write the if-statements that do it. That is the whole trade. You give up a system you can read line by line and audit directly, and in exchange you get one that handles cases you never anticipated and improves when you feed it more examples. Rules stay the right answer when the logic is known, stable, and legally or operationally required to be explicit.
children.deep_text:
Consider fraud detection on card transactions. The rule-based version starts easy: flag anything over five thousand, flag anything from a country the cardholder has never transacted in, flag more than three transactions in a minute. Each rule is readable and defensible. Then the exceptions arrive. Business customers legitimately spend twenty thousand. Travellers legitimately transact abroad. Fuel pumps legitimately produce rapid repeats. So you add conditions, and conditions on conditions, and eighteen months later you have four hundred interacting rules that nobody dares change because no one can predict what a change breaks. The rules did not become wrong; they became unmaintainable, because the real decision boundary was never a small set of thresholds.

The learned version takes the same historical transactions, each already marked fraudulent or not by chargeback records, and fits a function from transaction attributes to a fraud score. Nobody writes the thresholds. The thresholds — and the interactions between amount, hour, merchant category, and distance from the last transaction — come out of the fitting. When fraud patterns shift, you retrain rather than re-reason.

The common misconception is that learning replaces rules, and that a mature system has none. It is closer to the opposite. Production fraud systems are hybrids: hard rules for things that are non-negotiable regardless of what the data says, such as blocking a card reported stolen, and a learned model for the fuzzy majority. A rule is the right tool when you already know the answer and need it enforced exactly; a model is the right tool when you can recognise the answer but not state it.

The decision rule in practice: write rules when the logic is known, stable, low-dimensional, and must be explainable to an auditor or a regulator. Learn when the logic is genuinely unknown, when it involves many weakly-informative signals interacting, when it drifts over time, and when you have labelled examples in reasonable quantity. And be honest about the second condition — no labelled examples means no learning, and a project that starts by assuming labels will materialise usually stalls there. The cost side of the trade is real too: a learned system fails in ways you cannot inspect by reading it, so you need evaluation infrastructure that a rule engine never required.

interview.question: Why would you choose a hard-coded rule over a model even when you have plenty of training data?
interview.answer: Because some decisions must be guaranteed rather than predicted. If a card is reported stolen, it must be declined every time, and a model that gets it right 99.7% of the time is unacceptable. Rules also win when the decision has to be explained to a regulator or contested by a customer, since a threshold is defensible in a way that a learned weight is not.

interview.question: A team says their rule engine has become unmaintainable and they want to replace it with a model. What do you check first?
interview.answer: Whether they have labelled outcomes, and whether those labels are the thing they actually care about. A rule engine produces decisions, not ground truth, so if the only historical record is what the rules decided, training on it just reproduces the rules with worse readability. You need an independent signal — chargebacks, manual review outcomes, confirmed complaints — before replacement is even possible.

interview.question: When does moving from rules to a learned model make a system harder to operate rather than easier?
interview.answer: When the failure modes stop being readable. A broken rule is found by reading it; a broken model shows up as a slow drift in a metric nobody was watching. Adopting a model means adopting monitoring, held-out evaluation, and a retraining path, so if the organisation cannot support that, a mediocre rule set that everyone understands may genuinely be the better system.

children.title: The Three Learning Paradigms
children.text: What separates the major families of learning is what an example comes with. Supervised learning gets examples paired with the correct answer, so the learner can measure how wrong it was on each one. Unsupervised learning gets examples with no answers at all, so it can only find structure — groupings, directions of variation, things that look unusual. Reinforcement learning gets neither, just a consequence that arrives after a sequence of actions, often much later. Deciding which of these you are in is the first move on any new problem, because it determines which methods are even applicable.
children.deep_text:
Take a single dataset of customer records and watch the paradigm change with the question. You have a year of activity for two hundred thousand accounts: pages visited, purchases, support tickets, plan tier. If you also have a column recording which accounts cancelled in the following quarter, you are supervised: for each account there is a correct answer, and a learner can compare its prediction to that answer and adjust. If you have no such column and the question is which kinds of customers exist, you are unsupervised: the learner can group accounts that behave alike, but nothing tells it whether its groups are the right ones, because there is no right one defined. And if the question is what sequence of offers to send over six months to maximise retained revenue, you are in reinforcement: each offer changes what the customer does next, no single offer has a labelled correct value, and the only feedback is the revenue that shows up at the end.

The misconception worth killing early is that these are three difficulty levels, with reinforcement as the advanced version of supervised. They are three different feedback structures, and the differences are structural rather than ordinal. Reinforcement learning is not harder supervised learning; it is a setting where the training signal is delayed, sparse, and affected by the learner's own choices, which makes credit assignment the central problem rather than function fitting. Similarly, unsupervised learning is not supervised learning with the labels hidden as a challenge. It is a genuinely different objective, since with no target there is no unambiguous notion of correct, which is why evaluating it is hard in a way that evaluating a classifier is not.

The practical decision rule is to ask what feedback you can actually obtain, not what you would like. Labels are expensive; if getting them requires a human to review each example, the honest answer may be that you have ten thousand labels and two million unlabelled records, which points at approaches that use both. If the outcome you care about only becomes observable after a series of decisions and your system's own actions change what you observe, no amount of supervised framing will fix that mismatch. Most production systems are supervised, not because supervision is superior, but because it is the setting where feedback is cheapest to obtain and progress is easiest to measure.

interview.question: You are handed a dataset with no label column. Does that automatically make the problem unsupervised?
interview.answer: No — it often means the label has not been constructed yet. Many supervised problems are created by defining a target from raw history, such as marking an account churned if it had no activity for ninety days. The real question is whether the outcome you care about is recoverable from the data, not whether someone already put it in a column.

interview.question: Why can't you just frame a sequential decision problem as supervised learning over past decisions?
interview.answer: Because your past decisions determined what data you ever saw. Supervised learning on logged actions teaches the model to imitate whatever policy generated the logs, including its mistakes, and it has no way to evaluate an action nobody ever took. That feedback loop — actions shaping the data distribution — is exactly what the reinforcement framing exists to handle.

interview.question: How do you decide whether an unsupervised result is any good?
interview.answer: You usually cannot decide it from the data alone, because there is no defined correct answer to compare against. In practice you validate against something external: whether the discovered structure predicts a downstream outcome, whether domain experts recognise the groups as meaningful, or whether using it improves a system you can measure. If none of those are available, treat the result as a hypothesis rather than a finding.

children.title: Features, Labels, and Examples
children.text: An example is one row: one customer, one transaction, one image. Its features are the measured inputs — the columns the model is allowed to look at. Its label is the answer you want predicted, present only when someone or something recorded it. Stack the rows and you have a design matrix, conventionally n rows by d columns, with a separate vector of labels. Almost all practical difficulty lives in deciding what counts as one row and which columns are legitimately available at the moment a prediction has to be made.
children.deep_text:
Make it concrete with loan default prediction. One example is one loan application. The features might be applicant income, requested amount, employment length, number of prior accounts, and credit utilisation — say twelve numbers per application. The label is a single binary value, one if the loan defaulted within twenty-four months and zero otherwise. Fifty thousand applications gives a matrix with fifty thousand rows and twelve columns, plus a label vector of length fifty thousand. That is the entire input to a supervised learner.

Two decisions in that setup do more damage than any modelling choice. The first is the unit of an example. If the same applicant appears four times because they applied four times, the rows are not independent, and a random split will put the same person on both sides of it, which flatters your estimate of performance. The fix is to decide up front what the unit really is — applicant, or application — and to keep all rows belonging to one unit together whenever you divide the data.

The second is whether a feature is genuinely available at prediction time. Credit utilisation as of today is a fine feature for scoring an application today. Credit utilisation as recorded in the warehouse, which may have been refreshed after the default occurred, is not a feature at all — it is a peek at the answer. This is the single most common way a model that scores beautifully offline turns out to be worthless, and the discipline that prevents it is asking, of every column, what its value would have been at the exact moment the prediction was needed.

The misconception is that features are given rather than built. Raw tables rarely arrive in modelling shape. Twelve raw columns commonly become sixty after you encode categories numerically, bucket a skewed amount, and derive ratios such as requested amount over income, which is far more informative than either number alone. Categorical fields with many levels, dates that must become durations or cyclical positions, and free text that must be turned into numbers all require explicit choices, and those choices frequently matter more than which algorithm you then run.

The rule of thumb: fix the unit of observation first, then audit every candidate feature for availability at prediction time, and only then worry about representation. Reversing that order produces beautiful pipelines that answer the wrong question.

interview.question: Why does the definition of a single example matter so much before you write any modelling code?
interview.answer: Because it determines whether your rows are independent, and independence is what makes a held-out estimate meaningful. If one underlying entity generates many rows, splitting rows randomly puts correlated copies on both sides, and your measured performance is optimistic by an amount you cannot bound. Fixing the unit up front also fixes what your predictions are about, which is a product decision as much as a technical one.

interview.question: How would you audit a feature set for columns that won't be available in production?
interview.answer: Go column by column and ask what value that field held at the exact timestamp the prediction must be made, not what it holds in the warehouse today. Fields that are updated in place, backfilled, or derived from downstream events are the usual offenders. If the pipeline cannot reconstruct a point-in-time value, the feature should be dropped regardless of how predictive it looks.

interview.question: When is it worth investing in feature construction rather than a more expressive model?
interview.answer: Almost always when the data is tabular and the domain has known relationships. A ratio like debt-to-income encodes a relationship a model would otherwise have to infer from limited data, and giving it directly costs nothing. The exception is high-dimensional perceptual data such as images or audio, where hand-built features have generally been outperformed by learned representations.

children.title: The Hypothesis Space
children.text: A learner never searches all possible functions from inputs to outputs — that set is unimaginably large and searching it is hopeless. It searches a restricted family chosen in advance: all straight lines, all depth-five decision trees, all networks with a fixed architecture. That family is the hypothesis space, and choosing a model is precisely choosing it. Training is then a search within it for the member that fits best. Everything the learner can possibly express, and everything it can never express no matter how much data you give it, is fixed the moment you pick that family.
children.deep_text:
Take a one-dimensional regression problem: predict y from a single input x, with thirty observed points. If your hypothesis space is all functions of the form y equals ax plus b, it has exactly two free parameters, and training means finding the best pair. The space contains every straight line and no curves at all. If the true relationship bends, no amount of data helps — the best line remains a bad approximation, and the error it leaves behind is a property of your chosen space, not of your training procedure.

Widen the space to all polynomials of degree at most ten, and you now have eleven parameters and a family that contains every straight line as a special case plus a great many curves. With thirty points, some member of that family will pass close to nearly all of them. This is where the trade becomes visible: a larger space contains better approximations to the truth, and it also contains a great many functions that fit the observed points well by contorting between them. Which of those the search lands on depends on the data you happened to draw.

The standard misconception is that a bigger hypothesis space is straightforwardly better because it can represent more. Representation is only half the problem. A space you cannot search reliably, or cannot pin down with the data you have, gives you a function that fits your sample rather than the phenomenon. The reason restricted spaces work at all is that the restriction is itself information: choosing linear functions is a claim that the relationship is roughly linear, and when that claim is approximately right, it substitutes for data you do not have. This is the practical content of the no-free-lunch idea — a learner that assumes nothing about which functions are plausible has no reason to prefer any consistent explanation over any other, and averaged over all possible problems, no such preference beats any other.

The decision rule: pick the smallest space that plausibly contains something close to the truth, given what you know about the domain and how much data you have. Ten thousand examples and five features supports a rich family; two hundred examples and five features does not, and a linear fit there will usually beat a flexible one that has nothing to constrain it. Where you genuinely do not know the shape of the relationship, prefer families with an adjustable size — tree depth, number of basis functions — so you can let held-out data settle the question rather than guessing once and committing.

interview.question: What does it actually mean to say a model has high representational power, and why isn't that always desirable?
interview.answer: It means its hypothesis space contains a wide variety of functions, including good approximations to complicated truths. It is not automatically desirable because containing a good function is not the same as being able to identify it from finite data. With limited examples, a rich space also contains many functions that match your sample well and the underlying phenomenon poorly, and nothing in the fitting procedure distinguishes them.

interview.question: Why can adding a strong assumption about the functional form improve results rather than hurt them?
interview.answer: Because the assumption acts as free information. Restricting to monotone or additive functions rules out large regions of the space without spending any data, so the data you do have is spent distinguishing among plausible candidates instead. When the assumption is approximately right this is a clear gain; when it is badly wrong it puts a floor under your error that more data cannot lift.

interview.question: How would you explain the practical relevance of no-free-lunch to someone choosing a model?
interview.answer: It says that no model is best across all conceivable problems, so any claim that one algorithm dominates is really a claim about the problems you tend to face. Practically, it moves the question from which algorithm is best to which assumptions match your domain. That is why tabular problems with heterogeneous features and perceptual problems with spatial structure end up favouring different families.

children.deep_text:
The four parts here build a working vocabulary, and they are ordered from motivation to machinery.

Start with the contrast against explicitly programmed rules. This is the motivating move: it says what learning buys you and what it costs you, and it establishes why anyone would give up the readability of an if-statement. Everything after this is elaboration on how that trade is made.

Next comes the taxonomy of feedback signals. Once you accept that behaviour comes from examples, the immediate question is what an example carries with it — an answer, no answer, or a consequence — and that question partitions the entire field into families of methods. Knowing which family a problem belongs to is the first thing you do when handed a new task, so it comes early.

Third comes representation: the concrete anatomy of a dataset, and the precise meanings of the words that get used loosely everywhere else. This is deliberately placed after the taxonomy, because the taxonomy is what tells you whether a label column exists at all.

Fourth comes the hypothesis space — the set of functions the learner is permitted to consider. This is the most abstract of the four and the most load-bearing later, because choosing a model is exactly choosing this set, and the size and shape of the set is what the whole of generalisation is later argued about. Read it last, with the concrete vocabulary already in place, or it reads as empty formalism.

Taken together, these four give you enough language to state any supervised problem precisely: what a row is, what feedback it carries, which columns are inputs, and which family of functions you intend to search over it.

children.title: The Objective of Learning
children.text: Learning is search, and search needs a score. That score is where three separate ideas have to be pulled apart carefully. First, wrongness has to be defined numerically, and the definition you pick changes what the fitted model does. Second, there is a distinction between the average error over the finite sample you hold and the average error over everything you might ever see — the second is what you want and the first is all you can compute. Third, and following from that, driving the computable one to zero is not the objective and can actively defeat it.

children.title: Loss Functions as Definitions of Wrong
children.text: A loss function turns a mistake into a number, and it is not a neutral choice. Squared error says being off by ten is a hundred times worse than being off by one, so one large miss dominates many small ones. Absolute error says it is ten times worse, so a few extreme points barely move the fit. Same data, same model family, different fitted parameters — because you asked different questions. Picking a loss is deciding which errors you refuse to tolerate, and that decision belongs to the problem rather than the algorithm.

children.deep_text:
Take five delivery times in minutes: 20, 22, 21, 23, and 94, the last being a genuine outlier where a driver broke down. Fit a single constant prediction. Under squared error the best constant is the mean, 36 — a number that describes none of the five observations, dragged upward by the one bad day. Under absolute error the best constant is the median, 22, which is a good description of a typical delivery and simply accepts a large error on the outlier. Neither is wrong. The squared-error answer is correct if a ninety-minute delivery really is catastrophically bad and you want the prediction to reflect that risk; the absolute-error answer is correct if you want a typical-case estimate and consider the breakdown noise.

Classification makes the asymmetry starker. Counting misclassifications treats a missed fraud and a falsely-flagged legitimate purchase as identical costs. They are not: the first costs the chargeback amount, the second costs an annoyed customer and a support call. Once you attach real costs to the two error types, the threshold that minimises cost stops being one-half, and it moves toward whichever error is cheaper to make.

The misconception is that the loss is chosen for optimisation convenience and evaluated separately with the metric you care about. That is sometimes forced — some metrics are not differentiable and cannot be optimised directly, so a smooth surrogate is used instead — but it should be a known compromise rather than a default. When you train on one objective and report another, you have to check that improving the first still improves the second, and sometimes it does not. Squared error and a business metric that caps the penalty on large misses can move in opposite directions.

The decision rule: start from the cost structure of the actual decision. If large errors are disproportionately damaging, squared error encodes that honestly. If your data has heavy tails or contamination you cannot clean, prefer absolute error or a hybrid that is quadratic near zero and linear far from it, so single bad points cannot dictate the fit. If the two classes carry different costs, put those costs in the loss rather than hoping to fix it afterwards by moving a threshold. And write down the cost structure explicitly before choosing, because a loss chosen by default is still a claim about what matters.

interview.question: Why does switching from squared error to absolute error change the model, not just the reported number?
interview.answer: Because training optimises the loss, so a different loss has a different minimiser. Squared error is minimised by the conditional mean and absolute error by the conditional median, and those coincide only for symmetric error distributions. On skewed or outlier-contaminated data the fitted parameters can differ substantially.

interview.question: When would you accept training on a loss that isn't the metric you report?
interview.answer: When the reported metric is not usable as a training objective — ranking metrics and thresholded accuracy are flat or discontinuous, so gradients carry no signal. In that case you train a smooth surrogate that is known to be aligned with it. The obligation is to verify the alignment empirically on held-out data rather than assume it, because surrogates can improve while the target metric stalls.

interview.question: How do you encode asymmetric business costs into a model?
interview.answer: The cleanest way is weighting the loss so that the expensive error type contributes proportionally more, which makes the optimiser trade off correctly during fitting. The alternative is training on a symmetric loss and tuning the decision threshold afterwards against the real cost function, which is often good enough and is easier to revise when costs change. What you should not do is leave costs implicit and hope accuracy is a proxy for them.

children.title: Empirical Risk vs. True Risk
children.text: True risk is the average loss your model would incur over the entire distribution your data came from — every future example, weighted by how likely it is. That is the quantity you actually care about, and you can never compute it, because you do not have the distribution. Empirical risk is the average loss over the finite sample you do have, and it is computable. Learning proceeds by minimising the second and hoping it tracks the first. The whole discipline of evaluation exists because that hope needs to be checked rather than assumed.

Why Minimising Training Error Is Not the Goal

children.deep_text:
Empirical risk is a sample mean, and it inherits everything that is true of sample means. Suppose you evaluate a spam classifier on a thousand held-out emails and it misclassifies thirty, giving an empirical error of 3%. That 3% is an estimate of the true error, and like any estimate from a thousand draws it carries uncertainty of roughly a percentage point either way. If a colleague's model gets 2.6% on the same thousand, you have not shown it is better; you have shown a difference well inside the noise. This is the first practical consequence: empirical risk is a random quantity, and comparisons that ignore its variance manufacture conclusions.

The second consequence is more subtle and matters more. The estimate is unbiased only for a model chosen independently of the data being used to evaluate it. The moment you use a set to select among models — pick the best of twenty architectures by their score on it — the winner's score on that set is optimistically biased, because you selected partly on noise. Whichever model got the friendliest thousand emails wins, and its 2.6% overstates its true quality. With twenty candidates the effect is a fraction of a percent; with a hyperparameter sweep of two thousand configurations it can be several percent, which is often larger than the differences you are trying to detect.

The misconception to correct directly: unbiased is not the same as accurate. People hear that held-out error is an unbiased estimate of true risk and conclude the number can be taken at face value. Unbiasedness says that if you repeated the whole experiment many times the estimates would average out to the truth. It says nothing about how far any single estimate is from the truth, and with a small evaluation set that distance can be large. A five-hundred-example test set gives you an error bar of a couple of percentage points at best, so reporting a difference of half a percent from it is reporting noise with a decimal point.

The practical rule: treat every empirical risk as a point estimate with a spread, and size that spread before drawing conclusions. For binary outcomes, the spread narrows roughly with the square root of the evaluation set size, so quadrupling the set halves it. Keep any set used for selection separate from the set used for the final number, because the selection process is what breaks the unbiasedness. And when someone reports that a model achieves a particular figure, the first question is always how many examples that figure was computed on, and whether anything was chosen using them.

interview.question: Why is the score on a validation set biased upward for the model you selected with it?
interview.answer: Because selection uses the noise in that set as if it were signal. Each candidate's measured score is its true performance plus a random error from this particular sample, and picking the maximum tends to pick a model with a favourable error term. The more candidates you compare, the larger the expected overstatement, which is why a final untouched test set exists.

interview.question: Your model scores 94.1% and a colleague's scores 94.6% on the same 800-example test set. Is theirs better?
interview.answer: Not on that evidence. With 800 examples the standard error on an accuracy near 94% is around eight tenths of a percentage point, so a half-point gap is comfortably inside the noise. To distinguish them you would need a substantially larger evaluation set, or a paired comparison on the same examples that looks at where the two models actually disagree.

interview.question: If true risk can never be computed, what is the point of the concept?
interview.answer: It names the target precisely, which keeps you honest about what every measurement is an estimate of. It also frames the two distinct failure modes — the estimate can be biased because of how the data was selected, or noisy because the sample is small — and those have different fixes. Without the distinction, people treat a held-out number as the truth rather than as a measurement with error attached.

children.title: Why Minimising Training Error Is Not the Goal
children.text: Any sufficiently flexible model can drive training error to zero — memorise every example and look them up. That model is useless on anything it has not seen, and its perfect training score is evidence of nothing. Training error is the quantity you can measure and optimise; performance on unseen data is the quantity you want. Below a certain complexity these move together, so reducing training error genuinely helps. Past that point they diverge, and further reduction is bought by fitting the noise in your particular sample rather than the pattern behind it.

children.deep_text:
The cleanest demonstration is a nearest-neighbour lookup with one neighbour. For any training point, the closest point in the training set is itself, so its prediction is exactly its own label and training error is precisely zero on every dataset you will ever hand it. Nothing has been learned; the data has been stored. Now the same phenomenon in a less obvious form: fit a degree-twenty polynomial to twenty-one noisy points and it passes exactly through all of them, training error zero again, while oscillating wildly between them and predicting nonsense a short distance from any observation.

What makes this more than a curiosity is that the divergence is gradual and has a characteristic shape. Train a model while tracking error on both the training data and a held-out set. Early on, both fall — the model is capturing real structure and that structure is present in both. At some point held-out error flattens and then begins to rise while training error keeps falling. The gap opening between the two curves is the model spending capacity on the sample rather than the phenomenon. That crossing point is what you are looking for, and it is invisible if you only track the training curve.

The misconception, and it is common in people coming from conventional software, is that a model that fits its data perfectly has succeeded and one with residual training error has failed. In conventional software, passing all your tests is good news. Here, matching every training example exactly is at best uninformative and usually a warning, because the training set contains measurement error, mislabelled rows, and coincidences specific to those particular draws, and a model can only match them exactly by reproducing all of that too. A small amount of training error is often the sign of a model that has generalised.

This does not mean training error is useless. It is a diagnostic, read jointly with held-out error rather than alone. High training error and high held-out error means the model is too constrained to capture the pattern, and the fix is more capacity or better features. Low training error with much higher held-out error means it has capacity to spare and nothing constraining how it uses it, and the fix is fewer parameters, more data, or an explicit constraint on the fit. Low on both means you are done. Read as a pair the two numbers tell you which direction to move; read alone, either one misleads.

The operating rule: never tune anything against training error, never report it as a result, and treat a zero on it as a prompt to check for leakage or an over-flexible model rather than as a success.

interview.question: A model gets 100% on its training set. What are the possible explanations and how do you distinguish them?
interview.answer: Either the model has enough capacity to memorise, the task is genuinely trivial, or a feature is leaking the label. Check held-out performance first: if it is far lower, you are looking at memorisation; if it is also near-perfect, suspect leakage and audit the features for anything derived from the target. A genuinely easy task is the least likely explanation and should be the last one you accept.

interview.question: Why do you look at training and validation error together rather than validation alone?
interview.answer: Because validation error alone tells you the model is bad but not why. A large gap between the two points at excess capacity and calls for constraint or more data; both being high points at insufficient capacity or weak features and calls for the opposite. Acting on validation error without the training number means guessing which direction to move.

interview.question: When is it reasonable to deliberately train past the point where validation error starts rising?
interview.answer: Rarely, and only when you intend to recover with an explicit mechanism — for example when you are using the later phase of training with strong regularisation, or when the validation set is small enough that the apparent rise may be noise. The default is to stop at or near the minimum and keep the checkpoint from there. If you continue, you need a reason stated in advance and a second held-out set to check it against.

children.deep_text:
These three parts form a single argument, and the order is the argument's structure.

It opens with the definition of wrong. Before anything can be optimised, a number has to be attached to a mistake, and that number is a modelling decision rather than a neutral technicality. Different definitions of wrong make different predictions optimal on identical data, which is why this comes first: everything downstream is measured in the units this part chooses.

The second part introduces the quantity you actually care about and the quantity you can compute. The average loss over your sample is available; the expected loss over the whole distribution your data was drawn from is not, and it is the one that determines whether your system works. Naming both precisely, and being clear that one is an estimate of the other with a sampling error attached, is the piece of vocabulary the rest of the pathway leans on hardest.

The third part draws the consequence. Given that you can only minimise the sample quantity, the natural instinct is to minimise it as far as it goes, and that instinct is wrong. Pushed hard enough, minimising sample error stops improving the quantity you wanted and starts degrading it, because the extra fit is being spent on features of your particular sample rather than the phenomenon behind it.

Read in sequence, this section establishes the gap between what is measured and what matters. The section on generalisation that follows is a sustained study of that gap — where it comes from, how to decompose it, and what levers control it — so this is the vocabulary it will assume.

children.title: Generalisation
children.text: The gap between how a model performs on the data it was fitted to and how it performs on data it has never seen is the central problem of the field. This part studies that gap directly. It covers the two ways a model can fail at either end of the complexity range, a decomposition of prediction error into parts that trade against each other, the notion of capacity that controls where you sit on that range, the techniques that shrink capacity deliberately, and the way high-dimensional inputs make every part of this harder. These five ideas are one argument, not five topics.

children.title: Overfitting and Underfitting
children.text: Underfitting is a model too rigid to capture the structure in the data — it is wrong on the training set and equally wrong everywhere else. Overfitting is a model flexible enough to reproduce the training set's accidents as well as its patterns — it is nearly perfect where it was fitted and much worse anywhere new. You diagnose them from two numbers, not one. Both errors high means underfitting. Training error low with held-out error much higher means overfitting. The distance between those two numbers is the diagnosis, and the direction you should move follows from it.

must_not_cover: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial

children.deep_text:
Work through it with house prices. Fit a model that predicts a single constant, the average price, for every house. Training error is large and held-out error is large and roughly equal — say a mean absolute error of ninety thousand on both. That is underfitting in its purest form: the model has no capacity to express the relationship, so it is uniformly mediocre and more data changes nothing.

Now fit a deep decision tree with no depth limit on two thousand houses. It splits until each leaf holds a single house and predicts that house's exact price. Training error is zero. Held-out error is sixty thousand — better than the constant, because the early splits captured real structure like square footage and location, but far worse than the training number suggests, because the deep splits captured the fact that one particular house on Elm Street sold high because the seller was in a hurry. That is overfitting: a training-to-held-out gap of sixty thousand where a well-fitted model might show a gap of eight.

Between them sits a tree with depth capped at six, giving perhaps thirty-five thousand on training and forty-two thousand held out. Worse training error than the deep tree and much better held-out error, which is the point.

The common misconception is that overfitting is caused by training too long or by having too many parameters, full stop. It is caused by capacity that is large relative to the information in your data, and both of those are only proxies for it. Ten thousand parameters on fifty examples overfits badly; the same ten thousand on ten million examples may underfit. The ratio is what matters, which is why more data is a genuine remedy for overfitting and no remedy at all for underfitting.

The decision rule follows directly from the two numbers. If training error is unacceptably high, the model cannot express the pattern: add capacity, add features, or reduce constraint, and do not bother collecting more data because it will not help. If training error is acceptable but held-out error is much higher, the model is expressing too much: reduce capacity, constrain the fit, or collect more data, any of which narrows the gap. If both are acceptable and close, stop. The one thing you must not do is respond to a poor held-out number without looking at the training number first, because the two situations call for opposite actions and guessing wrong makes things worse in a way that is slow to detect.

interview.question: Held-out accuracy is poor. What do you look at before deciding what to change?
interview.answer: Training accuracy, because the two situations demand opposite responses. If training accuracy is also poor the model is underfitting and needs more capacity or better features. If training accuracy is high the model is overfitting and needs constraint or more data, and adding capacity would make it worse.

interview.question: Does more training data fix overfitting, underfitting, or both?
interview.answer: Overfitting only. More data reduces the variance of the fit, so a flexible model has less freedom to contort around individual points and the train-to-held-out gap narrows. Underfitting is a limitation of the model family — the family simply does not contain a good function — and no quantity of data changes what a family can express.

interview.question: Can a model overfit and underfit at the same time?
interview.answer: In the strict sense no, but in practice it appears constantly when performance is uneven across subgroups. A model can overfit a well-represented segment while underfitting a rare one, so aggregate errors look moderate while both problems are present. This is why you slice error by segment rather than trusting one global pair of numbers.

children.title: The Bias-Variance Decomposition
children.text: Expected prediction error at a point splits into three additive pieces. Bias is how far your model family's average prediction sits from the truth — error from the family being systematically wrong. Variance is how much your prediction moves when you refit on a different sample of the same size — error from being sensitive to which data you happened to draw. Irreducible noise is whatever the inputs cannot explain, and it sets a floor no model beats. The first two typically move in opposite directions as you change model flexibility, which is what makes it a trade.

must_not_cover: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial

children.deep_text:
The thought experiment that makes this concrete: imagine drawing a hundred independent training sets of the same size from the same source, fitting your model on each, and then predicting for one specific new input. You now have a hundred predictions for that input. Their average distance from the true value, squared, is the bias term. Their spread around their own average is the variance term. Whatever error remains when both are zero is noise in the target itself. For squared loss these three add up exactly to expected error, which is why the decomposition is more than a metaphor.

Make it numeric. The true value at some input is 100. A linear model fitted on a hundred different samples produces predictions clustered tightly between 88 and 92, averaging 90. Bias squared is 100, variance is small — call it 2. Total around 102 plus noise. A degree-fifteen polynomial on the same hundred samples produces predictions averaging 99.5, essentially unbiased, but scattered from 60 to 140. Bias squared is now under 1 while variance is perhaps 400. The flexible model is right on average and wrong on every individual run, which is exactly the failure that a single training run cannot show you.

The misconception worth being precise about: bias and variance are not properties of a fitted model, they are properties of a fitting procedure applied to a distribution of training sets. You cannot look at your one trained model and read off its variance, because variance is defined across samples you did not draw. This is why bagging reduces variance — averaging many fits on resampled data directly targets the spread term — and why it does essentially nothing for bias, since averaging biased predictors leaves the bias intact.

The second misconception is that the trade is a strict law, so any variance reduction must cost bias. It is a tendency across a family as you turn flexibility, not a conservation law. Better features can reduce bias without touching variance. More data reduces variance while leaving bias alone. Methods exist whose error keeps falling well past the point where the classical picture predicts a rise, so treat the U-shaped curve as the common case rather than the only one.

Used as a diagnostic, the decomposition tells you which lever to pull. A model that is consistently wrong in the same direction across retrains, or across data slices, is bias-dominated: change the family or the features. A model whose predictions swing noticeably when you retrain on a different subsample, or whose cross-validation folds disagree widely, is variance-dominated: constrain it, average several fits, or get more data. The cheap approximation of the experiment is to fit on several bootstrap resamples and look at how much the predictions move.

interview.question: Why can't you measure the variance of your model from a single training run?
interview.answer: Because variance is defined over the distribution of training sets, not over predictions within one fit. It asks how much your predictions would change if you had drawn a different sample of the same size, which one run cannot reveal. The practical approximation is refitting on bootstrap resamples or comparing predictions across cross-validation folds and measuring the spread.

interview.question: Why does bagging help some models a great deal and others hardly at all?
interview.answer: Bagging averages many fits on resampled data, which attacks the variance term and leaves bias essentially untouched. Deep unpruned trees are almost all variance, so averaging them yields a large gain. A linear model on a large sample already has low variance, so there is little for bagging to remove and the effort is mostly wasted.

interview.question: You retrain the same pipeline weekly and the predictions move a lot. Is that a bug?
interview.answer: Not necessarily — it is the signature of a high-variance procedure, and it is expected if the model is flexible relative to the data volume. Before treating it as a defect, check whether the training data itself shifted. If the data is stable and predictions still swing, reduce capacity, add regularisation, or average across seeds, since unstable predictions are an operational problem even when average accuracy is acceptable.

children.title: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial
children.text: Capacity is how much variety a model family can express — how many genuinely different input-output patterns it can realise. A straight line has very little; an unpruned decision tree has enough to isolate every training point. Capacity is not the same as parameter count, though the two correlate: what matters is the effective flexibility after any constraints are applied. Almost every family has a dial that controls it — polynomial degree, tree depth, number of hidden units, neighbourhood size in nearest neighbours. Setting that dial well relative to your data volume is most of practical modelling.

contract.must_cover: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial

children.deep_text:
The formal handle is the largest set of points a family can fit perfectly no matter how the labels are assigned. Straight lines in two dimensions can do this for any three points in general position and fail for some arrangements of four, which puts a precise number on how much they can express. The number itself is rarely used directly in practice, but the idea it captures is exactly right: capacity is the ability to accommodate arbitrary labellings, and a family that can accommodate anything has told you nothing when it accommodates your data.

Concretely, k-nearest-neighbours makes the dial unusually visible. With k equal to one, each prediction is the label of the single closest training point, the decision boundary is jagged, and training error is zero by construction — maximal capacity. As k rises the prediction averages more neighbours, the boundary smooths, and training error climbs. With k equal to the size of the training set, every prediction is the global average — a model with essentially no capacity at all. The same family spans the entire range, and one integer moves it. Held-out error traced across k typically falls, bottoms out somewhere in the range of five to twenty for moderate datasets, then rises again.

The misconception is that capacity equals parameter count. Two models with identical parameter counts can have very different effective capacity if one is heavily constrained — shrink the coefficients of a linear model hard enough and it behaves like a much simpler model despite having the same number of them. Weight sharing, early stopping, and architectural constraints all reduce effective capacity without removing a single parameter. This is why counting parameters is a poor guide and why the empirical behaviour of the train-to-held-out gap is the better one.

The amount of data is the other half of the picture. Capacity is only ever too high or too low relative to a dataset size. A rule of thumb that survives contact with practice: as you multiply the number of examples, you can afford to move the dial up, and the appropriate setting shifts steadily toward more flexibility. This is why the same architecture that overfits on two thousand rows is the right choice on two million.

In practice you rarely reason about capacity in the abstract. You pick a family, identify its dial, sweep it across a range, and pick the setting that minimises held-out error — accepting that the winning setting is specific to your current data volume and must be revisited when that volume changes materially. What the concept buys you is knowing which knob to sweep in an unfamiliar family, and knowing that the resulting curve should be U-shaped so that a monotone one means your range was too narrow.

interview.question: Why is parameter count a poor proxy for model capacity?
interview.answer: Because constraints change how much of that parameter space is actually reachable. A linear model with heavy shrinkage on its coefficients has the same parameter count as an unconstrained one but far less effective flexibility, and early stopping has a similar effect on a network without removing anything. What matters is the variety of functions the fitting procedure can actually produce, which is better read off the train-to-held-out gap than off a count.

interview.question: You sweep a complexity parameter and held-out error decreases monotonically across your whole range. What does that tell you?
interview.answer: That your range was too narrow — you have not reached the point where added flexibility starts costing you. Extend the sweep upward until error flattens or turns, and if it never does, the model is still capacity-limited for the amount of data you have. It can also mean regularisation elsewhere in the pipeline is absorbing the extra capacity.

interview.question: When your training set grows tenfold, what should change about your model choice?
interview.answer: The appropriate capacity goes up. Settings that overfit at the smaller size may now be well matched, so hyperparameters tuned on the old volume should be re-swept rather than carried over. This is a common oversight in production systems where the data grows continuously but the tuned configuration was frozen at launch.

children.title: Regularisation as Constrained Capacity
children.text: Regularisation lets you keep an expressive model family while restricting how freely the fitting procedure can use it. Instead of choosing between a rigid family and a flexible one, you take the flexible one and add a penalty for complexity — typically on the size of the parameters — so the fit has to justify every unit of complexity it takes on with a corresponding reduction in error. Turning the penalty up smoothly moves the model from flexible to rigid, giving you a continuous dial rather than a discrete choice between model families.

must_not_cover: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial

children.deep_text:
The mechanism is a modified objective: instead of minimising loss alone, you minimise loss plus a penalty term multiplied by a strength parameter. Penalising the sum of squared coefficients shrinks all of them toward zero proportionally, keeping every feature but reducing how much any one can swing the prediction. Penalising the sum of absolute coefficients pushes some of them to exactly zero, which performs feature selection as a side effect of fitting. The strength parameter is the dial: at zero you recover the unconstrained fit, and as it grows all coefficients head toward zero and the model approaches a constant.

Concretely, take a linear model on forty features with only three hundred rows. Unregularised, the fit produces coefficients ranging from minus eight hundred to plus nine hundred — large opposing weights on correlated features that cancel on the training data and produce wild predictions just off it. Add a squared-magnitude penalty and the same fit yields coefficients between minus four and plus six, training error rises modestly, and held-out error drops substantially. Nothing was removed from the model; the fitting procedure was simply forbidden from paying a high price in coefficient magnitude for a small gain in fit.

The misconception is that regularisation is a formula added to the loss and nothing more. It is better understood as any mechanism that restricts effective capacity, and most of these are not penalties at all. Stopping training before convergence limits how far the parameters can travel from their initialisation. Averaging several models fitted on resampled data restricts how much any one fit's idiosyncrasies survive. Adding noise to inputs, or dropping features at random during fitting, prevents the model from relying too heavily on any single signal. These are all regularisation in the meaningful sense, and treating the concept narrowly leads people to look for a penalty term when the effective constraint is elsewhere in the pipeline.

The second point people get wrong is the scale sensitivity of magnitude penalties. A penalty on coefficient size is only meaningful if the features are on comparable scales, because a feature measured in thousands will naturally carry a small coefficient and be penalised almost not at all, while the same quantity measured in units carries a large one and is crushed. Standardise before applying a magnitude penalty, always.

The decision rule: reach for regularisation when held-out error is materially worse than training error and you want to keep the current family. Choose the squared-magnitude form when you believe many features contribute a little and correlated features should share the weight; choose the absolute-value form when you believe most features are irrelevant and want a sparse model you can read. Set the strength by sweeping it against held-out error rather than by intuition, since the useful range spans orders of magnitude and varies with dataset size.

interview.question: Why must you standardise features before applying a magnitude-based penalty?
interview.answer: Because the penalty acts on coefficient size, and coefficient size depends on the units of the corresponding feature. A feature measured in thousands gets a naturally small coefficient and is barely penalised, while the same information in single units gets a large one and is shrunk hard. Without standardisation the effective strength of the penalty varies arbitrarily across features.

interview.question: How do you choose the regularisation strength in practice?
interview.answer: Sweep it across a logarithmic grid and pick the value minimising cross-validated error, since the useful range typically spans several orders of magnitude. Guessing a value rarely works because the right setting depends on dataset size and feature scaling. Where predictions must be stable, some practitioners deliberately pick a slightly stronger setting than the minimum, trading a little accuracy for a less variable fit.

interview.question: Is early stopping a form of regularisation, and why does that framing matter?
interview.answer: Yes — halting before convergence limits how far parameters travel from their starting point, which restricts effective capacity just as a penalty does. The framing matters because it stops you double-counting constraints: if you already stop early and then add a strong penalty, you may push the model into underfitting while looking for the source of the problem in the wrong place.

children.title: The Curse of Dimensionality
children.text: As the number of features grows, the volume of the input space grows exponentially, and any fixed number of examples becomes vanishingly sparse within it. Ten points cover a line reasonably; ten points in a hundred-dimensional space cover nothing at all. Distances between points also concentrate — in high dimensions the nearest and farthest neighbours of a query become nearly equidistant — which quietly breaks any method that relies on proximity meaning similarity. More features are not free. Each one buys some information and costs you sparsity, and past a point the cost dominates.

must_not_cover: Model Capacity and the Complexity Dial

children.deep_text:
Put numbers on the sparsity. To cover the unit interval so that no point is further than 0.1 from a sample, you need about ten points. In two dimensions the same coverage needs a hundred, in three a thousand, and in ten dimensions ten billion. This is not a subtle effect at the margins; it is exponential, and it means that in any space of even moderate dimension your data occupies an effectively empty region and every prediction is an extrapolation into territory where you have no neighbours.

The distance concentration effect is stranger and more damaging. Draw points uniformly at random in a high-dimensional cube and measure the distance from a query point to its nearest and farthest neighbour. In two dimensions the farthest is many times the nearest. By a few hundred dimensions the ratio approaches one — everything is roughly the same distance away. Any method whose logic is that close points share labels loses its footing, because nothing is meaningfully close. Nearest-neighbour methods and clustering that relies on Euclidean distance degrade for exactly this reason, and they do so silently, returning confident answers built on distances that carry no information.

The misconception is that high dimension is automatically fatal, which would make image and text modelling impossible. The resolution is that real data almost never fills its ambient space. A hundred-by-hundred grayscale image lives nominally in ten thousand dimensions, but the images that are actually photographs occupy a far lower-dimensional surface within it, because pixels are heavily correlated with their neighbours. What governs difficulty is this intrinsic dimension, not the column count. This is why methods that discover and exploit low-dimensional structure work well on data that looks hopelessly high-dimensional by the raw count.

The second misconception is that adding a weakly informative feature is harmless because the model can learn to ignore it. It is not free: each added dimension dilutes the sample, adds a parameter to estimate, and gives the fit one more direction in which to find a spurious pattern. With three hundred rows, going from twenty features to two hundred typically makes held-out performance worse even when the added features each carry a little genuine signal.

The operating rules that follow. Watch the ratio of examples to features and be suspicious when it falls below roughly ten to one for flexible models. Be sceptical of distance-based methods on raw high-dimensional inputs; either reduce dimension first or use a method that learns which directions matter. Prefer families that handle irrelevant features gracefully — those with built-in feature selection or strong shrinkage — when the feature count is large. And when adding features, verify the addition on held-out data rather than assuming that more information cannot hurt, because in this regime it very often does.

interview.question: Why do nearest-neighbour methods degrade in high dimensions specifically?
interview.answer: Because their entire premise is that the closest points are the most similar, and in high dimensions distances concentrate so that nearest and farthest neighbours become nearly equidistant. The ranking of neighbours then reflects noise more than similarity. The failure is quiet, since the method still returns neighbours and confident predictions built on distances that no longer carry information.

interview.question: If high dimensionality is so damaging, why do image models work at all?
interview.answer: Because natural images do not fill their nominal space — neighbouring pixels are heavily correlated, so real photographs occupy a much lower-dimensional structure inside the ambient one. Difficulty tracks that intrinsic dimension rather than the raw count of inputs. Architectures that assume spatial locality exploit exactly this, which is why they beat generic methods on the same pixels.

interview.question: A colleague wants to add two hundred weakly predictive features to a model trained on a few thousand rows. What's your response?
interview.answer: Ask for a held-out comparison before and after, because with that ratio the added dilution and estimation burden often outweighs the marginal signal. If the features are genuinely wanted, pair them with strong shrinkage or a sparsity-inducing penalty so the fit is forced to justify each one. The general point is that more information helps in principle and can easily hurt at finite sample sizes.

children.deep_text:
The order here is a build, and reading out of it makes the later parts look arbitrary.

It starts with the two observable failure modes: a model too constrained to capture the pattern, and one flexible enough to reproduce the sample's noise. These are the symptoms you actually diagnose from a pair of error numbers, so they come first, before any theory that explains them.

The decomposition of error comes second because it explains those symptoms rather than merely naming them. It splits expected prediction error into a part attributable to the model family being systematically wrong, a part attributable to sensitivity to which particular sample you drew, and a part that is irreducible. That split turns the two failure modes from opposites into two ends of a single quantitative trade.

Capacity comes third. Having established that there is a trade, you need the dial that controls it — what makes one model family more flexible than another, how flexibility relates to the amount of data you have, and why the same family can sit at either end depending on how it is configured.

Regularisation comes fourth, as the practical machinery. Once capacity is understood as a dial, the natural question is how to turn it down without abandoning an expressive family, and that is what constraining the fit achieves.

The curse of dimensionality comes last because it is the setting in which all four of the preceding ideas get worse simultaneously. It explains why methods that behave well with five features can fail with five hundred, and it makes the case for the dimension-reduction and feature-selection work that appears later in the pathway.

children.title: Data as the Substrate
children.text: Every claim about how a model will perform rests on assumptions about the data underneath it, and those assumptions break more often than any modelling choice goes wrong. This part covers four of them: how to partition your data so that a performance estimate means something, the specific ways information about the answer contaminates your inputs, the statistical assumption that training and deployment data come from the same source independently, and what happens when one outcome is far rarer than another. Each has a recognisable failure signature, and each is cheap to prevent and expensive to discover late.

children.title: Train, Validation, and Test Splits
children.text: You need three separate portions of data because you are answering three different questions. The training set fits the parameters. The validation set chooses between candidates — which model, which hyperparameters, when to stop. The test set is touched exactly once, at the end, to estimate how the chosen system will perform. Merging validation and test destroys the estimate, because any set used to make choices has already been partly fitted to. The number that goes in a report has to come from data that influenced no decision whatsoever.
children.deep_text:
A worked setup: sixty thousand labelled records split into 70% training, 15% validation, and 15% test — forty-two thousand, nine thousand, and nine thousand. You fit thirty candidate configurations on the training portion, score each on validation, and the best gets 91.2%. You then score that single configuration once on test and get 90.4%. The eight-tenths of a point difference is not a mistake; it is the selection bias in the validation number showing up, which is exactly what the test set was reserved to expose. Report 90.4%.

Three rules govern the split. First, split before you compute anything from the data. Fitting a scaler, imputing missing values with a column mean, or selecting features by correlation with the target must all happen on the training portion alone and then be applied to the others, because computing them on everything lets test information into the fitting. Second, split along the natural grouping, not along rows: if one patient contributed twelve records, all twelve go to the same side, or the model recognises the patient rather than the condition. Third, when the data is ordered in time, split by time — train on the earlier period, validate and test on later ones — because a random split lets the model see the future, and the future is precisely what it will not have in production.

When data is scarce, cross-validation replaces a fixed validation set: rotate which fold is held out, fit k times, and average the scores. This gives a lower-variance estimate and uses every row for fitting at some point, at k times the compute. It replaces the validation set and not the test set — a final untouched portion is still required, because the cross-validated score is what you selected on.

The misconception is that a fresh random split each run is harmless or even good practice. It leaks steadily. Across many experiments, examples rotate through the held-out portion, and choices accumulated over dozens of runs are informed by all of the data. Fix the split with a stored seed or, better, materialise the partitions and version them, so that six months of experiments are comparable and the test set stays genuinely untouched.

The practical rule on sizes: with hundreds of thousands of rows, 80/10/10 is ample and the held-out portions are large enough for tight estimates. With a few thousand, a fixed validation set is too noisy to select on and cross-validation is the right choice. And whatever the split, check that the held-out portions are large enough that the difference you are trying to detect exceeds their sampling error, or the whole apparatus is measuring noise carefully.

interview.question: Why isn't a validation set enough — what does the test set add?
interview.answer: The validation set stops being an unbiased estimate the moment you select on it, because the winning configuration is partly winning on that set's noise. The test set answers a different question: how does this one already-chosen system perform on data that influenced nothing. That is why it can be used once, and why looking at it and then changing the model quietly converts it into another validation set.

interview.question: When would a random split be the wrong choice?
interview.answer: Whenever rows are not exchangeable. Time-ordered data needs a chronological split, since a random one lets the model learn from periods that come after what it is asked to predict. Grouped data — multiple records per user, patient, or device — needs the group kept intact on one side, otherwise the model matches the entity rather than the pattern and held-out scores are inflated.

interview.question: You have four thousand labelled examples. How do you structure evaluation?
interview.answer: Hold out a test set of maybe eight hundred and run k-fold cross-validation on the remaining thirty-two hundred for all selection. A single fixed validation set of a few hundred is too noisy to distinguish candidates reliably, whereas cross-validation averages across folds and uses every row. Keep the test portion sealed until the configuration is final.

children.title: Data Leakage
children.text: Leakage is when information that will not be available at prediction time gets into training, making offline results look far better than anything achievable in production. It comes in two broad forms: a feature that encodes the answer, and a split that lets training and evaluation data share information. The signature is a model that performs implausibly well and then collapses on deployment. It is the most common serious defect in applied machine learning, it is almost never caught by looking at model code, and finding it means auditing where every column came from.
children.deep_text:
The most instructive example is mundane. A team builds a model predicting whether a hospital patient will be readmitted within thirty days. It reaches an area under the curve of 0.97, far above anything in the literature. The culprit turns out to be a feature called discharge_disposition, which for readmitted patients frequently records a value only assigned after the readmission occurred. The column existed in the training table because the warehouse was built for reporting, where it is perfectly valid. At prediction time — at discharge — that value is not yet known. Removing it drops performance to 0.71, which was the real number all along.

The forms it takes are worth listing because they are recognisable. Target leakage is a feature computed from, or updated after, the outcome: a payment_received flag when predicting default, a total_refund_amount when predicting returns. Temporal leakage is training on data from after the prediction point, which happens automatically when time-ordered data is split randomly. Group leakage is the same underlying entity appearing on both sides of a split — the same patient, the same product photographed twice, the same document with a duplicate in the corpus. Preprocessing leakage is subtler: fitting a scaler, an imputation value, or a feature selector on the full dataset before splitting means the training procedure has seen statistics of the evaluation data. That last one usually inflates results by a small amount rather than a large one, which is what makes it survive review.

The misconception is that leakage is a data-cleaning problem that a careful pipeline solves once. It recurs, because the pressure that creates it is structural: warehouses store current state rather than point-in-time state, and joining a feature table to a label table by entity id without a timestamp constraint is the natural thing to write. The durable defence is point-in-time correctness — every feature value must be the value that was knowable at the prediction timestamp — enforced in the join, not checked afterwards by inspection.

The practical detection rule: treat suspiciously good results as a bug report. When a model substantially beats what the domain considers achievable, look for leakage before celebrating. Rank features by importance and interrogate the top few by asking, of each, what its value would have been at the moment of prediction; leaking features almost always dominate importance rankings. Compare offline performance against a small live shadow run, since a large gap is the clearest possible signal. And when a result seems too good, the prior should be that it is, because a genuine large jump in a well-studied problem is far rarer than a mistake in a join.

interview.question: Walk me through how you'd investigate a model that scores far higher than expected.
interview.answer: Assume leakage and work backwards from feature importance, since a leaking feature almost always sits at the top. For each of the leading features, ask what value it held at the exact prediction timestamp and whether anything downstream of the outcome could have updated it. Then check the split for temporal ordering and for the same entity appearing on both sides, and confirm that all preprocessing was fitted on training data alone.

interview.question: Why does fitting a scaler on the full dataset before splitting count as leakage?
interview.answer: Because the scaler's parameters encode statistics of the evaluation data, so the training procedure has indirectly seen it. The effect is usually small — inflating results by a fraction of a point rather than transforming them — but it is real and it compounds with feature selection done the same way. The fix is to fit every transformation inside the training fold and apply it to the others.

interview.question: What does point-in-time correctness mean and how do you enforce it?
interview.answer: It means every feature value used for an example is the value that was actually knowable at that example's prediction timestamp, not the value in the warehouse today. You enforce it in the join by constraining feature records to those with an event time at or before the prediction time, rather than joining on entity id alone. Feature stores exist largely to make this the default, because doing it by hand in ad hoc SQL is where most leakage originates.

children.title: Independent and Identically Distributed Assumptions
children.text: Nearly every guarantee in machine learning assumes your examples were drawn independently from a single fixed distribution, and that future data comes from that same distribution. Independent means one example tells you nothing about another. Identically distributed means the source has not changed. Real data violates both routinely — measurements from the same user are correlated, behaviour drifts month to month, and the population you deployed into differs from the one you sampled. When these assumptions fail, held-out estimates stop predicting deployment performance, usually optimistically.
children.deep_text:
Independence fails whenever examples share a source. Twenty accelerometer readings from one wearer over a minute are near-copies of each other, so a dataset of a hundred thousand such readings from fifty people carries roughly fifty people's worth of information, not a hundred thousand readings' worth. Split those readings randomly and the model learns to identify wearers; it reports 96% and delivers 74% on a new person. The same structure appears with multiple sessions per user, multiple photographs of one object, and sentences from a single document. The fix is always the same: the unit of independence is the person, object, or document, and the split must respect it.

Identical distribution fails over time and across populations. Covariate shift is when the inputs change while the relationship between inputs and outcome holds — a lending model trained on applicants aged thirty to forty now sees applicants aged fifty, and the mapping from income to risk is unchanged but the input range is unfamiliar. Concept drift is when the relationship itself changes — a spam filter degrades because spammers adapt to it, so the same email features now imply a different label. These call for different responses: covariate shift can sometimes be handled by reweighting training examples toward the new input distribution, while concept drift requires new labels, because the thing being learned has genuinely changed.

The misconception is that violations are edge cases handled by a robustness flag. They are the normal condition of deployed systems. Any model serving users in a market that grows, a product that adds features, or a domain with adversaries is operating under shift permanently. The realistic goal is not to satisfy the assumption but to know how far you are from it and to detect when the distance grows — which is why input distribution monitoring is standard practice, and why it catches problems earlier than accuracy monitoring, since labels usually arrive late or never.

A second misconception concerns time series specifically: people apply cross-validation with random folds to sequential data and get an encouraging number. Random folds train on the future to predict the past. The correct structure is a rolling or expanding window where every evaluation period follows its training period, which typically yields a considerably worse and considerably more honest estimate.

The practical checklist: identify the unit of independence and split along it; if the data has a time dimension, split by time regardless of whether the task looks temporal; check whether the deployment population matches the training population on the obvious axes such as geography, device, and tenure; and instrument the input distribution in production so that shift is observed rather than inferred from a drop in a business metric months later.

interview.question: How do you tell covariate shift from concept drift, and why does the distinction matter operationally?
