interview.answer: Covariate shift changes the distribution of inputs while the input-to-outcome relationship holds; concept drift changes that relationship. It matters because the fixes differ: covariate shift can sometimes be addressed by reweighting or retraining on existing labels, whereas concept drift requires fresh labels since the mapping you learned is now wrong. Practically, you detect the first by monitoring input distributions and the second by monitoring accuracy on recently labelled data.

interview.question: Your model gets 96% in cross-validation and 74% in production. What are the first two things you check?
interview.answer: Whether the split respected the unit of independence — if several rows come from the same user, device, or document, a random split lets the model identify the entity and inflates the estimate. Second, whether the data has a time dimension that a random split ignored, which lets it train on periods after those it is evaluated on. Both produce exactly this pattern of a large, clean gap.

interview.question: Why monitor input distributions in production when you could monitor accuracy?
interview.answer: Because labels usually arrive late or not at all, so accuracy monitoring lags the problem by however long ground truth takes to materialise — often weeks. Input distributions are observable immediately and shift in them is a leading indicator. It is a weaker signal, since not every input change hurts performance, but it is available when the stronger signal is not.

children.title: Class Imbalance
children.text: When one outcome is far rarer than the other — 0.2% of transactions fraudulent, 3% of users churning — accuracy stops carrying information. A model that predicts the majority class for everything scores 99.8% and catches nothing. The problem is partly the metric and partly the training signal: the rare class contributes so few examples that the fit has little reason to model it well. Fixing it means changing what you measure, changing what the loss rewards, or changing the composition of the training data, and those are three separate decisions.
children.deep_text:
Start with the metric, because it is where most confusion lives. On a million transactions with two thousand fraudulent, a model predicting never-fraud is 99.8% accurate. Precision and recall on the rare class expose it immediately: recall is zero, so it catches none of the fraud. A useful model on this data might catch 60% of fraud at a precision of 30% — meaning of every ten alerts, three are genuine, and forty percent of fraud slips through. Those are ordinary numbers for a rare-event problem and they look terrible next to 99.8%, which is exactly why accuracy has to be abandoned first.

On the training side there are three levers. Weighting the loss so that errors on the rare class cost more makes the fit take them seriously without altering the data, and it is usually the first thing to try because it changes one parameter and leaves the pipeline intact. Resampling — discarding majority examples or duplicating and synthesising minority ones — changes the training distribution directly and can help when the imbalance is extreme, at the cost of throwing away data or manufacturing it. Threshold adjustment leaves the model untouched and moves the decision cut-off on its output scores, which is often the most effective and most reversible option because the ranking a model produces may already be good even when its default 0.5 cut-off is useless.

The misconception that causes real damage is that resampling must be applied to the whole dataset before splitting. Oversampling before the split places duplicates or synthetic points derived from the same original rows on both sides of it, so the model sees near-copies of evaluation examples during training and the reported recall is fiction. Resampling belongs strictly inside the training fold, and the validation and test portions must keep the true class proportions, because those proportions are what production looks like.

The second misconception is that imbalance itself is the problem. It often is not. If the classes are well separated, a model handles a 1000-to-1 ratio without complaint. The real difficulty is absolute scarcity — two hundred positive examples is little to learn from regardless of how many negatives accompany them — combined with overlap between the classes. Before reaching for resampling, check whether you have enough positives at all, since if you have fifty, no reweighting scheme rescues you and the honest answer is that you need more labelled positives or a rules-based first pass.

The decision rule: change the metric first and always, to precision and recall at an operating point chosen from real costs. Then try loss weighting. Reach for resampling only when weighting is insufficient, and keep it inside the training fold. Tune the threshold last, against the cost structure rather than against a symmetric score, and re-tune it whenever the base rate moves.

interview.question: Why is oversampling before the train-test split a serious error rather than a minor one?
interview.answer: Because duplicated or synthesised minority points derived from the same original rows end up on both sides of the split, so the model trains on near-copies of what it is evaluated on. Reported recall on the rare class becomes largely fictional, and the effect is severe precisely where you care most. Resampling must happen inside the training fold, with held-out data left at the true class proportions.

interview.question: Is class imbalance always a problem?
interview.answer: No — if the classes are well separated, a highly skewed ratio is handled without difficulty. The real problems are absolute scarcity of the rare class and overlap between the classes, and imbalance only makes those worse. Before applying any rebalancing technique, check the raw count of positives, because with a few dozen no reweighting scheme will save the model.

interview.question: How would you choose the decision threshold for a fraud model?
interview.answer: From the cost structure rather than from a symmetric score. Estimate the cost of a missed fraud and the cost of a false alert, including the reviewer time an alert consumes, and pick the threshold minimising expected total cost. In practice the constraint is often review capacity, so you set the threshold to produce the number of alerts the team can actually process and report the recall you achieve at that operating point.

children.deep_text:
The four parts here are ordered by dependency, and each one is a way the guarantees established earlier can silently fail.

Splitting comes first because it is the mechanism that makes any held-out estimate possible at all. Until you have partitioned the data into a portion for fitting, a portion for choosing among candidates, and a portion touched only once, you have no honest number to reason with. Everything else in this part assumes that machinery exists.

Leakage comes second because it is what breaks that machinery from the inside. A split can be structurally correct and still worthless if information about the answer has found its way into the features, or if related rows straddle the boundary. It is placed directly after splitting because the two are studied together — most leakage is discovered by interrogating exactly how the split was made and what was computed before it.

The distributional assumption comes third. Splitting and leakage are about the data you hold; this is about the relationship between that data and the data you will face. It names the assumption every estimate depends on — that examples are drawn independently from a single stable distribution — and describes the common ways real data violates it, which motivates the drift monitoring that appears later in the production section.

Imbalance comes last because it is where all three of the preceding concerns compound. When one class is rare, splits need to preserve its proportion, resampling fixes interact with leakage in ways that are easy to get wrong, and the headline metrics stop being informative. It is best read once the other three are in place.

This section splits along the causal chain of a learning system, and the order matters. First comes what learning from data means: the shift from writing rules to fitting a function, the shapes that shift can take, the vocabulary of features and labels, and the space of candidate functions a learner is allowed to search. Without that vocabulary the rest is unreadable.

Second comes the objective. Once you have a space of candidate functions, you need a way to rank them, which means committing to a numerical definition of wrong and being precise about what quantity you wish you could minimise versus the quantity you can actually compute. This is where most people's mental model is first tested, because the two are not the same quantity and the gap between them is the whole subject.

Third comes generalisation, which is that gap studied directly. It covers what goes wrong at both ends of model complexity, the standard decomposition of error into components you can trade off, the dial that controls complexity, the machinery for constraining it, and the way high-dimensional spaces make all of this harder.

Fourth comes data as the substrate. Everything above assumes the data you train on and the data you will be scored on come from the same place and were kept separate in the right ways. That assumption fails constantly and in specific, recognisable patterns, so it gets its own treatment last, once you understand what is at stake when it breaks.

Read in order. Each part supplies the vocabulary the next one uses without redefining.

children.title: Supervised Learning Algorithms
children.text: Supervised learning means you have labelled examples and you want a function that maps inputs to those labels. The interesting question is not whether that is possible but what shape the function should take, because every algorithm family makes a different structural bet. Linear models bet the relationship is a weighted sum. Tree-based models bet it is a series of threshold splits. Distance and margin based models bet that similar points share labels, or that a good boundary is a wide one. Neural networks bet that stacked simple transforms can learn the shape themselves. Picking a family is picking which bet fits your data.

children.title: Linear Models
children.text: A linear model predicts by multiplying each input feature by a learned weight and adding the results together. That is the entire hypothesis space, and its narrowness is the point: with few parameters you get fast training, stable behaviour on small datasets, and coefficients you can actually read. The family splits three ways. Plain linear regression fits continuous outputs by minimising squared error. Regularised variants add a penalty term that keeps weights small when features are many or correlated. Logistic regression bends the same weighted sum through a squashing function so the output becomes a probability for classification.

children.title: Linear Regression
children.text: Linear regression predicts a continuous number as a weighted sum of the input features. Fit it to house data and you get something like price equals eighty thousand plus two hundred times square footage plus fifteen thousand per bedroom — each coefficient is a readable statement about how the target moves when one feature moves. Three things are worth understanding separately. First, what exactly is being minimised when you fit it, and why squared error rather than something else. Second, whether to solve for the coefficients directly with linear algebra or approach them step by step. Third, what has to be true about your data for the answer to mean anything.

children.title: The Least Squares Objective
children.text: Fitting a line means picking the coefficients that make the errors smallest, and least squares defines smallest as the sum of squared residuals. For each training row you compute the prediction, subtract the actual value, square that gap, and add it up across all rows. Squaring does two things: it makes overshoots and undershoots count equally, and it punishes a single large miss far more than several small ones. That second property is a deliberate choice, not a mathematical accident. It also makes the objective a smooth bowl-shaped function of the coefficients, with exactly one lowest point and no local traps.
children.deep_text:
Suppose you have four houses with sizes 1000, 1500, 2000 and 2500 square feet selling for 200k, 260k, 340k and 380k. A candidate model predicting 100k plus 110 per square foot gives predictions of 210, 265, 320 and 375. The residuals are minus 10, minus 5, plus 20 and plus 5 thousand. Square them: 100, 25, 400, 25, summing to 550 in units of squared thousands. Any other pair of coefficients gives a different total, and least squares says the best pair is whichever makes that total as small as it can be. Notice how the third house dominates the sum. Its residual is four times the second house's but contributes sixteen times as much, and so it pulls the fitted line toward itself far harder than the others do.

That asymmetry is the most consequential property of the objective and the source of the most common misconception about it. People assume squaring is chosen because errors must be made positive and squaring is the natural way to do that. Taking absolute values would also do that, and it would weight all errors proportionally instead. The real reasons to square are that the resulting function is differentiable everywhere, which absolute error is not at zero, and that the objective becomes convex and quadratic, which is what makes the solution analytically tractable and reliably findable. There is also a probabilistic reading: minimising squared error is exactly maximum likelihood estimation when you assume the noise around the true line is Gaussian with constant spread.

The practical consequence is a decision rule. Use squared error when large errors genuinely are disproportionately bad — a delivery time estimate off by two hours hurts more than four times as much as one off by thirty minutes — and when your data has been cleaned of recording errors. Move to absolute error or a Huber loss, which is squared near zero and linear in the tails, when your target contains outliers you cannot remove, such as fraud amounts or sensor spikes. Fitting squared error on data with a handful of mistyped values will visibly drag the line toward them, and no amount of tuning elsewhere in your pipeline will undo that.

interview.question: Why squared error rather than absolute error when fitting a regression?
interview.answer: Squaring makes the objective differentiable everywhere and convex, which is what allows an exact analytical solution and makes iterative optimisation well behaved. Absolute error has a kink at zero that complicates both. It is also the maximum likelihood choice if you believe the noise is Gaussian with constant variance.

interview.question: A stakeholder says one bad prediction in your regression is unacceptable but many small ones are fine. How does that change your loss?
interview.answer: That preference is already what squared error encodes, since a residual twice as large contributes four times as much, so it is the right default there. The opposite preference — tolerate a few big misses, minimise typical error — argues for absolute error instead. If they want both, a Huber loss is squared near zero and linear in the tails.

interview.question: Your regression fit shifted noticeably after adding one new training row. What would you check?
interview.answer: Look at that row's residual under the old model. A single point with a very large residual dominates a squared error sum and can move the fit substantially, especially if it also sits far from the mean on the feature axes. Check whether it is a genuine observation or a data entry problem before deciding whether the shift is signal.

children.title: Closed Form vs. Iterative Solutions
children.text: Because the squared error objective is a smooth bowl, you can find its minimum two ways. The closed form solves an equation in one shot using matrix algebra — the normal equations — and hands you the exact coefficients with no tuning and no stopping decision. The iterative route starts from a guess and repeatedly nudges the coefficients downhill until the improvement stops mattering. Both land on the same answer for well-behaved data. The choice is about cost and conditioning: the direct solve involves inverting a matrix that grows with your feature count, and it breaks down entirely when features are exact duplicates of each other.
children.deep_text:
Concretely: with 50 features and 10,000 rows, the closed form builds a 50 by 50 matrix from your data, inverts it, and multiplies through. That is a fraction of a second and it is over. Go to 50,000 features — one-hot encoded product IDs, say — and you are asking for a 50,000 by 50,000 inversion, which is roughly a hundred trillion operations and tens of gigabytes just to hold the matrix. The iterative approach never forms that matrix at all. It computes predictions, measures the gradient of the error, takes a step, and repeats, touching only vectors the size of your feature count. That is why every large-scale system uses the iterative route regardless of the fact that an exact formula exists.

The common misconception is that iterative methods are approximate and the closed form is exact, so the closed form is better whenever you can afford it. The word exact is doing misleading work. The closed form is exact arithmetic on a matrix that may be numerically terrible. If two of your features are perfectly correlated — square feet and square metres of the same property — the matrix is singular and has no inverse; if they are nearly correlated it is invertible in principle but the computed inverse amplifies floating point noise into wild coefficients. Iterative methods degrade gracefully in the same situation, drifting slowly rather than exploding. In practice serious libraries do not use the naive normal equations even when they solve directly; they use a QR or SVD decomposition, which is numerically stabler and never forms the inverse explicitly.

The decision rule is straightforward. Feature count in the low thousands, data fits in memory, and you want a reproducible answer with no hyperparameters: solve directly, using a library routine rather than writing the inversion yourself. Feature count large, data streaming or too big for memory, or you plan to add a penalty term or swap in a different loss later: go iterative, since that machinery generalises and the closed form does not. If you are solving directly and the coefficients look implausible — enormous values with opposite signs on related features — suspect near-collinearity in the design matrix before you suspect the data.

interview.question: When would you avoid the normal equations even though the dataset is small enough to solve directly?
interview.answer: When the features are collinear or nearly so, since the matrix to invert is singular or ill-conditioned and the coefficients become numerically unreliable. Also when you intend to change the objective later, because the direct solve is specific to plain squared error while an iterative optimiser carries over unchanged. A decomposition-based solver handles the first case better than a literal inversion.

interview.question: Both methods minimise the same objective. Why does the industry default to the iterative one?
interview.answer: Cost and scale. The direct solve involves work that grows cubically in the number of features and requires holding the whole design matrix, which fails on high-dimensional or streaming data. Iterative updates touch only vectors and can process data in batches, so the same code runs on a laptop dataset and a cluster-scale one.

interview.question: How would you decide an iterative solver has actually converged?
interview.answer: Watch the change in the objective or in the coefficient vector between iterations and stop when it falls below a tolerance relative to the scale of the values. Watching held-out error rather than training error is safer, since it also tells you if you are past the useful point. A loss that is oscillating or increasing usually means the step size is too large, not that convergence is slow.

children.title: Assumptions of Linear Regression
children.text: Linear regression will return coefficients for absolutely any dataset, but whether those coefficients mean what you think depends on conditions the fitting procedure never checks. The relationship should actually be linear in the parameters. The residuals should have roughly constant spread across the range of predictions, not fan out as values grow. Observations should be independent of each other, which time series and repeated measures per user routinely violate. And the features should not be near-duplicates of one another. Violations do not always ruin prediction, but they quietly destroy the standard errors, confidence intervals and p-values that people read off the output.
children.deep_text:
Take a model predicting household spending from income across a hundred thousand rows. Fit it and the residuals fan out: at 30k income the errors cluster within a few hundred dollars, at 300k they spread across tens of thousands. That is heteroscedasticity, and it does not bias the coefficients — the estimate of the income slope is still centred on the right answer. What it does is invalidate the reported uncertainty, because the standard error calculation assumes one constant noise level. Your library prints a tight confidence interval on the slope and a tiny p-value, and both are fiction. If you then tell a product team that the effect is significant, you are handing them a number you have no support for. Log-transforming the target often flattens the fan and restores the assumption.

The most persistent misconception is that linear regression requires the features to be normally distributed. It does not, and there is no assumption about the distribution of the inputs at all. The distributional assumption is on the residuals, and even that only matters for inference on small samples, since with enough rows the central limit theorem carries the coefficient estimates toward normality regardless. Spending effort transforming a skewed feature to look Gaussian is usually wasted; spending it on whether the residual plot shows structure is not. The second persistent misconception is that linear in the parameters means linear in the features. Adding a squared term or a log of a feature keeps the model perfectly linear in the coefficients and is a standard way to capture curvature.

The practical rule is to match the assumption you check against the claim you want to make. If you only need predictions and you validate on held-out data, most violations are survivable and the held-out score is your real answer. If you want to say this feature causes that much change and quote an interval around it, then independence and constant variance are load-bearing and you must check them. Independence is the one people miss most often: repeated rows from the same user, or consecutive days from the same sensor, make your effective sample size far smaller than your row count, so every interval you compute is too narrow.

interview.question: Which regression assumption do you check first on a new dataset, and why that one?
interview.answer: Independence of observations, because it is the one most often violated silently and the one that most distorts your sense of how much evidence you have. Repeated measures from the same entity or a time ordering both mean the effective sample size is far below the row count. A residual plot will not reveal it; you have to know how the data was collected.

interview.question: Your residuals fan out with the fitted value. Do the coefficients still mean anything?
interview.answer: The coefficient estimates remain unbiased, so the predictions and the direction of the effects are still usable. What breaks is the reported uncertainty, since the standard errors assume a single constant noise level, so confidence intervals and p-values are not trustworthy. A log transform of the target or robust standard errors are the usual fixes.

interview.question: When would you not bother checking these assumptions at all?
interview.answer: When the model is purely predictive and you are judging it by held-out error rather than by coefficient interpretation. The assumptions underpin inference — intervals, significance, causal reading — not raw predictive validity. As soon as someone starts quoting a coefficient as an effect size in a meeting, the assumptions become load-bearing again.

children.deep_text:
Linear regression is the oldest and most transparent supervised algorithm, and it earns a careful treatment because so much of machine learning is a variation on it. The model itself takes about one line to state. The substance is in the three questions this unit splits into, and they are genuinely independent of each other, which is why they are separate.

The first question is about the objective. Fitting means choosing coefficients, and choosing requires a definition of what makes one set of coefficients better than another. That definition is a choice with consequences, not an obvious given, and it determines everything downstream including how the model behaves when your data contains extreme values.

The second question is about computation. Once the objective is fixed, there is a mathematically exact answer available and there are procedures that walk toward the answer instead. Both give the same coefficients in the well-behaved case. They differ sharply in cost as your dataset grows, and in what happens when the data is degenerate, so the choice is an engineering one that shows up in real systems.

The third question is about validity. The fitting procedure will happily return coefficients for any dataset you hand it. Whether those coefficients support the interpretation you want to place on them, and whether the standard errors and intervals your library prints mean anything, depends on conditions the algorithm never checks for you.

Take them in that order: what you are optimising, how you compute it, and when the result deserves your trust.

children.title: Regularised Linear Regression
children.text: Fit a linear model with more features than you have rows and it will nail the training set perfectly while producing coefficients that are enormous, unstable, and useless on new data. Regularisation fixes this by changing what you optimise: instead of minimising error alone, you minimise error plus a penalty that grows with the size of the coefficients. The model is now paying for complexity, so it only keeps weight on a feature if the error reduction is worth the charge. The three variants here differ in the mathematical shape of that penalty, and that shape decides whether coefficients get shrunk toward zero, driven exactly to zero, or both.

children.title: Ridge Regression and L2 Penalty
children.text: Ridge adds the sum of squared coefficients to the loss, so large weights are expensive and the fit is pulled toward smaller, more evenly distributed values. Because the penalty is smooth and quadratic, no coefficient ever reaches exactly zero — they all shrink toward it and stay. That turns out to be the right behaviour when your features are correlated. Where an unpenalised fit might assign a huge positive weight to one of two near-identical columns and a huge negative weight to the other, ridge splits the influence between them. It also has a closed form solution and stabilises the matrix inversion that plain regression struggles with.
children.deep_text:
Take a genomics-style problem: 5,000 expression features, 200 patients, target is a continuous biomarker level. Unpenalised least squares has more unknowns than equations, so it finds coefficients that reproduce all 200 training values exactly and generalise disastrously. Add a ridge penalty with a moderate strength and the picture changes: no single coefficient reaches an extreme value, the training fit is visibly imperfect, and held-out error drops sharply. Sweep the strength parameter across a log-spaced grid with cross-validation and you see the characteristic curve — held-out error high at zero penalty, falling to a minimum, then rising again as the penalty crushes all signal out of the model. You pick the bottom of that curve.

The mechanical reason it stabilises things is worth knowing. Ridge adds a constant to the diagonal of the matrix that plain regression has to invert. A matrix that was singular or nearly so — which is exactly what near-duplicate features produce — becomes safely invertible once you nudge its diagonal upward. That is the origin of the name, and it means ridge is not only a statistical device but a numerical one.

The misconception to clear is about feature selection. People assume shrinking coefficients toward zero is a soft form of dropping features, so a small ridge coefficient means an unimportant feature you could remove. Neither half holds. Ridge keeps every feature in the model with nonzero weight no matter how strong the penalty, so it never produces a sparse model, and a coefficient can be small simply because its feature shares information with several others that collectively carry the signal. Reading a ridge coefficient vector as an importance ranking is a common and misleading habit, especially with correlated columns where the shrinkage deliberately spreads weight around.

Reach for ridge when you believe most of your features carry some signal, when they are correlated, or when the feature count is large relative to the sample count and you want stability rather than a shorter model. Avoid it when the deliverable is a compact model — a scoring form a human fills in, or a model that must run on ten inputs instead of five thousand — because keeping every coefficient is precisely what it does. Standardise features first, and leave the intercept out of the penalty.

interview.question: Why does ridge help when features are correlated?
interview.answer: Correlated columns make the unpenalised solution unstable, since many very different coefficient vectors fit the data almost equally well and the fit can pick an extreme one with large offsetting weights. The quadratic penalty prefers spreading influence evenly over concentrating it, so it settles on a balanced split between correlated columns. The result moves far less when the training sample changes.

interview.question: How do you choose the penalty strength in practice?
interview.answer: Cross-validation over a log-spaced grid, because the useful range spans orders of magnitude and a linear grid wastes most of its points. Plot held-out error against the strength and take the minimum, or the largest value within one standard error of it if you want a more conservative model. Never tune it on the training error, which is monotone in the penalty and tells you nothing.

interview.question: You standardised the features before fitting. Why does that matter here specifically?
interview.answer: The penalty charges for coefficient magnitude, and a coefficient's magnitude depends on the units of its feature. A variable measured in dollars and one in millions of dollars get penalised completely differently for the same real effect. Standardising puts every feature on comparable footing so the penalty is applied fairly.

children.title: Lasso Regression and L1 Sparsity
children.text: Lasso penalises the sum of absolute coefficient values, and that absolute value changes everything. Because the penalty has a sharp corner at zero rather than a smooth curve, the optimum frequently lands exactly on that corner, setting coefficients to precisely zero rather than merely small. The result is a model that has selected a subset of your features and discarded the rest, all as a side effect of fitting. With a thousand candidate columns you might end up with a model that reads off forty of them. That makes lasso the tool of choice when you want a short, deployable, explainable model out the other end.
children.deep_text:
Picture a churn model with 1,200 candidate features assembled from event logs, billing records and support tickets. You fit lasso across a range of penalty strengths and watch the number of surviving nonzero coefficients: at very weak penalty nearly all 1,200 survive, and as you increase it the count falls to 300, then 80, then 25, then a handful. Cross-validated error typically bottoms out somewhere in the middle, and the model at that point might use 60 features. You ship those 60 columns and stop computing the other 1,140 in your feature pipeline, which is often a bigger operational win than the accuracy itself.

Why the corner produces exact zeros is worth the geometry. Think of the penalty as a budget region the coefficient vector must stay inside, and the error surface as ellipses expanding outward from the unpenalised solution. With an absolute value penalty that region is a diamond with vertices sitting on the axes, and an expanding ellipse is far more likely to first touch a pointed vertex than the flat face between vertices. Touching a vertex means every coordinate except one is zero. In higher dimensions the same argument produces sparsity along many axes at once.

The misconception is that the surviving features are the important ones and the zeroed ones are irrelevant. What lasso gives you is one sufficient subset, not the true set. Among a group of strongly correlated features it will typically retain one arbitrarily and zero the others, and which one it retains can flip with a different random split of your data — a real problem if a stakeholder wants to know which signals drive churn. Run lasso on several bootstrap resamples and count how often each feature survives; features that appear in most runs are the ones you can talk about, and features that appear in a third of runs are interchangeable members of a correlated cluster.

Reach for lasso when the feature count is large, you believe genuinely that most features contribute nothing, and a compact model has operational value. Avoid it when features are highly correlated and you need stable attribution, or when the signal is genuinely spread thinly across many weak features, because zeroing most of them throws away real information. Note also that it cannot select more features than you have training rows, which bites in very wide, short datasets. Standardise before fitting.

interview.question: Why does an absolute value penalty produce exact zeros when a squared one does not?
interview.answer: The absolute value penalty has a constant-magnitude pull toward zero that does not vanish as the coefficient shrinks, so a feature whose error contribution is smaller than that pull gets driven all the way to zero and stays. Geometrically the feasible region is a diamond with vertices on the axes, and the error contours tend to meet it at a vertex. Squared penalties have a smooth boundary with no corners, so they approach zero without reaching it.

interview.question: Lasso picked 40 features. Can you tell the business those 40 drive the outcome?
interview.answer: Not safely. Lasso returns one sufficient subset, and among correlated features it keeps one essentially arbitrarily, so a different data split can produce a different 40. Refit across bootstrap resamples and report selection frequency; features chosen in the large majority of runs are the ones worth naming.

interview.question: When would you deliberately not use lasso on a high-dimensional problem?
interview.answer: When you expect many weak but real effects rather than a few strong ones, since zeroing most of them discards genuine signal and hurts accuracy. Also when correlated feature groups exist and you need consistent attribution, because the selection becomes unstable. And it cannot retain more features than there are training rows, which is limiting on very wide, short datasets.

children.title: Elastic Net
children.text: Elastic net puts both penalty terms in the objective at once, with a mixing parameter controlling how much of each you get. The motivation is a specific failure mode: when a group of features is strongly correlated, a pure absolute-value penalty keeps one and discards the rest, and which one it keeps is unstable across data splits. Adding a quadratic component encourages correlated features to receive similar weights, so the whole group survives or the whole group goes together. You end up with a model that is still compact but selects in coherent blocks rather than picking arbitrary representatives. That grouping effect is the reason it exists.
children.deep_text:
Consider a text classification model with 30,000 n-gram features where phrases like flight delayed, delayed flight and my flight was delayed all fire on overlapping documents. These columns are close to interchangeable. A pure sparsity-inducing fit retains one of them and zeroes the rest, so refitting on next month's data can swap in a different member, and your model diff looks alarming even though nothing meaningful changed. Elastic net with a mixing parameter around 0.5 keeps all three with moderate, similar weights, and the model is stable across refits. It also sidesteps a hard limit: a purely sparse fit cannot retain more nonzero coefficients than you have training rows, which matters badly when you have 30,000 features and 2,000 documents, whereas elastic net can.

Tuning has two knobs rather than one, and they interact. The overall strength controls how much total penalty you apply; the mixing ratio controls the balance between the two components. The usual approach is a two-dimensional cross-validated search, but a coarse one — a handful of ratio values such as 0.1, 0.5, 0.9 crossed with a log-spaced strength grid — is almost always enough, since the error surface is broad in the mixing direction.

The misconception is that elastic net is a safe default that dominates both of its components, so you should always reach for it. It is more flexible, which is exactly the cost: you are fitting a second hyperparameter on the same finite validation data, and that extra search can overfit your validation split on small datasets. If your features are genuinely independent, or if you genuinely believe only a handful matter and correlation is not an issue, the extra knob buys you noise rather than accuracy. Elastic net earns its place specifically when you have correlated groups and want both compactness and stability.

The decision rule: look at your feature correlation structure before choosing. Blocks of related columns — n-grams, one-hot encodings of similar categories, lagged versions of the same series, expression levels of genes in a pathway — mean elastic net. Independent features and a clear expectation about how many matter mean you can pick one of the simpler penalties and spend your tuning budget elsewhere. Standardise features first, since both penalty components are scale sensitive.

interview.question: What problem does elastic net solve that its two components alone do not?
interview.answer: Stable selection among correlated feature groups. Mixing the two penalties makes correlated columns receive similar coefficients so they enter or leave the model together, rather than one being kept arbitrarily. It also removes the cap where a purely sparse fit cannot retain more features than there are training rows.

interview.question: How would you tune it without burning your validation set?
interview.answer: Search the mixing ratio coarsely — three or four values is usually enough since the error surface is flat in that direction — and the overall strength on a log-spaced grid. Use nested cross-validation or a held-out test set kept out of the search if you need an honest error estimate. On small datasets consider fixing the ratio from domain knowledge and tuning only the strength.

interview.question: Your features are all independent measurements. Is elastic net still worth it?
interview.answer: Usually not. The grouping effect it provides is only valuable when correlated blocks exist, and with independent features you are paying for a second hyperparameter that gives nothing back. That extra search can itself overfit a small validation set, so a single-penalty model is the better use of your tuning budget.

children.deep_text:
The prediction rule does not change anywhere in this unit. You still compute a weighted sum of features. What changes is the objective, which gains a second term measuring the magnitude of the coefficient vector, scaled by a strength parameter you choose by cross-validation. Setting that parameter to zero recovers unpenalised regression; pushing it high drives all coefficients toward nothing and the model toward predicting a constant. Everything useful happens in between, which is why tuning it is not optional.

The three children are best read as a progression rather than three alternatives on a shelf. Ridge comes first because its penalty is the smooth, differentiable one, which makes it the direct analogue of the plain least squares story and the easiest to reason about geometrically. It is also the one with a clean closed form, so it connects back to the machinery you already have. Lasso comes second because its penalty has a corner at zero, and that single geometric difference produces qualitatively different behaviour that would be hard to motivate before seeing the smooth case. Elastic net comes third because it is literally the sum of the other two penalties, so it only makes sense once you know what each contributes and why you might want both at once.

One idea underlies all three and is worth carrying through: regularisation is a bias-variance trade. You are deliberately accepting a slightly wrong model in exchange for one that moves much less when the training data changes. On a dataset where features outnumber rows, or where columns are strongly correlated, that trade is overwhelmingly favourable. On a large clean dataset with few, independent features it buys you little and may cost accuracy. Also note a shared prerequisite: all three penalise coefficient magnitude, so features measured on wildly different scales are penalised unequally. Standardise your features before fitting any of them.

children.title: Logistic Regression
children.text: Logistic regression predicts the probability that something belongs to a class, not a raw number. It gets there by computing the same weighted sum of features a regression would, then passing that score through a function that compresses any real value into the range zero to one. Because it outputs calibrated probabilities rather than bare labels, you can set your own decision threshold based on what a false positive actually costs. Three pieces make it work: the squashing function and what it does to the interpretation of coefficients, the loss function that replaces squared error, and the extension from two classes to many.

children.title: The Sigmoid and Log-Odds
children.text: The sigmoid takes any real number and squashes it into the interval between zero and one. Feed it zero and you get 0.5; feed it a large positive number and it saturates near one; large negative, near zero. What makes it more than a convenient squashing function is what it inverts to. The linear score your model computes is not the probability — it is the log of the odds, the log of p divided by one minus p. That means a coefficient of 0.7 on a feature says a one-unit increase multiplies the odds by about two, regardless of where you started.
children.deep_text:
Work an example. A loan default model has an intercept of minus 2 and a coefficient of minus 0.8 on a credit score expressed in hundreds of points. An applicant with a score of 600 gets a linear score of minus 2 minus 0.8 times 6, which is minus 6.8. That is the log-odds. Exponentiating gives odds of about 0.0011, which converts to a default probability near 0.11 percent. Push the score to 500 and the linear term becomes minus 6.0, odds of about 0.0025, probability near 0.25 percent. The absolute probability barely moved but the odds more than doubled — and doubling is exactly what the coefficient promised, since exp of 0.8 is about 2.2. That constancy in odds-space, and its non-constancy in probability-space, is the whole content of the log-odds interpretation.

The misconception this generates constantly is treating the coefficient as an effect on probability. People read a coefficient of 0.5 and say the feature raises the chance by 50 percent, or by 0.5, and both are wrong. The effect on probability depends entirely on where on the curve you are sitting. Near a linear score of zero, where the sigmoid is steepest, a small change in score moves probability a lot. Out at a score of minus 6, the curve is nearly flat and the same change moves probability almost not at all. This is why two applicants with the same coefficient change can see completely different probability shifts, and why explaining a model to a non-technical stakeholder in odds ratios is honest while explaining it in probability points requires you to name a baseline.

The practical consequences are two. First, when reporting coefficients, exponentiate them and speak in odds multipliers, which are genuinely constant. Second, the saturation is why very large coefficient magnitudes are a warning sign: if your classes are perfectly separable by some feature, the fit will push that coefficient toward infinity, since pushing the sigmoid closer to exactly zero or one always reduces the loss slightly. That is what regularisation prevents in practice, and it is the usual explanation when a fitted logistic model reports a coefficient of 30 and a convergence warning.

interview.question: What does a logistic regression coefficient of 0.7 actually tell a stakeholder?
interview.answer: That a one-unit increase in that feature multiplies the odds of the positive class by about two, holding everything else fixed. It does not say the probability rises by any fixed amount, because the effect on probability depends on the starting point on the curve. Exponentiating and speaking in odds ratios is the honest way to report it.

interview.question: Your fitted model has a coefficient of 28 and a convergence warning. What happened?
interview.answer: Almost certainly a feature that perfectly or near-perfectly separates the classes. Since the loss keeps decreasing as the predicted probability approaches exactly zero or one, the optimiser drives that coefficient toward infinity and never converges. Adding a penalty term bounds it, and it is worth checking whether that feature is leaking the label.

interview.question: Why map the score through a sigmoid rather than just clipping it to the zero-to-one range?
interview.answer: Clipping is not differentiable at the boundaries and gives zero gradient outside them, so an optimiser stuck in the clipped region gets no signal to improve. The sigmoid is smooth everywhere with a gradient that never fully vanishes at finite scores. It also gives the linear score a clean interpretation as log-odds, which clipping would not.

children.title: Cross-Entropy Loss
children.text: Cross-entropy scores a probabilistic prediction by taking the negative log of the probability the model assigned to the correct answer. Say the true label is positive and the model said 0.9 — the loss is small. Say it said 0.1 and the loss is much larger. Say it said 0.001 and the loss explodes toward infinity. That asymmetry is the point: being confidently wrong is punished far harder than being uncertain. It is the natural loss for a probability output because it falls directly out of asking which parameters make the observed labels most likely under the model.
children.deep_text:
Compare two models on four examples with true labels 1, 1, 0, 0. Model A predicts 0.6, 0.6, 0.4, 0.4 — timid but always on the right side. Model B predicts 0.9, 0.9, 0.4, 0.95 — sharper on the first two, but badly wrong on the last, asserting 0.95 for an example whose true label is 0. Model A's per-example losses are all minus log 0.6, about 0.51, averaging 0.51. Model B gets minus log 0.9 twice, about 0.105 each, minus log 0.6 for the third, about 0.51, and minus log 0.05 for the confident mistake, about 3.0. Model B's average is around 0.93, nearly double, despite being right three times out of four and more confident where it is right. A single confident error outweighed three good calls. Accuracy would have scored them 100 percent and 75 percent; cross-entropy scored the reverse ordering more harshly, and that is what makes it a training signal rather than just a report card.

The misconception is that squared error would work fine on probabilities and cross-entropy is a stylistic preference. It matters for optimisation. With squared error, an example the model has confidently got wrong produces a tiny gradient, because the sigmoid is saturated there and its derivative is nearly zero — the model has no pressure to fix its worst mistakes. Cross-entropy's log term cancels that saturation exactly, leaving a gradient proportional to the plain difference between predicted probability and label. So the most wrong examples generate the strongest corrections, which is what you want, and the objective is convex in the coefficients rather than non-convex.

Two practical consequences. Any predicted probability of exactly zero on a positive label gives infinite loss, so implementations clip probabilities away from the endpoints or compute the loss directly from the linear score in a numerically stable form; if you write the loss yourself, do not exponentiate then take a log. And because it rewards calibration rather than correct ranking alone, a model with excellent cross-entropy is one whose stated probabilities can be used in expected-value calculations — worth the loss you optimise when downstream decisions weigh costs, and less critical when you only need a ranking.

interview.question: Why not train a classifier on squared error?
interview.answer: The gradient vanishes exactly where you need it most. When the model is confidently wrong the output transform is saturated and its derivative is near zero, so squared error produces almost no correction for the worst examples. Cross-entropy's log cancels that saturation, leaving a gradient proportional to the raw prediction error, and the objective stays convex.

interview.question: Model A has better accuracy but worse cross-entropy than model B. Which do you ship?
interview.answer: Depends on the decision downstream. If you act on a fixed threshold and only correctness matters, accuracy is closer to the business metric. If the probabilities feed an expected-value calculation, or you need to tune the threshold later against changing costs, the better-calibrated model wins even at lower accuracy.

interview.question: Your loss returns NaN partway through training. Where would you look?
interview.answer: A predicted probability that hit exactly zero or one, since the log of zero is infinite. Usually that comes from computing the sigmoid and then the log separately instead of using a numerically stable combined form, or from a learning rate large enough to blow up the scores. Clipping probabilities away from the endpoints is the quick fix; the stable formulation is the right one.

children.title: Multiclass via Softmax and One-vs-Rest
children.text: With more than two classes there are two routes. Softmax trains one weight vector per class, exponentiates every class score, and divides each by the total, so the outputs are positive and sum to exactly one across classes. One-vs-rest instead trains a separate binary classifier per class — this class against everything else — and takes whichever is most confident. Softmax models the classes jointly and gives you a genuine probability distribution. One-vs-rest is simpler, parallelises trivially, and lets you swap in any binary classifier, but its scores come from independent models and do not add to one.
children.deep_text:
Take a support ticket router with five categories. Softmax learns five weight vectors, computes five scores for a ticket, exponentiates each and normalises. A ticket might come out at 0.55 billing, 0.30 account, 0.10 technical, 0.03 shipping, 0.02 other — summing to one, and directly usable as a confidence. One-vs-rest trains five separate binary models: billing versus not-billing, account versus not-account, and so on. Those five might output 0.7, 0.6, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1, summing to 1.7, which is not a distribution. You pick the argmax and get the same answer here, but the numbers themselves are not comparable in the way softmax outputs are, because each was fitted against a different negative set.

The misconception is that these are interchangeable implementations of the same thing. They differ in a way that shows up in production. Softmax enforces competition between classes: raising one probability necessarily lowers the others, so the model is forced to arbitrate between confusable categories, which usually helps when categories are mutually exclusive. One-vs-rest imposes no such coupling, so two classes can both be confident about the same input. That is a bug if exactly one label is correct and a feature if labels can co-occur — a ticket that is genuinely both billing and account. For genuine multi-label problems one-vs-rest is the right structure and softmax is simply the wrong model.

One-vs-rest also inherits a class imbalance problem the framing creates. With fifty categories, each binary problem is roughly two percent positive against ninety-eight percent negative even if the original classes are perfectly balanced. Those binary models need threshold care or class weighting. Softmax does not manufacture this imbalance, though it still suffers from imbalance genuinely present in the data.

The decision rule: exactly one label per example and mutually exclusive classes means softmax, which is what a modern library gives you by default and what any neural classifier uses. Multiple labels possible, or you need to plug in a binary learner that has no natural multiclass form, or you need to add a class later without retraining everything, means one-vs-rest. There is also one-vs-one, training a classifier per pair, which scales badly in class count but keeps each subproblem small and balanced.

interview.question: When would you choose one-vs-rest over softmax?
interview.answer: When examples can carry more than one label, since softmax forces the probabilities to compete and sum to one, which is wrong for multi-label problems. Also when you need to plug in a binary learner with no natural multiclass form, or add a new class without retraining the existing models. The cost is that the scores are not a calibrated distribution.

interview.question: Your one-vs-rest classifier over 40 classes performs poorly on rare classes. Why?
interview.answer: Each binary subproblem is severely imbalanced by construction — one class against the other thirty-nine — so even balanced original data becomes a two-and-a-half percent positive rate per model. The binary fits drift toward predicting negative. Class weighting or per-model threshold tuning helps, and a joint softmax fit avoids manufacturing the imbalance in the first place.

interview.question: Two of your softmax classes are constantly confused. Does the structure of the model tell you anything?
interview.answer: It tells you the linear scores for those classes are close, which means no linear combination of your features separates them well. Because softmax normalises jointly, probability mass genuinely shifts between them rather than both being independently confident, so the confusion is visible in the outputs. The fix is usually a feature that distinguishes them, not a change of loss or optimiser.

children.deep_text:
Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier. The regression part refers to the linear score underneath, which is fit in a broadly familiar way; the classification comes from what happens to that score afterward. This unit separates into three pieces that answer three different questions.

The first is about the output transformation. You need a function that turns an unbounded score into a valid probability, and the specific choice made here is not arbitrary — it has an interpretation that flows straight back into how you read the fitted coefficients. Getting that interpretation right is what lets you say something meaningful about a coefficient rather than just quoting its sign.

The second is about the objective. Squared error, which worked cleanly for continuous targets, behaves badly on probabilities: it produces an optimisation landscape with flat regions and it fails to punish a confident wrong answer as harshly as it deserves. A different loss is needed, and it comes from asking which parameters make the observed labels most likely.

The third is about scope. Everything up to that point handles two classes. Real problems routinely have five or fifty, and there are two distinct strategies for getting there — generalise the machinery to handle all classes jointly, or build a set of binary models and combine them. They differ in cost, in whether the output probabilities sum to one, and in how they behave with imbalanced classes.

Read them in order: the output transform defines the model, the loss defines how it is fit, and the multiclass extension defines how far it reaches. Note that regularisation applies here as directly as it does to continuous-target regression, and most library implementations apply a penalty by default whether you asked for one or not.

Everything in this subsection rests on one object, the linear score: a weighted sum of features plus an intercept. The three units differ in what they do with that score and in what they add to the objective used to fit it.

Start with linear regression, because it is the bare case. The score is the prediction, the loss is squared error, and the mathematics is clean enough that the solution can be written down in closed form. Working through it gives you the vocabulary — design matrix, residual, objective, fitted coefficients — that the other two units assume.

Regularised linear regression comes second because it is a modification of the first, not a new idea. The prediction rule does not change at all; only the objective does, gaining a term that charges you for large coefficients. This matters the moment your feature count approaches your sample count, or your features are correlated with each other, at which point unregularised fitting produces coefficients that swing wildly with small changes in the data. The variants inside that unit differ in the shape of the penalty, and that shape choice has consequences worth treating separately.

Logistic regression comes third because it changes the output side rather than the objective side. The score is passed through a function that maps any real number into the range zero to one, and the loss changes to match, since squared error on probabilities behaves badly. It is a classifier built from the same parts.

Read in that order and each unit is a single edit to the one before it.

children.title: Tree-Based Models
children.text: Tree-based models make predictions by asking a sequence of yes-or-no questions about a row and returning whatever the training data said at the leaf you land in. That single mechanism is remarkably flexible: it handles mixed numeric and categorical features, ignores feature scale entirely, and captures interactions nobody wrote down. It splits into three units. Decision trees give you the mechanism itself and its failure mode. Bagging and random forests attack that failure mode by averaging many independent trees. Gradient boosting attacks it differently, growing trees in sequence so each one repairs what the run so far still gets wrong.

children.title: Decision Trees
children.text: A decision tree splits your data with a chain of threshold tests: is income above 52,000, is the region code in this set, and so on down to a leaf that holds a prediction. Nothing about it assumes a linear relationship or a particular scale, which is why trees work on raw tabular data that would need heavy preprocessing for other models. This unit covers four things: how the algorithm picks each split, what number it is actually minimising when it picks, how you stop it growing forever, and why, left unconstrained, it memorises your training set instead of learning from it.

children.title: Recursive Binary Splitting
children.text: Growing a tree is a greedy loop. Look at every feature and every candidate threshold within it, score the two-way split each one would produce, take the best, and cut the data in two. Then run the same procedure independently on each half, and on their halves, until a stopping rule fires. Nothing looks ahead: the split chosen at the root is fixed forever even if a slightly worse root split would have enabled a far better pair of children. This is why the procedure is called greedy, and why the tree you get is a good tree rather than the best possible one.
children.deep_text:
Concretely, suppose you are predicting loan default from two features on 1,000 applicants, 200 of whom defaulted. For the numeric feature income, the algorithm sorts the distinct values and considers a threshold between each adjacent pair. Try income under 40,000: 300 rows go left with 120 defaults, 700 go right with 80. Try income under 60,000: 600 go left with 160 defaults, 400 go right with 40. It scores both, and every other candidate on every other feature, then keeps whichever produced the cleanest pair of children. Suppose income under 60,000 wins. That cut is now permanent. The 600 rows on the left are re-scanned from scratch as if they were the whole dataset, and the same happens on the right, so the two children can pick completely different features to split on.

For regression the same loop runs with a different score, usually the total squared error you would get by predicting each child's mean, and the leaf prediction is that mean rather than a class vote. For an unordered categorical feature the candidates are subsets of categories rather than thresholds, which is why high-cardinality categoricals are expensive and why libraries use tricks to avoid enumerating every subset.

A common misconception is that the tree is choosing the globally optimal set of splits. It is not, and it cannot be: finding the optimal tree is intractable, so the greedy loop is a heuristic that happens to work well. A direct consequence is the exclusive-or pattern, where neither feature alone is informative but the pair is. A greedy first split looks useless on both features and the algorithm may pick something irrelevant, though it usually recovers a level or two down.

The practical rule follows from the cost: the loop is roughly linear in the number of features times the number of distinct values per feature, at every node. Binning continuous features into a few hundred candidate thresholds costs almost no accuracy and makes large datasets tractable, which is precisely what production implementations do. Reach for a plain greedy tree when you want an interpretable model fast; do not reach for it when your signal lives in a smooth linear trend that a tree can only approximate as a staircase.

interview.question: Why is the splitting procedure greedy rather than optimising the whole tree at once?
interview.answer: Finding the tree that minimises error over all possible split sequences is combinatorially intractable, since every choice changes the subproblems below it. The greedy loop picks the locally best split at each node and never revisits it, which reduces the search to something linear in features times thresholds per node. It gives up global optimality in exchange for being fast enough to run on real data, and in practice the resulting trees are close enough that the tradeoff is almost always worth it.

interview.question: When would greedy splitting fail to find structure that is genuinely in the data?
interview.answer: When no single feature is informative on its own but a combination is, the classic case being an exclusive-or relationship between two binary features. Each feature scored alone splits the labels roughly evenly, so the greedy score sees nothing and may pick a noise feature at the root. The tree often recovers deeper down because the interaction becomes visible once the data is partitioned, but it may need more depth and more data than the pattern really warrants.

interview.question: How does the split search change when you move from classification to regression?
interview.answer: The loop is identical; only the scoring function and the leaf value change. Instead of measuring label mixture, you compute the sum of squared deviations from each child's mean and pick the split minimising the total, and the leaf predicts that mean. This is why regression trees produce piecewise-constant outputs, and why they approximate a smooth linear relationship as a staircase that needs many splits to look reasonable.

children.title: Gini Impurity and Entropy
children.text: To compare candidate splits you need a number saying how mixed a node's labels are. Gini impurity and entropy are the two standard answers. Both are zero when a node holds one class only, both peak when classes are balanced, and both are computed from nothing but the class proportions in the node. A split's quality is the impurity of the parent minus the weighted impurity of its children, so the algorithm is asking how much mixture this cut removed. Gini is the default in most libraries because it avoids computing logarithms; entropy comes from information theory and gives near-identical trees.
children.deep_text:
Take a node with 100 rows, 70 positive and 30 negative. Gini impurity is one minus the sum of squared proportions: 1 minus 0.49 minus 0.09, which is 0.42. Entropy is the negative sum of each proportion times its base-two logarithm, which for a 70/30 split comes to about 0.88 bits. Now score a candidate split. Suppose it sends 40 rows left, all 40 positive, and 60 rows right, holding 30 positive and 30 negative. The left child is pure, so its Gini is 0. The right child is perfectly balanced, so its Gini is 1 minus 0.25 minus 0.25, which is 0.5. The weighted child impurity is 0.4 times 0 plus 0.6 times 0.5, or 0.3, and the gain is 0.42 minus 0.3, or 0.12. A competing split producing children at 0.35 and 0.20 would be scored the same way and the larger gain wins. When entropy is the measure, the same subtraction is called information gain.

The misconception worth killing is that the choice between Gini and entropy matters. It rarely does. The two functions have the same shape over the unit interval and disagree only in narrow regions, so on real data they produce trees that agree on the overwhelming majority of splits and score within noise of each other. Time spent tuning that flag is time not spent on depth, minimum leaf size, or feature engineering, all of which move the needle far more.

One thing that genuinely does matter is that both measures are biased toward features with many distinct values. A near-unique identifier column can produce many tiny, perfectly pure children and therefore an enormous apparent gain, even though it carries no real signal. Information gain ratio, which normalises the gain by how much the split fragments the data, exists to correct this. In practice the more common fix is to drop identifier-like columns before training.

For regression trees neither measure applies; the analogue is variance or total squared error in the node, but the subtract-the-weighted-children structure is identical. And a caution on interpretation: total impurity reduction attributed to each feature is what many libraries report as feature importance, which inherits exactly the same high-cardinality bias.

interview.question: Why do most libraries default to Gini rather than entropy?
interview.answer: Because the two produce essentially the same trees and Gini is cheaper. Gini needs only squares of proportions, while entropy needs a logarithm per class per candidate split, and that cost is paid millions of times during training. The functions have the same shape and the same zeros and maximum, so they disagree only on splits that are nearly tied anyway, which means the default is a performance choice rather than a statistical one.

interview.question: A colleague reports that customer ID is the most important feature by impurity reduction. What do you tell them?
interview.answer: That impurity-based scores are biased toward high-cardinality features, and an ID column is the extreme case. It can carve out many tiny pure leaves, each contributing real-looking impurity reduction, while generalising to nothing at all. I would drop the column, and separately check the other importances with a permutation-based measure on held-out data, which does not inherit that bias.

interview.question: How would you score splits if the target were continuous instead of categorical?
interview.answer: You swap impurity for a spread measure, normally variance or the sum of squared deviations from the node mean, and keep the rest of the procedure unchanged. The split score is still parent spread minus the size-weighted spread of the two children, so you are still asking how much of the target's variability this cut explains. Mean absolute error is available when you want robustness to outliers, at the cost of a slower split search.

children.title: Pruning and Depth Control
children.text: Left alone, the splitting loop keeps cutting until every leaf is pure, which produces a tree far more elaborate than the data supports. Two families of controls stop that. Pre-pruning halts growth during construction with limits on depth, minimum samples per leaf, minimum samples to split, or a minimum required gain. Post-pruning does the opposite: grow the tree fully, then collapse the branches that do not earn their keep, judged on validation data or by a complexity penalty. Post-pruning is generally the stronger of the two because it can see what a split eventually enabled before deciding to remove it.
children.deep_text:
Cost-complexity pruning is the standard post-pruning method and is worth understanding concretely. You score a subtree as its total training error plus alpha times the number of leaves, where alpha is a penalty per leaf. With alpha at zero the full tree wins. As you raise alpha, the weakest branch collapses first, then the next, producing a small ordered sequence of candidate trees rather than a continuum. Suppose the full tree has 180 leaves and 0 training errors, and pruning back to 24 leaves raises training error to 40 of 1,000 rows. On held-out data the 180-leaf tree might land near 74 percent accuracy while the 24-leaf tree reaches the low 80s. You pick alpha by cross-validation, evaluating each tree in that sequence and keeping the one with the best held-out score.

The misconception to correct is that pre-pruning and post-pruning are interchangeable. They are not, because pre-pruning is myopic in the same way the split search is. A minimum-gain threshold rejects a split whose immediate improvement is small, even when that split is the one that exposes an interaction and unlocks two excellent splits below it. Growing the tree first and cutting afterwards avoids that trap, because the eventual payoff is already visible when the decision is made. The price is compute: on a large dataset, growing to purity can be expensive enough that a depth cap is the only practical option.

The practical decision rule is straightforward. If the tree is the deliverable, because someone must read and defend its rules, prune properly and accept the extra work, since the number of leaves is also your interpretability budget. If the tree is one member of an ensemble, do not prune for accuracy at all: bagged trees are deliberately left deep, and boosted trees are deliberately kept shallow, for reasons belonging to those methods rather than to pruning. And when you only need a quick guard, a depth limit around 4 to 8 plus a minimum leaf size of a few dozen rows removes most of the damage for almost no effort. Set minimum leaf size in absolute rows on small data and as a fraction on large data, and remember that a leaf of one row is a memorised row, not a rule.

interview.question: Why is post-pruning usually preferred to a minimum-gain stopping rule?
interview.answer: Because a minimum-gain rule makes an irreversible decision using only the immediate improvement of a single split. A split that barely helps on its own can partition the data so that two very strong splits become available beneath it, and a stopping rule kills that branch before the payoff appears. Post-pruning grows the tree first, so it judges each branch by everything below it, and its only real drawback is the compute spent growing structure you then discard.

interview.question: How would you choose the pruning strength in practice?
interview.answer: With cost-complexity pruning the penalty per leaf generates a short sequence of nested subtrees, not a continuous space, so I cross-validate over that sequence and keep the subtree with the best held-out score. If interpretability is the real constraint I would also cap the number of leaves at whatever a stakeholder can actually read, even at a small accuracy cost. What I would not do is pick the depth by looking at training error, which always favours the largest tree.

interview.question: Would you prune the trees inside an ensemble the same way?
interview.answer: No, and usually not at all for accuracy reasons. Ensembles set tree size for reasons specific to how they combine trees, so the right depth there is a property of the ensembling method rather than something you tune per tree on a validation curve. The one time I do constrain depth in an ensemble is for memory and inference latency, where hundreds of deep trees become an expensive artefact to ship.

children.title: Why Single Trees Overfit
children.text: The splitting loop keeps cutting until each leaf is pure, so with enough depth it can put nearly every training row in its own leaf. That tree scores perfectly on data it has seen and poorly on data it has not, because the deepest splits are fitted to a handful of rows and are therefore fitted to noise. The second symptom is instability: change a few training rows and the root split can flip, giving a structurally different tree with different rules. High variance in this precise sense, not bias, is the defining weakness of a single tree, and it is what every tree ensemble exists to fix.
children.deep_text:
Watch the numbers on a concrete run. Train an unrestricted tree on 1,000 rows with a moderately noisy binary target. Training accuracy is 100 percent, because the tree has manufactured enough leaves to cover every row. Held-out accuracy might be around 72 percent. Cap depth at 5 and training accuracy falls to perhaps 86 percent while held-out accuracy rises into the low 80s. The gap between the two curves is the overfitting, and the fact that hurting the training score improves the test score is the clearest possible evidence that the extra structure was noise.

The mechanism is data starvation with depth. The root split uses all 1,000 rows, so its threshold is estimated from plenty of evidence. Ten levels down, a node might hold 6 rows, and the algorithm still dutifully searches every feature and every threshold for the best cut of those 6. With enough features, some split will separate them perfectly by pure chance. That rule is now permanent, and it will be applied to real users at inference time. The tree has no notion of statistical significance and no way to say a split was not worth making.

Instability is the same variance viewed from a different angle. Because the procedure is greedy, the root split is chosen and then never reconsidered, so two candidate splits that score 0.118 and 0.117 are effectively decided by a coin flip that a handful of rows can flip. Resample the data and you may get a tree that partitions on an entirely different feature at the root and looks unrelated to the first, even though both make similar predictions overall.

The misconception here is that overfitting means the tree is too complicated in some vague aesthetic sense, and that a smaller tree is always better. The real statement is sharper: the tree has low bias and high variance. It can represent almost any decision boundary, and that flexibility is genuinely valuable. What it lacks is any mechanism for distinguishing signal from noise as the sample per node shrinks. That framing is what makes the fix predictable. Anything that averages away variance without adding much bias will help enormously, which is exactly the opening that bagged and boosted tree ensembles walk through. The decision rule: use a single tree when a human must read the rules or when you need predictions in microseconds; reach for an ensemble whenever accuracy is what you are being paid for.

interview.question: Explain in mechanical terms why a deep tree overfits.
interview.answer: Each split consumes data, so the number of rows supporting a decision shrinks geometrically with depth. Near the leaves the algorithm is choosing among thousands of candidate thresholds using only a handful of rows, and with enough candidates one of them will separate those rows perfectly by chance. The tree has no significance test, so it commits to that split as if it were signal, and applies it to every future record that reaches the node.

interview.question: Two trees trained on 90 percent samples of the same data look completely different. Is something broken?
interview.answer: No, that is the expected behaviour and it is exactly what high variance means for trees. Split scores are often nearly tied, and because the search is greedy a tiny change in the data can flip the root, which then changes every subproblem beneath it. The two trees can still make similar predictions on most rows despite having unrelated structure, which is also a warning about reading a single tree's rules as a causal story.

interview.question: Would you describe a decision tree as a high-bias or high-variance model, and why does the answer matter?
interview.answer: High variance and low bias: given enough depth it can represent nearly any boundary, but the fit changes a lot with the training sample. It matters because it tells you which fixes will work. Averaging many versions of a high-variance, low-bias learner reduces the variance without introducing much bias, which is why tree ensembles are so effective, whereas the same trick on an already-biased model buys you very little.

children.deep_text:
The four pieces build on each other in sequence. Recursive binary splitting is the construction procedure: the greedy loop that picks one feature and one threshold, cuts the data in two, and recurses on each half. That loop needs a scoring function to decide which of thousands of candidate splits is best, and Gini impurity and entropy are the two standard scores for classification, both measuring how mixed the labels in a node still are.

With construction and scoring in place, the natural next question is when to stop.
