It deliberately hunts for the maximum of a noisy objective, so it is more likely than blind sampling to find a configuration that scored well by luck on your particular folds. The mitigations are the usual ones: use repeated or nested cross-validation for the search score, and confirm the winner on a test set that the search never saw.

children.title: Cross-Validation Strategies
children.text: A single train-validation split gives one number, and that number has real variance — reshuffle and the ranking of your candidate models can flip. Cross-validation reduces that noise by splitting the data several ways, training and scoring on each, and averaging. K-fold is the standard: divide into k parts, hold each out in turn. But the right splitting scheme depends on your data. Imbalanced classes need stratification, repeated measurements on the same subject need grouping, and time-ordered data must never train on the future.
children.deep_text:
Concretely, 5-fold cross-validation on 10,000 rows means five models: each trains on 8,000 rows and scores on the 2,000 it did not see, and you average the five scores. If those five come out as 0.82, 0.79, 0.85, 0.81, and 0.83, the mean is 0.82 and the spread of roughly 0.03 tells you how much confidence to place in it. That spread is the number people ignore and shouldn't: if two candidate configurations differ by 0.01 while the fold-to-fold spread is 0.03, you have not shown one is better.

Stratification matters when classes are imbalanced. With 3 percent positives, a plain random 5-fold split can produce a fold with 1 percent positives and another with 6 percent purely by chance, so scores swing for reasons unrelated to the model. Stratified splitting preserves the class proportion in every fold and removes that source of variance for free.

Grouping matters when rows are not independent. If you have 200 patients with 10 measurements each, a random split puts the same patient in both train and validation, and the model can recognise that individual rather than learn the underlying pattern. Your score then measures memorisation of specific patients and collapses on new ones. Group-aware splitting keeps all of a patient's rows on one side of every split.

Time ordering is the strictest constraint. Standard k-fold trains on rows that occurred after the validation rows, which is impossible at prediction time and inflates the score, sometimes enormously. Forward-chaining is the fix: train on the first three months and validate on the fourth, then train on four and validate on the fifth, and so on. It gives fewer folds and less training data in the early ones, and that is the honest cost.

The common misconception is that more folds is always better. Leave-one-out cross-validation, where k equals the number of rows, gives an almost unbiased estimate but a high-variance one, because the training sets across folds are nearly identical and the individual scores are perfectly correlated errors on single rows. It also costs one fit per row. Five or ten folds is the usual sweet spot between bias, variance, and compute.

The second and more consequential point: when cross-validation is used to select hyperparameters, the resulting best score is not an unbiased estimate of future performance, because the selection consumed the folds. Nested cross-validation — an inner loop for tuning, an outer loop purely for estimation — is the rigorous fix, at the cost of multiplying the fits. A single clean held-out test set is the cheap approximation most teams actually use.

The decision rule: default to stratified k-fold with 5 or 10 folds. Switch to group-aware splitting the moment rows share an entity, and to forward-chaining the moment prediction happens forward in time. Never do both a search and a final estimate on the same folds.

interview.question: Why is standard k-fold wrong for time series data?
interview.answer: Because folds are assigned randomly, so most training sets contain rows from after the validation period. The model gets to see the future while predicting the past, which is impossible in deployment, and the resulting score is inflated — often dramatically when the series is autocorrelated. Forward-chaining, where each fold trains only on data preceding its validation window, is the correct scheme.

interview.question: You have multiple rows per customer. What splitting scheme do you use and why?
interview.answer: Group-aware splitting keyed on customer, so every row for a given customer lands entirely in train or entirely in validation. A random split lets the model recognise individual customers from their other rows, which is memorisation that will not transfer to new customers. The grouped score is lower, but it is the number that reflects what happens in production.

interview.question: You used 5-fold cross-validation to pick hyperparameters and your best mean score was 0.88. Is that your expected production performance?
interview.answer: No — those folds were consumed by the selection, so 0.88 is the maximum over many noisy estimates and is biased upward. The rigorous answer is nested cross-validation, with an inner loop doing the tuning and an outer loop producing the estimate. In practice most teams hold out a test set that the search never touched and report that instead.

children.deep_text:
The first part is definitional but load-bearing: until you can say which numbers the fitting procedure sets and which you set yourself, the rest of the topic has no object. It also explains why hyperparameters cannot simply be optimised alongside the parameters — they are chosen on a different criterion, evaluated on different data.

The middle two parts are competing search strategies, and they sit next to each other on purpose. Exhaustive and random sampling of the space are the baseline approaches: simple, embarrassingly parallel, and requiring no assumptions. They are also blind, spending exactly as much effort on hopeless regions as on promising ones. The alternative builds a model of how settings map to performance and uses it to decide where to look next, which costs bookkeeping and sequential dependency but converges in far fewer trials. Understanding the first makes the second's motivation obvious, so the order matters.

The final part is the foundation the other three stand on, placed last because its necessity is clearest once you have seen the search. Every strategy compares candidates by a score, and if that score is noisy or contaminated, the search optimises the noise. A single train-validation split has enough variance that the reported winner is frequently arbitrary, and repeated evaluation against the same split gradually fits the search to it. Resampling strategies control both problems, and knowing which strategy suits which data — imbalanced classes, grouped observations, time-ordered rows — determines whether the whole exercise produced anything real.

The practical thread connecting all four: tuning is an outer loop, and its cost is the number of candidates multiplied by the cost of evaluating one. Every decision here is a trade between those two factors.

The order here is deliberate. Gradient descent comes first because it is the engine underneath most of what follows: it explains what "training" physically does, why it can stall, and why the shape of your data matters to it. Once you understand that training is a repeated small step downhill on an error surface, the second part stops being a list of chores and starts being obvious. Rescaling columns, encoding categories as numbers, filling gaps, dropping useless inputs, and compressing correlated columns are all ways of reshaping that error surface so descent has an easier time and the model has less noise to fit. Feature preparation is optimisation-aware data work, not hygiene for its own sake.

Hyperparameter tuning sits last because it is the outer loop wrapped around the other two. Learning rate, regularisation strength, tree depth, the number of components you kept — none of these are learned by the descent procedure. They are chosen, and choosing them well means running training many times and comparing honestly. That honesty requirement is why validation strategy lives in this part rather than being assumed.

Read them in order the first time. In practice you will cycle: tuning reveals that a feature is scaled wrong, fixing the scaling changes which learning rate works, and the search restarts. What stays constant is the diagnostic habit — when a model underperforms, ask three questions in order. Did the optimiser fail to converge, so the loss never actually got low? Did the features carry no usable signal, so there was nothing to converge to? Or were the settings simply never searched, so a better version of the same model was always available and you never looked? Those three questions map onto the three parts of this section, and answering them in that order saves you from tuning a model whose inputs were broken all along.

children.title: Evaluation and Model Selection
children.text: A model that has finished training is just a set of numbers until you can say how good it is, and "good" is not one thing. Deciding that means answering three separate questions: how do you score a classifier that outputs labels, how do you score a model that outputs numbers or probabilities, and how do you decide that one candidate is genuinely better than another rather than luckier on this particular test set. Those three questions have different mathematics behind them, so this section splits along exactly those lines. Get the metric wrong and every downstream decision inherits the error.

children.title: Classification Metrics
children.text: A classifier can be wrong in two different ways, and almost every argument about model quality comes down to which of those two ways you mind more. Once you write the model's predictions against the truth as a table of counts, you can pull out a whole family of scores, each answering a different question about the same predictions. This part works through that table, the two headline ratios that come out of it, the standard ways to combine them into one number, the two curve-based summaries that sweep across every possible threshold, and finally why the most obvious score of all is often the worst one to trust.

children.title: The Confusion Matrix
children.text: Line up a classifier's predictions against the truth and every prediction falls into one of exactly four buckets. It said positive and it was positive: a true positive. It said positive and it was negative: a false positive. It said negative and it was negative: a true negative. It said negative and it was positive: a false negative. Arrange those four counts in a two-by-two grid and you have the confusion matrix. It is not a metric; it is the raw material every classification metric is computed from, and reading it directly tells you things a single score never will.
children.deep_text:
Take a fraud detector run over 1000 transactions, of which 10 are genuinely fraudulent. Suppose the model flags 18 transactions in total, and 7 of those flagged are real fraud. That gives you 7 true positives. The other 11 flagged transactions were legitimate, so 11 false positives. Of the 10 real frauds, 3 were not flagged, so 3 false negatives. Everything else, 979 transactions, was legitimate and unflagged: 979 true negatives. Check the arithmetic: 7 + 11 + 3 + 979 = 1000. Those four numbers are the confusion matrix, and every score anyone might quote about this detector is some ratio of them.

The naming convention trips people up constantly, so decode it mechanically. The second word is what the model predicted. The first word says whether the model was right. A false negative is therefore a case the model called negative and was wrong about, meaning it was actually positive. In the fraud example, false negatives are the frauds that got through, which is usually the expensive bucket.

The common misconception is that the confusion matrix is symmetric, or that swapping which class you call positive is a cosmetic relabelling. It is not. Choosing which class is positive determines the meaning of every derived score, and the choice is a modelling decision you should make deliberately. Convention is to make the rare, interesting, or costly class positive: fraud, disease, defect. If you silently let a library pick alphabetically, you can end up reporting near-perfect numbers about the ability to detect ordinary non-fraudulent transactions, which is worthless.

For more than two classes the matrix becomes k-by-k, with rows for true classes and columns for predicted ones. The diagonal holds correct predictions and every off-diagonal cell tells you which specific confusion the model makes, which is enormously more informative than any summary. A digit classifier that confuses 4 with 9 and nothing else is a very different engineering problem from one that scatters errors uniformly, and only the matrix reveals that.

The decision rule is simple: always look at the matrix before looking at any score. It costs one function call, it takes ten seconds to read, and it catches the degenerate cases, a model predicting one class always, a class with almost no support, an off-by-one label mapping, that a single aggregate number will happily conceal from you.

interview.question: Your model reports 96% accuracy and the confusion matrix shows a nearly empty positive row. What do you conclude?
interview.answer: That the model is predicting the negative class almost unconditionally and the positive class is rare enough that this still scores well. The near-empty positive row means true positives and false positives are both tiny, so the model has essentially learned the prior rather than a decision boundary. This is exactly the failure the matrix catches and the accuracy figure hides.

interview.question: Why does it matter which class you label as positive?
interview.answer: Because the labels of the four cells, and therefore every metric derived from them, are defined relative to that choice. Swap it and false negatives become false positives, and scores that looked strong can invert. The convention is to make the rare or costly class positive so the metrics describe the thing you actually care about detecting.

interview.question: When would you look at a full multi-class confusion matrix instead of a per-class summary score?
interview.answer: Whenever the errors are likely to be structured rather than random, which is most of the time. Per-class scores tell you a class is weak but not what it is being mistaken for. The off-diagonal cells identify the specific pairs being confused, which usually points straight at a labelling ambiguity, a missing feature, or two classes that should be merged.

children.title: Precision, Recall, and the Trade-Off
children.text: Precision asks: of everything the model flagged, what fraction was right? Recall asks: of everything that should have been flagged, what fraction did the model catch? They answer genuinely different questions, and they pull against each other. Lower the decision threshold and the model flags more things, catching more of the real positives but sweeping in more junk, so recall rises and precision falls. Raise it and the reverse happens. There is no threshold that maximises both, so choosing one means deciding which kind of mistake your application can better afford.
children.deep_text:
Return to the fraud detector over 1000 transactions with 10 real frauds. Suppose at its default threshold it flags 18 transactions and 7 of them are real fraud. Precision is 7 out of 18, about 0.39: fewer than two in five alerts are worth an analyst's time. Recall is 7 out of 10, or 0.70: it catches seven of the ten frauds. Now drop the threshold so the model flags 50 transactions and catches 9 of the 10 frauds. Recall jumps to 0.90, but precision collapses to 9 out of 50, or 0.18. Push the other way, flag only the 5 most confident, and suppose 5 are fraud: precision is a perfect 1.00 while recall sinks to 0.50. Same model, same learned scores, three completely different report cards. Nothing changed but a number you chose.

That last point is the one people miss. Precision and recall are not properties of a model, they are properties of a model plus a threshold. When someone says their classifier has 0.9 recall, the honest follow-up is "at what precision, and at what threshold?" A model that outputs continuous scores has an entire curve of achievable pairs, and quoting one point is quoting one arbitrary choice from that curve.

The common misconception is that the trade-off is a flaw to be engineered away. It is not; it is arithmetic. Flagging more items can only increase the true positives you capture and can only increase the false positives you incur. The only way to improve both at once is to improve the underlying model's ranking of examples, which is a modelling problem, not a threshold problem. Tuning the threshold moves you along the curve; better features or a better model move the curve itself.

The decision rule follows from what a mistake costs. Optimise recall when missing a positive is the expensive outcome and a false alarm is merely annoying: disease screening, safety-critical defect detection, an initial filtering stage that a human or a second model will review anyway. Optimise precision when acting on a flag is costly or damaging: auto-blocking a paying customer's account, sending an accusatory email, surfacing a recommendation that burns user trust.

In practice the cleanest way to set the threshold is to fix the constraint the business actually has and maximise the other quantity subject to it. If the fraud team can review forty alerts a day, do not chase an abstract balance point; find the threshold that produces roughly forty alerts and report the recall you achieve there. That converts a metric argument into an operations question, which is usually where it belonged.

interview.question: A stakeholder asks you to improve both precision and recall. How do you respond?
interview.answer: By separating the two ways that can happen. At a fixed model, they trade off, so moving the threshold improves one at the other's expense and there is nothing to negotiate. Improving both simultaneously requires a better ranking of examples through better features, more data, or a different model class. Framing it this way turns a vague ask into a concrete decision about where to spend effort.

interview.question: When would you deliberately ship a model with very low precision?
interview.answer: When the model is a recall-oriented first stage feeding something with more capacity to filter. A screening step that surfaces candidates for a human reviewer or an expensive second-stage model can tolerate a lot of false positives, because the cost of a false positive is one review rather than a bad user-facing action. The thing you cannot recover from is a positive that never enters the funnel.

interview.question: How would you actually pick an operating threshold in production?
interview.answer: Start from the operational constraint rather than the metric. Review capacity, alert budget, or an acceptable false-alarm rate usually fixes one axis, and then you choose the threshold that maximises the other quantity subject to it. Validate that threshold on held-out data from the deployment period, since the score distribution can drift even when the model does not.

children.title: F1 and F-Beta Scores
children.text: F1 collapses precision and recall into one number by taking their harmonic mean: two times precision times recall, divided by their sum. The harmonic mean is chosen deliberately because it punishes imbalance. A model with precision 1.0 and recall 0.0 has an arithmetic mean of 0.5 but an F1 of 0, which is the honest answer. F-beta generalises this with a knob: beta greater than one weights recall more heavily, beta less than one weights precision more heavily. F2 and F0.5 are the common choices when the two errors are not equally costly.
children.deep_text:
Take the fraud detector that flags 18 transactions out of 1000 and catches 7 of the 10 real frauds. Precision is 7/18 = 0.389, recall is 7/10 = 0.70. F1 is 2 times 0.389 times 0.70 divided by (0.389 + 0.70), which is 0.544 / 1.089 = 0.50. Note where that sits: closer to the weaker of the two inputs than the midpoint of 0.545. That pull toward the smaller number is the entire point of the harmonic mean. Now suppose a second candidate model achieves precision 0.55 and recall 0.50. Its F1 is 2 times 0.275 divided by 1.05 = 0.524, slightly higher, so on F1 the second model wins, even though it catches fewer frauds.

That comparison is exactly why F-beta exists. If missing fraud costs ten times what a wasted investigation costs, F1's implicit assumption that precision and recall matter equally is simply wrong for you. F-beta is defined as (1 + beta squared) times precision times recall, divided by (beta squared times precision, plus recall). With beta = 2, recall is weighted four times as heavily as precision, and recomputing the two candidates flips the ordering back toward the higher-recall model. The rule of thumb worth memorising is that beta is the number of times you consider recall more important than precision, so F2 for screening problems and F0.5 for problems where acting on a false positive is expensive.

The common misconception is that F1 is the neutral, assumption-free choice, the metric you use when you have not thought about it. It is the opposite: F1 encodes a specific and quite strong assumption, that a false positive and a false negative cost precisely the same. Almost no real application satisfies that. Choosing F1 by default is making a cost assumption silently rather than making it explicitly, which is worse than choosing F2 for a reason.

A second thing F1 hides is that it ignores true negatives entirely. That is often a feature, since it stops a huge easy negative class from inflating the score, but it means F1 says nothing about how the model behaves on the bulk of your traffic. Two models with identical F1 can flag wildly different volumes.

The decision rule: use F-beta when you genuinely need a single number to rank many candidates automatically, in a hyperparameter sweep or a model registry, and you have thought about beta. Do not use it as the number you report to a stakeholder. Report the precision and recall pair alongside the threshold, because those map to things people can act on, alert volume and miss rate, in a way a fused score never does.

interview.question: Why the harmonic mean rather than the arithmetic mean?
interview.answer: Because the arithmetic mean rewards a degenerate model. Predict everything positive and recall is 1.0 while precision equals the base rate, and the arithmetic mean still looks respectable. The harmonic mean is dominated by the smaller of the two values, so it collapses toward zero unless both are decent, which is the behaviour you want from a summary score.

interview.question: When would you choose F2 over F1?
interview.answer: When a missed positive is meaningfully more expensive than a false alarm. Medical screening, safety inspection, and any first-stage filter that feeds a human reviewer all fit. F2 weights recall four times as heavily as precision, which makes model selection prefer the candidate that catches more of the real positives even at the cost of extra review load.

interview.question: Is F1 a good metric to put on a dashboard for non-technical stakeholders?
interview.answer: Usually not. It is a single opaque number that assumes both error types cost the same and cannot be translated back into anything operational. Precision and recall at a stated threshold map directly onto alert volume and miss rate, which stakeholders can reason about and set targets against. Keep F1 for automated ranking of candidates.

children.title: ROC Curves and AUC
children.text: A model that outputs scores rather than hard labels has no single performance number until you pick a threshold. The ROC curve avoids picking one: it plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate as the threshold sweeps from strictest to loosest, tracing every operating point the model can reach. The area under that curve, the AUC, has a clean interpretation. It is the probability that a randomly chosen positive example receives a higher score than a randomly chosen negative one. AUC 0.5 is coin-flipping, 1.0 is perfect separation, and it measures ranking quality, not calibration.
children.deep_text:
The two axes are both rates, and both are normalised within a class. The true positive rate is the fraction of actual positives the model catches at a given threshold; the false positive rate is the fraction of actual negatives it wrongly flags. Sweep the threshold from infinitely strict, where you flag nothing and sit at the origin, to infinitely loose, where you flag everything and sit at the top right, and the path between those corners is the curve. A useless model traces the diagonal. A good one bulges toward the top-left corner, where you capture most positives while flagging few negatives.

The probabilistic reading of AUC is the one to hold in your head, because it makes clear what the metric is and is not measuring. Take the fraud detector's 10 fraudulent and 990 legitimate transactions. There are 9900 possible fraud-legitimate pairs. If the model scores the fraud higher in 9207 of them, ties aside, AUC is 0.93. That is a statement purely about ordering. Apply any monotonic transformation to every predicted score, square them, take logs, divide them all by 100, and the AUC does not change by a hair, because the ranking is untouched. The scores could all be wildly wrong as probabilities and AUC would not notice.

The common misconception is that a high AUC means the model is ready to deploy. It means the model can separate the classes if you find the right threshold, which is a necessary condition and not a sufficient one. AUC 0.95 tells you a good operating point exists somewhere on the curve. It does not tell you which one, what the precision is there, or whether the predicted probabilities can be fed to a downstream cost calculation. Those are separate questions handled by the threshold-specific metrics and by calibration.

AUC's real strengths are threshold independence and comparability. Because it summarises the entire curve, it is the right metric when you have not yet decided on an operating point, when different teams will deploy the same model at different thresholds, or when you are ranking dozens of candidates in a sweep and want a single ordering-quality number that no threshold choice can game.

The decision rule is about when the false positive rate is a meaningful denominator. It is when negatives are plentiful and the cost of a false positive scales with the fraction of negatives you disturb, as in a ranking or retrieval setting. When the negative class massively outnumbers the positive one, the false positive rate denominator is so large that thousands of false alarms barely move the axis, and the curve looks flattering while the alert queue is unusable. That is the situation the precision-recall curve is built for, and it is the standard reason to reach for that instead.

interview.question: What does AUC actually measure, in one sentence?
interview.answer: The probability that a randomly drawn positive example is scored higher than a randomly drawn negative one. That makes it a pure measure of ranking quality across all thresholds. It says nothing about whether the scores are usable as probabilities or which threshold you should deploy at.

interview.question: Two models have identical AUC but you can only ship one. How do you choose?
interview.answer: Look at the shape of the curves rather than the areas, because equal area can come from very different trade-offs. One model may dominate in the low false-positive-rate region where you actually intend to operate while the other catches up only at loose thresholds nobody would use. Compare them at the operating point your application requires, then bring in calibration and latency.

interview.question: Why is AUC unchanged if you rescale all the predicted scores?
interview.answer: Because it depends only on the relative ordering of scores, and a monotonic transformation preserves ordering. This is convenient when comparing models whose outputs live on different scales, such as an SVM margin against a probability. It is also the limitation: a model can have excellent AUC while its stated probabilities are systematically too confident.

children.title: Precision-Recall Curves for Imbalanced Data
children.text: A precision-recall curve plots precision on the vertical axis against recall on the horizontal one as the decision threshold sweeps across its range. Both quantities depend on the positive class, which is exactly the point: nothing in the curve is dominated by a huge easy negative class. Summarise it with average precision, the area under it. The crucial difference from a ROC curve is the baseline. Random guessing traces a flat line at the positive class prevalence, so with 1% positives a useless model scores 0.01, and any real score has to be read against that floor.
children.deep_text:
Consider a fraud detector on 1000 transactions with 10 frauds, a 1% positive rate. Suppose at some threshold it flags 200 transactions and catches 9 frauds. On the ROC axes, the false positive rate is 191 wrongly flagged out of 990 legitimate, about 0.19, which sits well up the curve and looks tolerable. On the precision-recall axes, the same operating point is recall 0.90 and precision 9/200 = 0.045. That second pair is the one an analyst would recognise: twenty-two alerts to review for every real fraud found. Both descriptions are arithmetically correct; only one is informative about whether the system is usable.

The reason for the divergence is which denominator each axis uses. The false positive rate divides by the count of negatives, and when negatives number in the hundreds or millions, hundreds of false alarms barely register. Precision divides by the number of things flagged, so every false alarm counts against you at full weight. When the positive class is rare, the negative class is the one with the enormous denominator, and any metric normalised by it becomes insensitive to the errors you care about.

The common misconception is that a precision-recall curve is simply a better ROC curve. It is not better in general; it answers a different question and it is not comparable across datasets. Because the random baseline equals the class prevalence, an average precision of 0.30 on a dataset with 1% positives is a strong result, roughly thirty times the floor, while 0.30 on a balanced dataset is worse than useless. ROC AUC always has a 0.5 baseline regardless of prevalence, which makes it portable but insensitive here. Never compare an average precision figure between two datasets with different base rates without stating both prevalences.

The curve is also noticeably jagged at the high-precision end, and this is real rather than a plotting artefact. At very strict thresholds only a handful of examples are flagged, so a single example changing from correct to incorrect swings precision from 1.0 to 0.75. Read that region with suspicion, especially with small positive counts, and prefer to report an operating point with enough support behind it to be stable.

The decision rule: reach for the precision-recall curve when positives are rare and when the cost of your errors is driven by the volume of false alarms relative to true finds. Fraud, intrusion detection, rare-disease screening, content moderation, information retrieval. Keep ROC when classes are roughly balanced or when you need a prevalence-independent number to compare models across differently sampled evaluation sets. Plotting both is cheap and the disagreement between them is itself diagnostic.

interview.question: Why does a precision-recall curve show a problem that a ROC curve hides on rare-positive data?
interview.answer: Because precision divides by the number of predictions flagged while the false positive rate divides by the total negatives. With a vast negative class, thousands of false alarms are a negligible fraction of negatives but can be the overwhelming majority of the alerts you produce. The precision axis registers that at full weight and the false positive rate axis does not.

interview.question: A colleague reports average precision of 0.4 and calls it weak. What do you ask?
interview.answer: The positive class prevalence, because that is the random baseline. At 1% positives, 0.4 is roughly forty times the floor and genuinely strong. At 40% positives it is exactly chance. Average precision has no fixed reference point, so the number is meaningless without the base rate attached.

interview.question: Why is the left end of a precision-recall curve so noisy, and what do you do about it?
interview.answer: At very strict thresholds only a few examples are flagged, so precision is computed over a tiny denominator and a single misclassification swings it dramatically. Do not choose an operating point from that region on the basis of a single evaluation run. Either report points with enough flagged examples to be stable, or put confidence bands on the curve via bootstrapping.

children.title: Why Accuracy Misleads
children.text: Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that were correct, and it is the first metric everyone reaches for because it is the easiest to explain. It is also the one that breaks most reliably. Its problem is that it treats every prediction as equally important and every error as equally bad. When one class dominates the data, a model that ignores the input entirely and always predicts that class scores extremely well while being completely useless. The rarer and more valuable the thing you are trying to detect, the more thoroughly accuracy lies to you.
children.deep_text:
Take the fraud detector one final time: 1000 transactions, 10 of them fraudulent. Write a classifier consisting of the single line "return not fraud". It has never seen a feature and cannot learn. Its accuracy is 990 out of 1000, or 99%. A real model that catches 7 of the 10 frauds at the cost of 11 false alarms gets 7 + 979 = 986 correct, an accuracy of 98.6%. By accuracy, the useless constant model wins. This is not a contrived edge case; it is the default outcome whenever the interesting class is rare, and rare classes are exactly what most detection systems exist to find. Push the prevalence to 1 in 10,000, as in some medical screening or intrusion settings, and the constant model scores 99.99% while providing literally zero information.

The mechanism is that accuracy sums correct predictions with no regard for which class they belong to. The abundant class contributes almost all the terms, so the score is essentially a measurement of performance on the easy majority, with the minority class's contribution rounded away. A model can improve its accuracy by getting worse at the only task you cared about, as long as it compensates on the majority.

The second failure is unequal error costs, and it is independent of imbalance. Accuracy counts a false positive and a false negative as one mistake each. In a cancer screen, missing a tumour and calling a healthy patient back for a second scan are not remotely comparable outcomes, but accuracy averages them together as though they were. Even on a perfectly balanced dataset, accuracy is the wrong objective whenever the two mistakes have different consequences.

The common misconception is that the fix is to rebalance the training data so accuracy becomes valid again. Resampling changes the distribution the model sees, but if you then evaluate on rebalanced data your accuracy no longer describes performance in production, where the original prevalence still holds. The number becomes optimistic rather than meaningful. Evaluation should reflect the deployment distribution; class imbalance is handled in training and thresholding, not by editing the test set.

The decision rule is narrow. Accuracy is defensible when classes are roughly balanced, when the errors genuinely cost the same, and when you need one number a non-specialist can interpret without training. That triple condition holds in some benchmark settings and rarely in production. Otherwise, quote accuracy only next to the majority-class baseline so the reader can see the headroom, and lean on the metrics that separate the two error types. If a report shows accuracy alone with no baseline and no per-class breakdown, the correct response is to ask for the confusion matrix.

interview.question: Your team reports 99% accuracy on a detection task. What is your first question?
interview.answer: What fraction of the data is the positive class, because that gives the accuracy of a constant model that predicts the majority every time. If positives are 1% of the data, the trivial baseline is also 99% and the model has demonstrated nothing. Accuracy is only interpretable relative to that floor.

interview.question: Can accuracy be the wrong metric even when classes are balanced?
interview.answer: Yes, whenever the two error types have different costs. Accuracy weights a false positive and a false negative identically, so on a balanced fraud or diagnostic problem it will happily prefer a model that makes many expensive mistakes and few cheap ones. Balance fixes the base-rate problem, not the cost-asymmetry problem.

interview.question: Should you oversample the minority class in your test set so accuracy becomes meaningful?
interview.answer: No. The test set should mirror the distribution the model will actually see, otherwise no metric computed on it estimates production behaviour. Rebalancing the evaluation data makes accuracy look better without the model improving. Handle imbalance in training and threshold selection, and evaluate with metrics that are informative at the true prevalence.

children.deep_text:
Everything here is downstream of a single idea: a binary classifier's performance on a given test set is fully described by four counts, and every metric you have ever heard of is some arithmetic combination of those four. Start with the table itself, because without it the other topics are just formulas to memorise, and memorised formulas do not survive contact with a stakeholder asking why the numbers disagree.

From the table come the two ratios that matter most in practice. They point in opposite directions, and tightening the decision threshold improves one while degrading the other, which is why they are always discussed as a pair rather than individually.

Because managers and leaderboards want one number rather than two, there is a standard way to fuse the pair into a single score, with a knob that lets you say which of the two you weight more heavily. That is a convenience, and like all conveniences it hides information you sometimes need.

The two curve-based topics take a different approach: instead of fixing a threshold and reporting scores, they sweep the threshold across its whole range and summarise the resulting trade-off as an area under a curve. The two curves answer different questions and disagree sharply when one class is rare, which is why they are treated separately rather than as one topic.

Finally, there is an explicit treatment of why plain accuracy, the score everyone reaches for first, breaks down in the situations you most care about. Read that last: it lands harder once you know what the alternatives are.

children.title: Regression and Probabilistic Metrics
children.text: When a model predicts a number rather than a label, being wrong is no longer binary. A house price prediction off by five thousand and one off by five hundred thousand are both errors, and any useful metric has to distinguish them. That raises questions a classifier never faces: how heavily should large errors be punished relative to small ones, how do you express error as a fraction of something rather than in raw units, and if the model outputs a probability rather than a quantity, does that number mean what it claims. Those three questions organise this part.

children.title: MSE, RMSE, and MAE
children.text: Three ways to average how wrong a numeric prediction is. Mean squared error squares each error before averaging, so a single large miss dominates. Root mean squared error takes the square root of that, returning the number to the units of the target so it can be read directly. Mean absolute error just averages the size of the errors with no squaring, so every unit of error counts the same. The choice is not cosmetic: squaring says large errors are disproportionately bad, and absolute error says they are not.
children.deep_text:
Take a house price model evaluated on five properties, with errors in thousands of dollars of 10, 20, 10, 15, and 100. That last one is a mansion the model badly misjudged. Mean absolute error is (10 + 20 + 10 + 15 + 100) / 5 = 31. Mean squared error is (100 + 400 + 100 + 225 + 10000) / 5 = 2165, and RMSE is the square root of that, 46.5. Notice that the single 100 error contributes 10000 of the 10825 squared-error total, over 92% of the score, while contributing only 65% of the absolute-error total. Now suppose a second model trades that one bad prediction for slightly worse performance everywhere: errors of 25, 30, 25, 30, 40. Its MAE is 30, marginally better than 31. Its RMSE is 30.4, dramatically better than 46.5. Two metrics, opposite verdicts about which model to ship.

The gap between RMSE and MAE is itself a diagnostic. They are equal only when all errors have identical magnitude, and RMSE is always at least as large as MAE. A ratio near 1 means errors are uniform, and a ratio well above it, as with 46.5 against 31 above, means the total is being driven by a small number of large misses. That is worth checking before you tune anything, because it tells you whether to chase broad improvement or to go find the specific cases that are blowing up.

There is a deeper consequence people rarely notice. Because squared error is minimised by the conditional mean and absolute error by the conditional median, choosing MSE as your training loss makes the model predict an average, which is pulled by outliers, whereas absolute error makes it predict a typical value. If ten percent of your delivery-time labels are corrupted with impossible values, an MSE-trained model will shift all of its predictions to accommodate them, while an MAE-trained model largely ignores them. The metric you optimise changes what the model learns, not just how you score it.

The common misconception is that MSE and RMSE rank models differently. They cannot: the square root is monotonic, so any model with lower MSE has lower RMSE. MSE survives because it is smooth and convenient to differentiate; RMSE exists purely so humans can read the number. Report RMSE, optimise MSE, and never present both as if they were independent evidence.

The decision rule: use RMSE when large errors are genuinely disproportionately costly, which is common when the error feeds a physical or financial consequence that scales badly, such as underestimating peak power demand. Use MAE when your labels contain outliers or noise you do not want the model chasing, and when a stakeholder needs a number meaning "typically off by about this much". If the two disagree about which model wins, that disagreement is the actual finding, and you resolve it by asking what a large error really costs.

interview.question: When would you prefer MAE to RMSE?
interview.answer: When the target has outliers or noisy labels that you do not want to dominate either the score or the training signal. RMSE lets a handful of extreme cases determine which model looks best, which is right if those cases are genuinely catastrophic and wrong if they are data errors. MAE also communicates more cleanly to stakeholders as a typical error magnitude.

interview.question: Your RMSE is roughly twice your MAE. What does that tell you?
interview.answer: That the error distribution is heavy-tailed: most predictions are decent and a small subset are badly wrong. The two are equal only when all errors are the same size, so a large gap points at a distinct failing subpopulation rather than uniform mediocrity. The productive next step is to isolate the worst errors and look for what they have in common.

interview.question: Does it matter that you train on MSE but report MAE?
interview.answer: Yes, because they target different statistics. Squared error is minimised by the conditional mean and absolute error by the conditional median, so an MSE-trained model is systematically pulled toward outliers and will not be the best MAE model available. If MAE is what you are judged on, train on absolute error or a robust loss such as Huber.

children.title: R-Squared and Its Failure Modes
children.text: R-squared answers a specific question: how much of the variation in the target does the model explain, compared to just predicting the mean every time? It is one minus the ratio of the model's squared error to the squared error of that mean-only baseline. An R-squared of 0.8 means the model removed 80% of the variance the baseline left behind. Because it is a ratio it carries no units, which makes it comparable in ways raw error is not. It also has several failure modes serious enough that it should never be quoted alone.
children.deep_text:
Work it concretely. Suppose you predict house prices for 100 homes whose actual prices vary with a total sum of squared deviations from the mean of 500 million dollars-squared. Your model's total squared error is 100 million. R-squared is 1 minus 100/500 = 0.80. The baseline it is measured against is the constant model that guesses the average price for every house, so 0.80 means your model eliminated four fifths of the error that guessing the mean would have incurred. Zero means you matched that baseline, and negative values are entirely possible and simply mean you did worse than guessing the mean, which happens on test data more often than people admit.

The first failure mode is that R-squared never decreases when you add a feature, no matter how irrelevant. Add a column of random numbers to a linear regression and the fit can only improve or stay flat, because the model can always assign the new feature a coefficient of zero. Add enough random columns and R-squared marches toward 1.0 on the training set while the model learns nothing. Adjusted R-squared applies a penalty for the number of predictors and partly addresses this, but the real defence is computing R-squared on held-out data rather than on the data you fitted.

The second failure mode is dependence on the variance of your particular sample. The denominator is the spread of the targets in your test set, so the same model scores differently on different test sets. Evaluate a house price model across an entire country, where prices range enormously, and R-squared looks excellent. Evaluate the identical model within one neighbourhood where prices are tightly clustered and it collapses, possibly below zero, despite the predictions being just as accurate in dollar terms. This makes cross-dataset R-squared comparisons close to meaningless unless the target variances are comparable.

The common misconception is that high R-squared means the model is correct or that the relationship is causal. It measures variance explained under a squared-error criterion and nothing else. Anscombe's quartet is the classic demonstration that datasets with wildly different structures, one linear, one curved, one with a single dominating outlier, can produce identical fit statistics. A model with R-squared 0.9 can still be systematically biased in exactly the region you care about, and only a residual plot will reveal that.

The decision rule: use R-squared to communicate how much signal exists relative to a naive baseline, especially to an audience who will not know whether an RMSE of 46 is good. Do not use it to compare models across different datasets, do not use it as a training-set model selection criterion without adjustment, and never quote it without the corresponding error in real units next to it. R-squared says how much you beat the mean, RMSE says how wrong you actually are, and a decision usually needs both.

interview.question: Can R-squared be negative, and what does it mean?
interview.answer: Yes, on held-out data. It means the model's squared error exceeds that of simply predicting the training mean for every case, so the model is actively worse than a constant. It typically indicates severe overfitting or a distribution shift between train and test, and it is a strong signal to stop tuning and look at the data.

interview.question: Why is a higher R-squared on the training set not evidence of a better model?
interview.answer: Because it is monotonically non-decreasing in the number of features. Adding pure noise columns can only leave it flat or raise it, since the fitting procedure can always zero out a useless coefficient. Any comparison that uses training R-squared to choose between models of different complexity will systematically pick the most complex one.

interview.question: The same model scores 0.85 on one region's data and 0.2 on another's. What is happening?
interview.answer: Most likely the target variance differs between the regions, since it forms the denominator. Where prices or values are tightly clustered there is little variance to explain, so even accurate predictions yield a low ratio. Compare RMSE in the original units across the two regions to see whether the model's actual error changed at all.

children.title: Calibration of Predicted Probabilities
children.text: A model that outputs 0.8 is claiming something specific: among all cases it scores 0.8, the event should happen about eighty percent of the time. When that holds, the model is calibrated. Many models rank cases beautifully while being badly miscalibrated, systematically overconfident or underconfident, and nothing in a ranking metric will detect it. You check calibration by bucketing predictions and comparing each bucket's predicted probability to its observed frequency. It matters the moment a downstream system multiplies your probability by a cost, because then the number itself, not just its order, is load-bearing.
children.deep_text:
The check is mechanical. Take 10,000 predictions from a click model, sort them into ten buckets by predicted probability, and for each bucket compare the mean prediction against the fraction that actually clicked. If the 1,200 cases predicted around 0.30 clicked 298 times, an observed rate of 0.248, the model is overconfident in that region. Plot observed against predicted for all ten buckets and a perfectly calibrated model lies on the diagonal. A curve sagging below it means systematic overconfidence, and one bowing above it means the model is too timid. Summarise the gap with expected calibration error, the bucket-size-weighted average of the absolute differences, or score the whole thing with the Brier score, the mean squared difference between predicted probability and the zero-one outcome.

Why it goes wrong differs by model. A support vector machine's distance from the margin is not a probability at all and only resembles one after a transformation. Naive Bayes multiplies correlated features as though they were independent, which drives its outputs toward 0 and 1 and makes it notoriously overconfident. A random forest averages many trees and rarely produces extreme values, so it tends to be underconfident at both ends. Training with heavy class rebalancing or class weights shifts outputs away from true prevalence too. The fixes are post-hoc: Platt scaling fits a logistic function mapping raw scores to probabilities, and isotonic regression fits a free monotonic mapping, which is more flexible and needs more data to avoid overfitting. Both must be fitted on a held-out calibration split, never the training data.

The common misconception is that a high AUC implies good probabilities. It does not, and the reason is structural: both Platt scaling and isotonic regression are monotonic transformations, so applying them leaves the ranking, and therefore the AUC, completely unchanged while potentially fixing the probabilities entirely. Discrimination and calibration are separate axes, and a model can be excellent on one and useless on the other. The converse also holds: a model that always outputs the base rate is perfectly calibrated and has no discriminative power whatsoever, so calibration alone is never sufficient either.

The decision rule: calibration matters whenever the probability is consumed as a number rather than as a rank. Expected-value calculations, insurance and credit pricing, medical risk communication, bidding systems that multiply a predicted click probability by a bid, and any threshold set from a cost analysis rather than a validation sweep. It matters much less if you only ever take the top-k results or compare scores against each other, since a monotonic distortion is harmless there. Check it cheaply with a reliability plot before shipping any model whose output leaves your system as a number, and keep a calibration split aside for that purpose from the start.

interview.question: Why can a model with excellent AUC still be dangerous to deploy?
interview.answer: Because AUC only measures ordering, and any monotonic distortion of the scores leaves it untouched. A model can rank every positive above every negative while reporting 0.95 for cases that occur half the time. If a downstream system multiplies that number by a cost or a bid, the ranking being right does not save you.

interview.question: When would you not bother calibrating?
interview.answer: When the probability is only ever used comparatively: retrieving the top ten results, ranking a feed, or picking a threshold empirically on a validation set. A monotonic recalibration cannot change any of those outcomes. Spend the held-out data elsewhere and revisit the decision if a consumer of the score starts treating it as a real probability.

interview.question: Platt scaling or isotonic regression?
interview.answer: Platt scaling when calibration data is limited or the miscalibration looks like a smooth sigmoidal squash, since fitting two parameters is hard to overfit. Isotonic regression when you have a few thousand held-out examples and the distortion has an irregular shape, because it can fit any monotonic mapping. Either way, fit on a dedicated split, since fitting on training predictions reproduces the original overconfidence.

children.deep_text:
Continuous predictions bring in magnitude, and magnitude forces choices that discrete labels do not.

The first topic covers the family of average-error metrics. They differ mainly in how they treat outliers: squaring errors before averaging makes a few large misses dominate the score, while averaging absolute errors treats every unit of error the same regardless of where it occurs. That is not a technicality, it is a statement about what you consider a serious failure, and it also determines which quantity of the target distribution the model is implicitly trying to predict.

The second topic addresses a different need. Average-error metrics carry the units of the target, which makes them concrete but makes them impossible to compare across problems, and impossible to interpret without knowing how much the target varies in the first place. The standard fix normalises the model's error against the variance of the data, producing a unitless proportion. That normalisation is genuinely useful and also introduces failure modes severe enough to need explicit treatment.

The third topic is different in kind. When a model outputs a probability, you can ask whether that probability is honest: among all the cases assigned 0.8, does the event actually happen about eighty percent of the time. This is orthogonal to whether the model ranks cases correctly, so it needs its own tooling and its own metrics. It matters whenever a downstream system multiplies the probability by a cost, which covers most decision systems that do anything more sophisticated than thresholding.

The order is deliberate: raw error, then normalised error, then the reliability of probabilistic outputs.

children.title: Choosing Between Models
children.text: Having a metric is not the same as having a decision. Two candidates produce two numbers, one is higher, and none of that tells you whether to ship it. You still need something to compare against so you know whether either candidate is worth anything at all, a way to tell a real gap from sampling noise, an honest accounting of what the two kinds of mistake actually cost your organisation, and a tiebreaker for when two models are genuinely close. Those four considerations, in that order, turn a leaderboard into an engineering decision.

children.title: Baselines and Why You Always Need One
children.text: A baseline is the score of something so simple it required no modelling: predict the majority class, predict the training mean, predict yesterday's value, or use the rule the business already runs on. Its job is to convert an uninterpretable number into a comparison. RMSE of 46 means nothing on its own; RMSE of 46 against a baseline of 48 means your model has bought you almost nothing for all its complexity. Baselines also catch pipeline bugs early, because a sophisticated model that cannot beat a constant usually indicates a broken feature join rather than a hard problem.

contract.must_cover: Baselines and Why You Always Need One
must_not_cover: The Cost of Errors Is Rarely Symmetric

children.deep_text:
Build them in a specific order of ambition. Start with the trivial statistical baseline: for classification, predict the most common class; for regression, predict the training mean or median; for time series, predict the previous observed value, which is remarkably hard to beat. Then add the domain baseline: whatever heuristic or rules engine the business is currently using, since that is the thing you actually have to outperform to justify a deployment. Then, if you are building something complex, add a simple-model baseline like logistic regression or a shallow gradient-boosted tree on the obvious features, because a large neural network that ties a linear model on tabular data is a strong hint to stop.

A concrete case makes the point. A demand forecasting model reports RMSE of 120 units. Impressive or not? Compute the baselines. Predicting last week's demand gives RMSE 130, and predicting the trailing four-week mean gives 118. The sophisticated model is losing to a four-line function. That is a decision, not a diagnostic detail: you ship the four-line function, or you go back and find out why the model is not capturing what the moving average captures.

The common misconception is that baselines are a formality for a report, computed after the model is built to make the results look good. The value is almost entirely diagnostic and it is front-loaded. Compute baselines before you train anything. They tell you the achievable headroom, so you know whether an eight-week modelling effort has room to earn its cost. They tell you whether your evaluation harness works, because if the majority-class baseline scores something impossible, the harness is broken. And when a complex model comes in below the trivial baseline, the cause is nearly always a leak, a misaligned join, or a label shifted by one row, and you find that in an afternoon rather than after the launch review.

Baselines also give you the vocabulary to say no. "The new model improves recall by 0.4 points over the existing rules engine while adding a GPU dependency and a retraining pipeline" is a sentence that ends a project cleanly and honestly. Without the baseline you only have "the model achieves 0.83 recall", which sounds like progress regardless of whether it is.

The decision rule is unconditional: every evaluation reports at least one baseline, and the baseline set is built before the model. The only judgement call is which baselines are worth including, and the answer is the trivial one plus whatever the system in production does today. If your model cannot beat both by a margin that survives the significance check, you do not have a result yet.

interview.question: Why compute baselines before training rather than after?
interview.answer: Because they tell you the headroom and validate your evaluation harness before you spend weeks on modelling. Knowing that a moving average already achieves most of the achievable accuracy changes whether the project is worth starting. Computed afterwards, a baseline only confirms or embarrasses a decision you have already made.

interview.question: Your deep model underperforms a majority-class classifier. What do you check first?
interview.answer: The data pipeline, not the model. A model with capacity to fit the training set that cannot beat a constant almost always indicates a broken feature join, misaligned labels, a train-test leak that inverted, or a preprocessing step dropping signal. Hyperparameters are the last thing to suspect, not the first.

interview.question: What baseline would you use for a time series forecasting problem?
interview.answer: The persistence forecast, predicting the last observed value, and a seasonal version predicting the value from the same point in the previous cycle. They are trivially cheap and they are surprisingly strong, since most series are highly autocorrelated. Any forecasting model that cannot clearly beat both has not demonstrated that it learned anything about the dynamics.

children.title: Statistical Significance of Model Differences
children.text: Model A scores 0.847 and model B scores 0.851 on your test set. That gap is real only if it would survive a different test set drawn from the same distribution, and often it would not. A test set is a finite sample, so every score carries sampling error, and the difference between two scores carries more. Treating a fourth-decimal improvement as a result is how teams ship rewrites that were noise. The tools are standard: bootstrap the test set to get confidence intervals, or use a paired test that exploits the fact both models saw identical examples.

must_not_cover: Baselines and Why You Always Need One
The Cost of Errors Is Rarely Symmetric

children.deep_text:
Start with a rough sense of scale. With a test set of 1000 examples and an accuracy near 0.85, the standard error is roughly the square root of 0.85 times 0.15 divided by 1000, about 0.011. A 95% interval spans roughly plus or minus 2.2 points, so 0.847 against 0.851 is comfortably inside the noise. To distinguish a half-point difference reliably you need tens of thousands of evaluation examples, which is a fact worth internalising before you start celebrating small gains.

The practical tool is the bootstrap, because it works for any metric including ones with no closed-form variance such as AUC or F1. Resample the test set with replacement to the same size, compute both models' scores on that resample, record the difference, and repeat several thousand times. You now have a distribution of the difference. If its 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles straddle zero, you cannot claim one model is better. Crucially, compute the difference within each resample rather than bootstrapping each model separately, because both models are being evaluated on the same examples and that shared variation cancels out. Ignoring the pairing throws away most of your statistical power.

The same pairing logic drives McNemar's test for classifiers. It ignores every example both models got right and every example both got wrong, since those carry no information about which is better, and looks only at the disagreements: cases where A was right and B wrong, against cases where B was right and A wrong. If those counts are 40 and 25, the question is whether 40 versus 25 is meaningfully lopsided, and the test answers it directly. For cross-validated comparisons, the folds overlap in training data so the fold scores are not independent, and a naive paired t-test over folds is anticonservative, reporting significance too readily. Corrected variants exist; the safer habit is to use a held-out test set for the final claim.

The common misconception is that a p-value below 0.05 means the difference matters. It means the difference is probably not zero, which is a much weaker claim. With a million evaluation examples, a 0.0004 improvement can be highly significant and completely irrelevant to anyone. Report the effect size and its confidence interval, not just the verdict, and ask separately whether an improvement of that magnitude justifies the added complexity and operational cost.

A second trap is multiplicity. Comparing twenty hyperparameter configurations and reporting the best one against the baseline means you have run twenty tests, and the winner is selected precisely for having got lucky. Selection on the test set invalidates the test. Choose the configuration on validation data and touch the test set once.

The decision rule: for gaps under roughly one percentage point on a test set of a few thousand examples, assume noise until a paired bootstrap says otherwise. For larger gaps, the interval still belongs in the report, because the reader needs to know the precision of the estimate to weigh it against the deployment cost.

interview.question: Why use a paired test rather than comparing two independent confidence intervals?
interview.answer: Because both models were evaluated on the same examples, so much of the variation is shared and cancels when you take the difference per example. Comparing two separate intervals and checking for overlap is a much weaker test and will miss real differences. Pairing typically gives substantially more power for the same amount of data.

interview.question: You ran a 20-configuration sweep and the best one beats the baseline with p = 0.03. Do you believe it?
interview.answer: Not on its own. Selecting the maximum of twenty comparisons and then testing that maximum inflates the false positive rate well beyond the nominal level. The right procedure is to select on validation data and then evaluate the single chosen configuration once on the untouched test set, or to apply a multiple-comparison correction.

interview.question: When would you accept a difference that is not statistically significant?
interview.answer: When the models are effectively tied on the metric but differ on something else that matters, such as inference cost, latency, interpretability, or maintenance burden. A non-significant result says the metric does not distinguish them, which is licence to decide on other grounds. It is never licence to claim the higher-scoring model is better.

children.title: The Cost of Errors Is Rarely Symmetric
children.text: Metrics count mistakes. Businesses pay for them, and the two prices are almost never the same. Missing a fraudulent transaction costs the value of the fraud plus a chargeback; blocking a legitimate one costs a few minutes of support time and some goodwill. Once you write those costs down, model selection stops being about which candidate scores higher and becomes an expected-cost calculation, which frequently picks a different model and almost always picks a different threshold. The hard part is not the arithmetic; it is getting anyone to commit to a number for what a mistake is worth.

contract.must_cover: The Cost of Errors Is Rarely Symmetric
must_not_cover: Baselines and Why You Always Need One

children.deep_text:
Do it with numbers. A fraud detector sees 1000 transactions with 10 frauds averaging 500 dollars each. A missed fraud costs 500 dollars. A false alarm costs 20 dollars in review time and customer friction. At its current threshold the model catches 7 frauds and raises 11 false alarms: expected cost is 3 misses times 500, plus 11 false alarms times 20, which is 1500 + 220 = 1720 dollars. Now loosen the threshold so it catches 9 frauds at the cost of 40 false alarms: 1 times 500 plus 40 times 20 = 500 + 800 = 1300 dollars. The looser threshold is worse by precision, worse by accuracy, and 420 dollars a day better for the business. Loosen further to catch all 10 at 90 false alarms and you get 0 + 1800 = 1800, worse again. The cost curve has a minimum, and finding it is the actual optimisation problem.

The general form is straightforward: expected cost equals the count of false negatives times their unit cost plus the count of false positives times theirs, evaluated at each candidate threshold, and you pick the minimum. What this formalises is that the optimal threshold shifts toward flagging more cases in proportion to how much more a miss costs than a false alarm. When the ratio is 25 to 1, as above, the threshold should sit far from the naive 0.5.

This also reaches back into training. Most libraries accept class or sample weights, and setting them from the cost ratio rather than from class frequencies makes the model optimise something closer to what you actually pay. Threshold adjustment on a well-calibrated model is usually the simpler route to the same destination, since it needs no retraining when the costs change.

The common misconception is that costs must be known precisely for this to be worthwhile. They almost never are, and it matters less than people fear, because the result is insensitive to exact values and sensitive mainly to the ratio. Even an order-of-magnitude estimate, a miss costs roughly twenty times a false alarm, moves the threshold somewhere materially better than the default. Run the calculation across a plausible range of ratios; if the same threshold wins for ratios from 10 to 50, you can stop arguing about the number.

Some costs resist pricing, and you should be explicit rather than pretend. Reputational damage, regulatory exposure, and harm to an individual user are hard to denominate in dollars. Handle those as constraints rather than costs: minimise expected financial cost subject to a false negative rate below a hard ceiling.

The decision rule: any system whose outputs trigger an action with a material consequence deserves this analysis before the threshold is set. It takes an hour, it usually moves the operating point substantially, and it replaces an argument about metrics with a conversation about money.

interview.question: How do you set a decision threshold when you have cost estimates?
interview.answer: Sweep the threshold across its range, and at each point compute expected cost as false negatives times the cost of a miss plus false positives times the cost of a false alarm, using counts from a held-out set. Choose the minimum. The result depends mainly on the ratio of the two costs, so precise absolute figures are less important than getting the ratio roughly right.

interview.question: The business will not give you a cost for a missed detection. What do you do?
interview.answer: Invert the question and present the trade-off instead. Show what each candidate threshold implies in concrete operational terms, so many extra alerts to review in exchange for so many more detections, and let them choose a point. That is an implicit cost ratio, and people commit to a trade-off far more readily than to a dollar figure for a bad outcome.

interview.question: When would you use class weights during training instead of just adjusting the threshold?
interview.answer: When the model is not well calibrated or lacks capacity to represent the rare class properly, since in those cases no threshold recovers a good operating point. Weighting changes what the model learns rather than only how you cut its output. The downside is that it distorts the predicted probabilities and requires retraining whenever the costs change, so threshold adjustment on a calibrated model is usually the first thing to try.

children.title: Occam's Razor and Model Simplicity
children.text: When two models perform about the same, take the simpler one. This is not aesthetic preference. A simpler model has fewer parameters to have quietly fitted noise, so its held-out score is more likely to reflect real signal and to hold up when the data shifts. It is also cheaper to serve, faster to debug at three in the morning, easier to explain to a regulator, and less likely to break when a feature pipeline changes. The complexity has to earn its place with a measured improvement that matters, not a plausible story about capacity.

must_not_cover: Baselines and Why You Always Need One
The Cost of Errors Is Rarely Symmetric

children.deep_text:
The statistical argument comes first. A model with more free parameters can fit more patterns, including patterns that exist only in your particular training sample. Two models scoring 0.84 and 0.845 on a test set are not equally likely to score that on next month's data: the one with three hundred parameters has less room to have absorbed sampling noise than the one with thirty million, so its estimate is the more trustworthy of the two. This is why regularisation works at all, and why the razor is a defensible prior rather than a slogan.

The engineering argument usually dominates in practice. Consider a real choice: a gradient-boosted tree on twelve features scoring 0.847 AUC against a deep model on four hundred features scoring 0.851. The gap is four thousandths, likely within sampling noise on a typical test set. The second option brings a GPU serving dependency, a feature store with four hundred columns that each need monitoring for drift, retraining that takes eight hours instead of four minutes, and no way to answer a customer asking why they were declined. Priced honestly, the simpler model wins decisively and the comparison is not close.

The common misconception is that Occam's razor means always choosing the simplest model available. It does not. It is a tiebreaker, and it only applies when the performance difference is genuinely negligible. If the complex model is five points better on a metric that maps to real money, complexity is exactly what you should buy, and refusing it on principle is as much an error as reaching for a transformer to fit a straight line. The razor tells you what to do when the evidence is indifferent, not how to ignore evidence.

A subtler version of the mistake is counting the wrong thing. Parameter count is a poor proxy for complexity. A deep network trained with strong regularisation and early stopping can have a smaller effective capacity than an unregularised polynomial with far fewer coefficients. What matters is how much the model can adapt to noise, which is why techniques like cross-validated selection and information criteria such as AIC and BIC try to penalise fitted flexibility rather than raw parameter counts.

The decision rule to actually use: when the confidence interval on the performance difference includes zero, or the difference is real but too small to change any downstream decision, take the simpler model. When the difference is real and material, take the better model and be honest about the operational cost you have just accepted. In the middle, ask what the improvement is worth in the units the business cares about, and compare that to a year of maintenance. That framing settles most of these arguments in about ten minutes.

interview.question: Your complex model beats the simple one by 0.4 points of AUC. Which do you ship?
interview.answer: It depends on whether that gap survives a paired bootstrap and whether it translates into anything anyone cares about. If the interval on the difference includes zero, the models are tied and simplicity decides. If it is real but worth less than the ongoing cost of a second serving stack and a larger feature pipeline, simplicity still decides.

interview.question: Is parameter count a good measure of model complexity?
interview.answer: Not really. What matters is effective capacity, how much the model can contort itself to fit noise, and regularisation, early stopping, and parameter sharing all reduce that without reducing the count. A heavily regularised large network can generalise better than a small unconstrained one. Cross-validated performance stability is a more honest measure than any parameter tally.

interview.question: When is preferring the simpler model the wrong call?
interview.answer: When the performance difference is real, comfortably outside noise, and maps to material value, or when the simple model has a structural blind spot such as being unable to represent interactions that clearly exist in the data. The razor is a tiebreaker for indifferent evidence, not a licence to discard a genuine improvement because the winning model is harder to maintain.

children.deep_text:
The metrics sections tell you how to score a model. This part is about what to do with the scores, and it decomposes into four questions that get asked roughly in sequence.

First, a score means nothing in isolation. Before comparing two models to each other you need a floor: the performance of something trivial that required no modelling effort. Without that reference, an impressive-looking number can represent zero learned signal, and you have no basis for judging whether the complexity you are about to take on is buying anything.

Second, once you have two real candidates, the difference between their scores is itself an estimate computed on a finite sample. Small gaps evaporate on a different test split. Deciding whether an observed difference reflects a genuine improvement or the particular examples that happened to land in evaluation is a statistical question with standard tools, and skipping it is how teams end up shipping a rewrite that was noise.

Third, aggregate scores flatten the fact that different mistakes have wildly different consequences. A model that is worse on the headline metric can be clearly better once the errors are priced correctly, and making those prices explicit often changes both the model choice and the threshold you deploy at.

Fourth, when candidates are genuinely close after all of that, there is a principled tiebreaker. The simpler model is preferred, not out of aesthetics but because simplicity buys you things that do not appear in the metric: cheaper inference, easier debugging, fewer failure modes, and less capacity to have fitted noise.

They compose naturally: establish a floor, verify the gap is real, price the errors, then break ties on simplicity.

Evaluation is where most real machine learning projects quietly fail. The training loop converges, the notebook prints a number, and nobody asks whether that number is the one the business actually cares about. This section is organised around the three distinct decisions you have to make.

The first is classification metrics. When a model emits a discrete label, all the information about its errors lives in a small table of counts, and every familiar score is a different ratio pulled out of that table. Understanding which ratio answers which question, and which ones stop being informative when one class is rare, is the whole content of that part.

The second is regression and probabilistic metrics. Here the model emits a real number or a probability, so errors have magnitude rather than just presence.
