interview.answer: Almost certainly feature retrieval and serialisation, not the model. I would break down the span into feature-store round trips, any synchronous calls to upstream services, and payload parsing. Common fixes are batching the lookups into one multi-get, caching entity-level features that change slowly, and precomputing anything expensive into a materialised aggregate rather than deriving it in the handler.

interview.question: What is the risk of a hybrid design where some features come from a nightly table and some are computed live?
interview.answer: You get two different notions of time inside one feature vector, and the model was trained on whatever combination the training pipeline happened to produce. If training used same-timestamp values for all features but serving mixes day-old aggregates with live ones, the relationships the model learned no longer hold. It is manageable, but the training set has to be constructed with the same staleness pattern the serving path will have.

children.title: Feature Stores
children.text: A feature store is a system where a feature is defined once and then served two ways: as a historical table for building training sets, and as a low-latency lookup for scoring live requests. The point is that both come from the same definition, so a feature cannot mean one thing in the training job and something subtly different in the request handler. The second thing it buys you is reuse. If three teams each independently compute days_since_last_purchase, you have three slightly different definitions and three chances to be wrong; a store gives you one, with an owner and a schema.
children.deep_text:
Picture a lending team defining a feature called applicant_income_12mo_avg. In the store it is registered with an entity key of applicant_id, a transformation over a source table, and a freshness contract, say updated hourly. Two things then happen automatically. The offline side materialises a history of that feature with timestamps, so that when a data scientist asks for a training set of ten thousand loan applications, the store performs a point-in-time join and returns, for each application, the value of the feature as it stood at the moment of that application rather than its value today. The online side keeps the current value per applicant in a key-value store, so the scoring service does a single lookup by applicant_id. The same registered definition produced both.

The point-in-time join is the part that is genuinely hard to build yourself and the main reason teams adopt a store rather than two hand-rolled pipelines. Doing it wrong is subtle: joining a training set to an aggregate table on entity id alone, with no timestamp condition, gives every historical row today's value and leaks the future into the past. A store makes the correct join the default rather than the thing you remember to do.

A store typically also gives you a registry with lineage and ownership, so you can answer who defined this, what upstream tables it reads, and which models currently consume it. That last question is what makes it safe to change a feature at all.

The common misconception is that a feature store is a database. It is not; it is a definition layer plus two materialisation paths, usually sitting on top of a warehouse for offline and something like Redis or DynamoDB for online. Buying one does not make features good. If your team computes features in the request handler from raw payloads, adopting a store changes nothing until the definitions actually move into it.

The decision rule: a feature store earns its keep when you have online inference, multiple models sharing features, or a real need for point-in-time correct training sets. If you have one batch model owned by one team, a well-documented SQL pipeline plus a scheduled materialisation gives you most of the benefit at a fraction of the operational cost. Adopting a store to serve a single nightly scoring job is infrastructure looking for a problem.

interview.question: What problem does a feature store solve that a well-organised set of SQL pipelines does not?
interview.answer: Two things: guaranteed consistency between the offline training path and the online serving path from a single definition, and correct point-in-time joins when assembling training sets. Plain SQL pipelines can do both, but nothing enforces it, so the training query and the serving query drift apart over time. The store makes the consistent behaviour the default rather than a convention someone has to maintain.

interview.question: When would you tell a team not to adopt one?
interview.answer: When they have a single batch model, one team owning the features, and no online serving. The operational cost of running offline and online materialisation, plus a registry, is substantial, and a documented pipeline with a scheduled refresh covers the same ground. I would revisit the decision when a second model wants to reuse the features or when online inference appears.

interview.question: How does a feature store help you change an existing feature safely?
interview.answer: The registry tells you which models currently consume the feature, which is the question you cannot answer with ad hoc pipelines. Usually you register the modified logic as a new version rather than editing in place, backfill its history, retrain and evaluate consumers against it, and migrate them one at a time. Editing a live definition in place silently changes the inputs of every model reading it.

children.title: Model Serialisation and Versioning
children.text: Serialisation is turning a fitted model into bytes you can move to another machine; versioning is knowing which of those byte blobs answered a given request. Both matter more than they sound. A pickle file carries no record of the library version that wrote it, so an environment upgrade can make it refuse to load or, worse, load and behave differently. And a model saved as model_final_v2.pkl on someone's laptop is not something you can roll back to. What you want is an immutable artefact with an identifier, its training inputs recorded, and that identifier attached to every prediction it makes.
children.deep_text:
Python's pickle serialises object references, not a self-describing model. Unpickle a scikit-learn estimator under a different library version and you may get an outright failure, a warning, or silently different behaviour because an internal attribute was renamed or a default changed. The standard mitigation is to pin the environment alongside the artefact: store the model bytes together with the exact library versions and, ideally, ship them in the same container image used to train. The alternative is an interchange format such as ONNX or PMML, which describes the computation graph rather than Python objects, so it survives an environment change and can be executed by a runtime in another language. The cost is that not every estimator or custom transformer converts cleanly, and you should verify a converted model reproduces the original's predictions on a held-out sample before trusting it.

A useful concrete setup: on every training run, write an artefact to immutable storage under a content hash or a run id, and record alongside it the training data snapshot identifier, the code commit, the hyperparameters, the environment lockfile, and the evaluation metrics. Then have the serving layer resolve a symbolic alias, say fraud-scorer:production, to a specific run id, and stamp that run id into every prediction log line. When somebody asks in three weeks why a particular transaction was declined, you can identify exactly which artefact scored it. Rolling back is then repointing the alias, which is seconds, rather than rerunning a training job, which is hours.

The common misconception is that versioning the model file is enough. It is not: the same code and the same hyperparameters on different data produce a different model, and the same data with a different preprocessing commit produces a different model. The version identity of a deployed model is the tuple of artefact, code, data snapshot, and environment. If any of the four is unrecorded you cannot reproduce or reason about the artefact.

The decision rule: pickle plus a pinned container is fine when the same team trains and serves in the same language and you control the runtime. Reach for an interchange format when the serving runtime is a different language, when you need to embed the model in a mobile or edge target, or when you must keep old models loadable across years of library upgrades. Either way, never let an alias point at a mutable path, and never deploy an artefact whose training run you cannot identify.

interview.question: What are the risks of pickling a scikit-learn model and loading it in your serving environment?
interview.answer: Pickle stores references to classes rather than a self-describing graph, so a version mismatch between the training and serving environments can fail to load or silently change behaviour. It also executes code on load, so an artefact from an untrusted source is a remote code execution risk. The usual mitigations are pinning the environment and shipping the model inside the same image used to train it, or converting to an interchange format when the serving runtime differs.

interview.question: A model in production started behaving differently and nobody deployed anything. How do you find out what changed?
interview.answer: I would check whether the artefact identity actually stayed fixed, which requires the run id to be stamped on prediction logs; a common cause is an alias pointing at a mutable path that a retraining job overwrote. If the artefact really is unchanged, the change is upstream, in the feature data or a dependency, and I would compare recent input distributions against the ones logged before the shift.

interview.question: What do you need to record for a model version to be genuinely reproducible?
interview.answer: The artefact itself, the code commit that trained it, an identifier for the exact training data snapshot, the hyperparameters, and the environment lockfile. Missing any one of these means you can describe the model but not rebuild it. Recording metrics alongside is what makes the record useful later when comparing candidates.

children.deep_text:
These four topics are not a random list of ops chores; they are one problem seen from four angles. The central problem is that training and serving are two different programs operating on the same conceptual data, and every difference between them is a potential bug that your test set cannot catch.

Training-Serving Skew names the failure directly and is the right place to start, because it gives you the vocabulary for why the other three exist. Once you understand how a feature computed one way in a batch job and another way in a request handler silently degrades a model, the rest of the subsection reads as a set of responses.

Batch versus online inference is the architectural fork. It determines whether features are computed ahead of time over a whole table or on demand for a single entity, and that choice cascades into latency budgets, freshness guarantees, and which skew risks you inherit. Read it second because it frames the constraints the remaining topics operate under.

Feature stores are the organisational answer to skew: define a feature once, materialise it for both paths, and guarantee the training set sees the values that were current at the time of the historical event rather than today's values. They only make sense after you have felt the problem they solve.

Model serialisation and versioning is the last mile. It covers turning a fitted estimator into a portable artefact and tracking which artefact answered which request, so that when monitoring later tells you something regressed, you can identify what changed and roll back deliberately rather than by guesswork.

children.title: Monitoring and Maintenance
children.text: A deployed model is a perishable asset. It encodes relationships that held in the data it was trained on, and the world it operates in does not agree to stay still. Worse, the thing you most want to watch, accuracy, is usually invisible in real time because the labels arrive weeks later or never arrive at all. So production monitoring is largely the craft of inferring health from what you can see. This part covers what actually shifts underneath a model, what you measure when you have no labels, what should trigger a retrain, and how to release the replacement without betting all your traffic on it at once.

children.title: Data Drift and Concept Drift
children.text: Data drift is the input distribution moving: the users, transactions, or documents arriving today do not look like the ones you trained on. Concept drift is the relationship changing: the same inputs now imply a different outcome. These need separating because the responses differ. Data drift on a feature the model barely uses is harmless noise. Concept drift is always a real problem, because whatever mapping the model learned is now partly wrong. And concept drift can occur with input distributions that look completely stable, which is exactly why watching inputs alone gives false comfort.
children.deep_text:
Concretely, a credit risk model trained on applications from a company's original market sees its input mix shift when marketing opens a new region: median applicant age drops, a previously rare employment category becomes common, and one feature that was almost never null is now null a third of the time. That is data drift. The model may still be roughly correct on each individual applicant; it is just being asked about a population it saw little of, so its predictions in that region carry more uncertainty. If the new region's applicants land in regions of feature space the training data covered densely, the impact can be near zero.

Concept drift looks different. Suppose interest rates rise sharply. Applicants with identical income, tenure, and debt-to-income now default at a materially higher rate than the same profile did last year. The input distribution barely moved; the conditional distribution of the outcome given the inputs did. Every threshold calibrated on the old relationship is now mis-set, and the model will systematically under-predict risk until it is retrained on data from the new regime.

Drift also has characteristic shapes worth recognising. Sudden drift is a discrete break, typically caused by something in your own systems, an upstream schema change, a new app release that stops sending a field, a partner API that starts returning codes in a different case. Gradual drift is a slow population shift over months. Recurring drift is seasonal: retail features in December do not resemble features in February, and retraining on the anomaly rather than accommodating it makes things worse.

The common misconception is that drift detection is a sufficient health check. It is not: statistical tests over large traffic volumes flag differences that are statistically significant and practically irrelevant, so a raw p-value alarm on a high-volume feature fires constantly. Weight drift alerts by the feature's importance to the model, use effect-size measures such as population stability index or a Wasserstein distance rather than significance alone, and set thresholds from observed historical variation rather than from a textbook default.

The decision rule: on a data drift alert, first check whether it is an upstream data bug rather than the world moving, because a sudden break in one feature almost always is. If the data is genuinely fine and the drifted features matter, treat it as a signal to look, not an instruction to retrain. Concept drift, when you can confirm it against arriving labels, is a direct instruction to retrain on recent data, and usually to reweight or window the training set toward the new regime.

interview.question: Why is it not enough to monitor input distributions alone?
interview.answer: Because concept drift changes the relationship between inputs and the target while leaving the inputs looking identical, so no input-side test will fire. A rate change or a policy change can make the same applicant profile carry different risk with a stable feature distribution. Input monitoring catches population shifts and upstream data bugs, which is valuable, but it has a blind spot exactly where the damage is worst.

interview.question: A drift test on one of your features fires every day. What do you do?
interview.answer: First check whether it is practically meaningful: with high traffic, significance tests detect differences far too small to affect predictions. I would switch to an effect-size measure like PSI, weight the alert by that feature's importance in the model, and calibrate the threshold from historical week-to-week variation. If it still fires constantly on an important feature, I would look upstream for an unstable data source before assuming the world is moving.

interview.question: How would you distinguish a genuine population shift from an upstream data bug?
interview.answer: The shape and timing. Bugs are almost always sudden and localised, appearing as a step change in one or two features at a deploy or schedule boundary, often accompanied by a jump in null rate or a change in category casing. Genuine shifts are usually gradual and correlated across several features that plausibly move together. I would check the deploy log and the upstream schema before concluding anything about the world.

children.title: Monitoring Models Without Ground Truth
children.text: In most production systems you do not learn whether a prediction was right for weeks, and often you never learn at all. A loan default takes months to materialise. A fraud decision that blocked a transaction has no counterfactual. So the accuracy dashboard you would like to have does not exist. What you monitor instead is everything upstream and downstream of the label: the distribution of the inputs going in, the distribution of the scores coming out, the rate at which features are missing, and whatever business consequence follows quickly enough to observe. These are proxies, and knowing their limits is the skill.
children.deep_text:
Start with the prediction distribution, because it is cheap and surprisingly informative. Log the score for every request and track the histogram, not just the mean. A fraud model that has been emitting scores above 0.8 on roughly 2% of traffic for months and jumps to 6% overnight has told you something real, even though not one of those transactions has a label yet. Similarly, a model whose score distribution collapses toward a single value usually means a feature stopped arriving and every request is hitting the same default path. Track the rate at which each feature is null or defaulted, per feature, as a first-class metric; in practice it catches more incidents than any distributional test.

On the input side you compare the live feature distribution against a fixed training reference and against a recent rolling window. The reference comparison tells you how far you have travelled from the model's training world; the rolling comparison tells you what changed this week. Both are useful and they answer different questions.

Some proxies are stronger than distributional checks. Delayed labels still arrive, so build the pipeline to backfill them and compute true accuracy on a lag, accepting that it reports on last month. Where a fast downstream signal correlates with correctness, use it: click-through on a recommendation, whether a flagged case was confirmed by a human reviewer, whether a routed ticket got reassigned. Sampling for manual labelling is the underrated option; having reviewers label a few hundred stratified predictions a week gives a real, if noisy, accuracy estimate on a schedule you control.

The common misconception is that a stable prediction distribution means the model is fine. It does not. A model can emit a perfectly stable score histogram while being wrong about which specific entities get which score, because the mapping changed and the marginal did not. Distributional monitoring is a smoke detector, not a thermometer: it reliably catches breakage and reliably misses degradation.

A second trap is feedback loops corrupting your proxies. If the model blocks transactions it scores as fraud, you never see whether those would have been fraud, and the labels you do collect describe only the transactions the model let through. Any accuracy computed on that population is biased. Reserving a small random holdout that bypasses the model's decision is the standard remedy, expensive but the only clean source of unbiased labels.

The decision rule: instrument prediction distributions, per-feature null rates, and input drift on day one, because they cost almost nothing and catch the loud failures. Add a delayed-label evaluation and a small human-labelled sample when the cost of quiet degradation is high. Do not let a green monitoring dashboard substitute for a periodic honest evaluation against real labels.

interview.question: Labels for your model arrive 90 days late. What do you monitor in the meantime?
interview.answer: Input feature distributions against both the training reference and a recent rolling window, the full prediction score histogram rather than just its mean, and per-feature null or default rates, which in practice catch the most incidents. I would add any fast downstream proxy that correlates with correctness, such as human reviewer agreement on flagged cases. In parallel I would build the backfill so that when labels do land, true accuracy is computed on a lag rather than not at all.

interview.question: The score distribution is unchanged but you suspect the model has degraded. Is that possible, and how would you check?
interview.answer: Yes. The marginal distribution of scores can stay identical while the assignment of scores to entities becomes wrong, which is what concept drift looks like from the outside. I would check by getting real labels on a sample, either from delayed labels that have arrived or from a stratified batch sent for manual review, since no input-side or output-side distributional check can detect that failure.

interview.question: Why can the labels you collect in production be biased, and what do you do about it?
interview.answer: Because the model's own decisions filter which outcomes you get to observe. If it blocks the transactions it scores highest, those never generate an outcome, so accuracy computed on the surviving population understates the model's error on exactly the cases it cares about. The standard fix is a small random holdout that bypasses the model's action, which is costly but the only unbiased sample available.

children.title: Retraining Cadence and Triggers
children.text: Retraining is not free and not automatically an improvement, so the real question is what policy decides when it happens. Two policies exist. Scheduled retraining runs on a calendar, weekly or monthly, whether or not anything changed. Triggered retraining fires when a monitored signal crosses a threshold: measured performance falls, an important feature drifts materially, or enough new labelled data has accumulated to be worth using. Most mature systems run both, with a schedule as the floor and triggers for the surprises. The hard part is not the pipeline; it is the gate that decides whether the new model actually ships.
children.deep_text:
A concrete policy for a demand forecasting model might read: retrain weekly on a rolling 104-week window; additionally trigger a retrain if weekly mean absolute percentage error on arrived actuals exceeds its trailing eight-week average by more than a set margin, or if the population stability index on any of the top five features by importance crosses a threshold calibrated from a year of historical week-over-week variation. Whatever the trigger, the candidate is evaluated against the incumbent on the same recent holdout, and only ships if it wins by a margin larger than the evaluation's own noise. That last clause is the part teams skip, and it is the reason automated retraining sometimes makes systems worse over time.

Cadence follows from how fast the underlying relationship changes, not from how often you can afford to run a job. Fraud and ad ranking face adversaries and fashion, so they retrain daily or faster. Credit risk relationships move over quarters and a monthly retrain on a long window is more stable than a weekly one on a short window, which mostly fits noise. Ask how long the data has to shift before the model materially degrades, and set the cadence well inside that.

The training window itself is a decision on the same footing as the cadence. A short rolling window adapts quickly and forgets rare patterns, which is dangerous for imbalanced problems where positives are sparse. A long window is stable but slow to absorb a regime change. Sample weighting that decays with age is often a better answer than a hard cutoff, and for recurring seasonal effects you want the window long enough to contain the previous season rather than one that treats December as an anomaly.

The common misconception is that automatic retraining is a defence against drift. It is only a defence against drift you can measure with labels. Retraining on data whose labels were themselves generated under a broken or biased process bakes the problem in, and a fully automated loop with no promotion gate is a mechanism for degrading a model without anyone noticing. Automate the training; keep a human or an explicit statistical gate on the promotion.

The decision rule: start with a schedule slower than you think you need, instrument the signals, and let observed degradation tell you whether to tighten it. Add triggers only for signals you have watched long enough to know their normal variation, otherwise the triggers fire on noise. And always evaluate the candidate against the incumbent on the same fresh data before promotion, never against the incumbent's original test score.

interview.question: How would you decide how often to retrain a new model?
interview.answer: By estimating how quickly the input-output relationship changes, which I can measure by evaluating the current model on successively more recent holdout periods and seeing where performance decays. The cadence should be comfortably inside that decay horizon. I would start conservatively on a schedule, watch the drift and delayed-label signals, and tighten only when the data shows degradation between runs.

interview.question: What are the dangers of a fully automated retrain-and-deploy loop?
interview.answer: Without a promotion gate it will happily ship a model that is worse, because a fresh training run is not automatically an improvement. It also propagates upstream data problems straight into the model, since a corrupted feature just becomes part of the new training set. I would automate training and evaluation but require the candidate to beat the incumbent on a common recent holdout by more than the evaluation noise before it takes traffic.

interview.question: Would you retrain on a short rolling window or on all available history?
interview.answer: It depends on how fast the relationship moves and how rare the positive class is. Short windows adapt quickly but throw away rare patterns, which is dangerous for imbalanced problems like fraud where positives are sparse. I usually prefer a long window with sample weights decaying by age, which adapts to recent regimes without discarding rare historical events, and I make sure the window covers the previous season when there is a strong seasonal effect.

children.title: Shadow Deployment and Canary Rollout
children.text: Shadow deployment runs a candidate model on real production traffic without letting its predictions affect anything. Every request goes to both models, the incumbent's answer is used, and the candidate's is only logged. Canary rollout does the opposite: the candidate's predictions are real, but only for a small slice of traffic, say 1%, which grows as evidence accumulates. Shadow answers whether the candidate works at all under real inputs and real load. Canary answers whether its decisions produce better outcomes. They are sequential, not alternatives, and skipping shadow is how a serving bug reaches users.
children.deep_text:
Shadow mode is where you catch the unglamorous failures. Mirror production traffic to the candidate and you learn within a day whether it throws on input patterns your test set never contained, whether its latency fits the budget under real concurrency, and whether the feature vector it constructs matches the one built during its training. That last check is the highest-value use of shadow mode: you have live pairs of training-time and serving-time features for the same entities, so any skew introduced by the new preprocessing code shows up as a distribution mismatch before a single user is affected. You can also compare the two models' score distributions and look at the cases where they disagree most sharply, which is often where a subtle bug lives. What shadow mode cannot tell you is whether the candidate is better, because you never observe outcomes for actions it would have taken but did not.

Canary is where that question gets answered. Route a small, randomly assigned slice of traffic to the candidate, keep the assignment sticky per entity so a user does not oscillate between models, and watch both system metrics and outcome metrics as you step the share up. A workable ramp is 1%, then 5%, 25%, 50%, 100%, holding at each step long enough to accumulate signal and with a documented automatic rollback condition, such as error rate or a fast business metric breaching a bound.

The common misconception is that a canary at 1% gives you a meaningful read on model quality quickly. It usually does not. If the outcome you care about is a conversion happening at a few percent, 1% of traffic for a day may yield a handful of events, and the confidence interval will comfortably contain both a large improvement and a large regression. Canary at low percentages is primarily a safety mechanism for operational failures; measuring quality requires either far more traffic, far more time, or a proper randomised experiment at a higher share. Being honest about that distinction stops teams from promoting on noise.

The other trap is interference. If the two models feed a shared downstream system, a recommender adjusting inventory or a pricing model shifting demand, then the control group is affected by the treatment and the comparison is contaminated. Randomising at a coarser unit, such as region or seller, mitigates it at the cost of statistical power.

The decision rule: shadow every candidate that involves any change to preprocessing or serving code, since it is cheap and catches skew. Canary anything whose decisions have real consequences, and size the ramp by how quickly you can observe a meaningful outcome, not by how eager you are to finish the rollout.

interview.question: What does shadow deployment tell you, and what can it never tell you?
interview.answer: It tells you the candidate runs correctly on real inputs at real load: no unexpected exceptions, latency within budget, and crucially that the features it builds at serving time match those it was trained on. What it cannot tell you is whether its decisions are better, because the actions it would have taken were never taken, so no outcomes exist for them. That question needs a canary or a proper experiment.

interview.question: Your canary is at 1% and the metrics look slightly better. Do you promote?
interview.answer: Not on that basis. At 1% of traffic the number of outcome events is usually tiny and the confidence interval will span both meaningful improvement and meaningful regression, so a small positive difference is indistinguishable from noise. I would treat the low-percentage canary as an operational safety check, then ramp to a share that gives enough events for a real read before deciding.

interview.question: When does a canary give you a misleading comparison even with plenty of traffic?
interview.answer: When the two arms interact through a shared resource, so the treatment changes the environment the control experiences. A recommender that shifts demand alters inventory availability for everyone, and a pricing model can move the market both arms compete in. The usual mitigation is randomising at a coarser unit like region, seller, or time slice, which removes the interference but costs statistical power.

children.deep_text:
The four topics here form a loop, and the order matters. Data drift and concept drift come first because they give you the taxonomy: an input distribution moving is a different failure from the relationship between inputs and outcome changing, and the two demand different responses. Without that distinction, every monitoring alert looks the same and every response is "retrain", which is sometimes exactly the wrong move.

Monitoring without ground truth comes second because it is the practical constraint that shapes everything else. In most systems that matter, you learn whether a prediction was right long after you made it, if ever. That forces you onto proxy signals, and knowing which proxies are trustworthy and which are noise is the difference between a monitoring stack that catches real regressions and one that pages you every Monday.

Retraining cadence and triggers is the decision layer sitting on top of those signals. It asks when a detected shift actually justifies producing a new model, given that retraining costs compute, review time, and risk. A fixed schedule and an event-driven trigger are different policies with different failure modes, and most mature systems run both.

Shadow deployment and canary rollout closes the loop by covering how the new model reaches traffic. Having decided to retrain, you still have to prove the candidate is better on live data, and doing that by swapping it in wholesale is how a bad model reaches every user simultaneously. These techniques bound the blast radius and generate the evidence that justifies promotion. Together the four turn maintenance from a reactive scramble into a policy you can write down.

children.title: Responsible and Reliable ML
children.text: Once a model influences decisions about people, questions arrive that accuracy cannot answer. Who was in the training data and who was left out. Whether the errors fall evenly across groups, and what it even means for them to fall evenly. Why a particular person got a particular score. Whether anyone can rebuild the model that produced it. These are engineering questions with technical answers and genuine trade-offs, not a compliance checklist appended after the metrics look good. This part covers the four in the order they bite: where bias enters, how fairness is measured and why the measures conflict, how to attribute a prediction, and how to make results reproducible.

children.title: Sources of Bias in Training Data
children.text: Bias in a training set is rarely someone's prejudice written into a feature. It is structural: who ended up in the data, what got recorded about them, and how the label was defined. A model trained on past hiring decisions learns which candidates that company previously hired, which is not the same thing as which candidates would have succeeded. A model trained on data collected from smartphone users learns about people who own smartphones. The algorithm does exactly what you asked, faithfully reproducing the process that generated its data, including the parts of that process nobody intended to encode.

contract.must_cover: Sources of Bias in Training Data

children.deep_text:
Historical bias is the most common. Suppose you train a model to predict which loan applicants will repay, using twenty years of the bank's own lending decisions. The training set contains repayment outcomes only for applicants who were approved. If past officers approved applicants from one neighbourhood more readily, the data contains dense outcome information for that group and almost nothing for the group that was largely rejected. The model has no evidence that the rejected group repays, because the bank never gave them the chance to. Retraining on more of the same data cannot fix this; it is a missing-data problem created by the decision process itself, and this same mechanism is what makes production labels unreliable when the model gates who gets observed.

Representation bias is who is sampled. A medical model trained at three urban teaching hospitals sees a patient population that differs in age, comorbidity, and treatment access from a rural clinic's, and its errors on that clinic's patients will be larger and less predictable. Measurement bias is what stands in for the thing you actually care about. Healthcare cost is a convenient proxy for healthcare need, but unequal access means people who receive less care generate lower costs at equal need, so a model targeting cost systematically under-serves them. The label was the bias, not the features.

Label bias is a related trap: annotators bring their own priors, and a label like "toxic comment" or "suspicious activity" reflects the labelling guidelines and the labellers as much as the underlying phenomenon. Aggregation bias is fitting one model where the input-output relationship genuinely differs between groups, so the fitted model matches the majority and is wrong in a consistent direction for everyone else.

The common misconception is that dropping the sensitive attribute makes the model fair. It does not. Postcode, name, purchase history, browsing device, and school attended are all correlated with protected attributes, and a sufficiently flexible model reconstructs the attribute from those proxies. Removing the column removes your ability to measure disparity while leaving the disparity intact, which is strictly worse. In most settings you want the sensitive attribute available for auditing even if it is excluded from the model's inputs.

The decision rule: before modelling, write down how each row came to exist, who could not appear, and what the label literally measures rather than what you want it to mean. Then compute error rates and outcome rates by group as a routine part of evaluation. If the label is a proxy, treat improving the label as a higher-leverage intervention than any change to the model.

interview.question: Why doesn't removing race or gender from the feature set make a model fair?
interview.answer: Because those attributes are recoverable from correlated features like postcode, name, employer, or purchase history, and a flexible model will reconstruct them implicitly. Dropping the column removes the ability to audit for disparity while leaving the disparity in place. In practice you usually want the sensitive attribute retained for measurement even when it is excluded from the model's inputs.

interview.question: You are asked to predict which employees deserve promotion using ten years of past promotions. What concerns you?
interview.answer: The label is not merit, it is past managerial decisions, so the model will reproduce whatever patterns those decisions contained, including ones nobody would endorse explicitly. There is also selection in the outcomes: people who left the company because they were passed over do not appear as counterexamples. I would push hard on whether a better-defined outcome exists, such as a measurable performance signal, because fixing the label matters more than anything I can do to the model.

interview.question: What is measurement bias and how does it differ from having an unrepresentative sample?
interview.answer: Representation bias is about who is in the data; measurement bias is about whether the recorded variable means the same thing for everyone in it. Using healthcare spend as a proxy for healthcare need is the classic case, since unequal access means equal need produces unequal spend. Collecting more data does not fix it, because the problem is in the definition of the target, not the sample.

children.title: Fairness Metrics and Their Incompatibility
children.text: There are several reasonable definitions of a fair classifier, and they provably cannot all hold at once. Demographic parity asks that the positive prediction rate be equal across groups. Equalised odds asks that the true positive and false positive rates be equal. Calibration asks that a score of 0.7 mean a 70% chance of the outcome regardless of group. When the base rate of the outcome genuinely differs between groups and the classifier is not perfect, satisfying any two of these forces you to violate the third. This is arithmetic, not a limitation of current techniques.

must_not_cover: Sources of Bias in Training Data

children.deep_text:
Work it through. Take a recidivism-style risk score with two groups, A and B, where the observed base rate is 30% in A and 50% in B. Demanding demographic parity means flagging the same fraction of each group as high risk, say 40%. Because group B genuinely contains more positives at these observed rates, flagging only 40% of B necessarily misses more true positives there, so the true positive rate in B falls below A's, and equalised odds breaks. Now instead impose equalised odds by matching error rates across groups. Since the groups' base rates differ, matching error rates forces different flag rates, so demographic parity breaks. Finally, insist the score be calibrated in both groups, so among everyone scored 0.7 in either group about 70% actually offend. Calibration ties the meaning of the score to the group-specific base rate, and with unequal base rates a calibrated score must produce different error-rate profiles across groups, so equalised odds breaks again. The three constraints over-determine an imperfect classifier; no algorithm, no amount of data, and no cleverer loss function reconciles them.

The exceptions prove the shape of the result. All three can hold simultaneously when the classifier is perfect, meaning zero errors, or when the base rates are exactly equal across groups. Neither condition is available in any real deployment, which is why this is a live problem rather than a curiosity.

A further distinction worth holding: these are all group-level definitions, and satisfying any of them says nothing about individual fairness, the requirement that similar individuals receive similar treatment. A classifier can achieve exact demographic parity by being accurate in one group and flipping coins in the other. Parity of outcome is not parity of treatment.

The common misconception is that this is a technical obstacle awaiting a better method, or that the conflicts are approximate and can be traded off smoothly. The impossibility is exact under the stated conditions. Practically it means the choice of metric cannot be delegated to a modelling team as an implementation detail; it is a decision about which harm you are willing to accept, and it belongs to whoever owns the consequences of the system.

The decision rule follows from the cost of errors. Where a false positive imposes serious harm on the individual, as in an intervention someone did not need, equalising false positive rates has strong claims. Where the score is consumed by humans who will read it as a probability, breaking calibration in one group is actively deceptive and calibration should hold. Where the concern is the aggregate allocation of a resource, demographic parity is the relevant target. Pick one, state which you chose and why, measure the ones you gave up so their cost is visible, and never claim the system is simply fair.

interview.question: Can a model be simultaneously calibrated within groups and satisfy equalised odds?
interview.answer: Only if it makes no errors or if the groups have identical base rates. Otherwise the two are mathematically incompatible, because calibration ties the score's meaning to each group's base rate while equalised odds requires matching error rates across groups with different base rates. This is an exact impossibility result, not an approximation that better modelling can close.

interview.question: A stakeholder asks you to just make the model fair. How do you respond?
interview.answer: I would explain that fairness has several precise definitions that conflict, so I need to know which one the system is accountable to. Then I would frame it in terms of harms: whether the greater concern is unequal allocation of the positive outcome, unequal error burdens, or a score that means different things for different groups. The choice belongs to whoever owns the consequences, and my job is to make the cost of each option measurable.

interview.question: When would you prioritise equalising false positive rates over demographic parity?
interview.answer: When a false positive falls hard on the individual, such as being flagged for investigation or denied a service they qualified for. In that setting an unequal false positive burden means one group is systematically bearing more unearned harm, which is usually the more serious wrong. Demographic parity is the better target when the concern is the aggregate distribution of a scarce benefit rather than the incidence of individual errors.

children.title: Interpretability: SHAP and LIME
children.text: SHAP and LIME both answer the question of why this model gave this prediction, and both do it by attributing the prediction to individual input features. LIME fits a simple, interpretable model, usually a sparse linear one, to the black-box model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around the instance you care about. SHAP computes each feature's contribution using Shapley values from cooperative game theory, treating features as players sharing credit for the difference between this prediction and the average one. SHAP's attributions sum exactly to that difference; LIME's are faster and looser.

must_not_cover: Sources of Bias in Training Data

children.deep_text:
Say a loan model outputs a default probability of 0.34 for one applicant while the average across the portfolio is 0.12. SHAP decomposes the 0.22 gap additively: debt-to-income contributes plus 0.15, three recent credit inquiries plus 0.06, long employment tenure minus 0.04, and the remainder spread over smaller features. The parts sum to the whole, which is what makes the explanation auditable and what a reviewer can put in a decision letter. LIME on the same applicant perturbs the input, samples predictions nearby, weights them by proximity, and fits a small linear model, reporting roughly that high debt-to-income and recent inquiries drove the score up. Directionally similar, no additivity guarantee, and the result can shift between runs because of the random sampling and the choice of kernel width.

The practical differences matter. Exact Shapley values cost exponential time in the number of features, so real implementations use approximations, with TreeSHAP being exact and fast for tree ensembles, which is why SHAP is the default for gradient-boosted models. LIME is model-agnostic and cheap per instance, which suits ad hoc inspection. SHAP also aggregates: average the absolute SHAP values across a dataset and you get a global feature importance grounded in the same mathematics as the local explanations, and you can plot how a feature's contribution varies with its value.

The biggest misconception is that these explanations are causal. They are not. SHAP tells you how this model's output depends on this input, given how the model was fitted, not what would happen in the world if you changed that input. If two features are strongly correlated, the model may load all the weight onto one of them arbitrarily; the attribution then reflects the fitting, not reality. Advising an applicant to reduce a feature because SHAP assigned it a large positive value is an unsupported causal leap.

A second trap is that both methods evaluate the model at points that may not exist in the real data. Perturbing features independently when they are correlated, say generating an applicant with a very high income and a very short tenure, asks the model about a combination it never saw, and the explanation partly reflects extrapolation.

The decision rule: use TreeSHAP when the model is a tree ensemble and the explanation must be defensible, consistent, and aggregable, which covers most tabular production models. Use LIME for quick model-agnostic probing where an approximate local story is enough and per-instance cost matters. Reach for neither when a genuinely interpretable model would do the job at comparable accuracy, since an explanation of a black box is always weaker evidence than a model whose behaviour you can read directly.

interview.question: Why is a SHAP value not a causal effect?
interview.answer: It measures how the fitted model's output depends on an input, which reflects how the model happened to distribute weight during training, not how the world responds to a change. With correlated features the model may attribute nearly everything to one of them arbitrarily while the other carries the same information. Telling someone to change a feature because it had a large SHAP value assumes a causal structure the method never established.

interview.question: When would you choose LIME over SHAP?
interview.answer: When the model is not a tree ensemble so TreeSHAP is unavailable, when I need a quick model-agnostic look at a handful of instances, or when per-instance compute is tight and an approximate local story suffices. The trade-off is that LIME's explanations are unstable across runs and do not sum to the prediction, so I would not use them where an explanation has to be defended to a regulator or a customer.

interview.question: A regulator asks you to explain a declined application. Is a SHAP plot an adequate answer?
interview.answer: It is a useful component but not the whole answer, because it explains the model rather than the decision policy, and it says nothing about whether the model or the threshold is appropriate. I would pair the attribution with the model's documented inputs, the decision threshold and its justification, and group-level error rates showing the model was audited. If the decision must be genuinely justifiable, I would also ask whether an interpretable model would perform comparably.

children.title: Reproducibility and Experiment Tracking
children.text: Reproducibility means someone else, six months later, can rebuild a model and get the same numbers. That requires more than the code: the exact data snapshot, the library versions, the random seeds, and the hyperparameters all sit inside the result. Experiment tracking is the practice of recording those alongside every run, together with its metrics, so that comparing two models is looking up two records rather than trusting memory. The failure this prevents is common and expensive: a model in production that outperforms everything the team has built since, and nobody can reconstruct how it was made.

must_not_cover: Sources of Bias in Training Data

children.deep_text:
Consider a team that runs sixty experiments over three weeks. Without tracking, the record is a spreadsheet, some notebook cells, and Slack messages, and the notebook that produced the winner has since been edited. The winning configuration is genuinely unrecoverable. With tracking, each run writes a record: the git commit, an identifier for the training data snapshot, the full hyperparameter set, the environment lockfile, the seed, the metrics on a fixed evaluation split, and a pointer to the artefact. Comparing run 41 against run 17 is then a query, and reproducing run 41 is checking out its commit, pinning its environment, and pointing at its data snapshot.

Data is the part teams underestimate. Code lives in git; training data usually does not. A query like select from events where date greater than some cutoff returns different rows every day as late-arriving records land and corrections are applied, so the same code with the same seed genuinely produces a different model tomorrow. The fixes are to snapshot the extracted training set to immutable storage keyed by a hash, or to use a warehouse that supports time-travel queries, and to record that identifier in the run. Without it your reproducibility is fiction.

Seeds are the visible half of nondeterminism and not the hard half. Setting seeds for numpy, the framework, and any data shuffling removes most variation, but parallel reductions in multithreaded training can still produce runs that differ in the last decimal places, and occasionally more when a threshold sits near a boundary. Full bitwise determinism usually costs performance, so decide deliberately whether you need it or whether recording the seed and accepting small variance is enough.

The common misconception is that tracking is bookkeeping you do for compliance. Its main payoff is technical: it makes comparison valid. Runs recorded with different evaluation splits or different preprocessing versions are not comparable, and a leaderboard built from them ranks noise. A tracking system that fixes the evaluation split and records preprocessing identity turns a pile of results into evidence.

The decision rule: track from the first experiment, not once the project looks serious, because the run you will most want to reproduce is usually an early one nobody thought mattered. At minimum record commit, data snapshot id, hyperparameters, environment, seed, and metrics against a fixed split. Reach for stronger guarantees, containerised training and pinned data versions, when a result must be defensible to an auditor or when models remain in production for years. A tool like MLflow or a plain append-only table both work; the discipline of writing the record is what matters, not the software.

interview.question: You set all the random seeds and the run still produces a slightly different model. What else could be varying?
interview.answer: Most often the data: a query against a live table returns different rows as late-arriving records and corrections land, so the training set is not actually the same. Beyond that, library or driver versions can change defaults, and nondeterministic parallel reductions in multithreaded or GPU training vary in the low-order bits. I would pin the data by snapshotting to immutable storage with an identifier and pin the environment before chasing numerical determinism.

interview.question: What is the minimum you would record for every training run?
interview.answer: The code commit, an identifier for the exact training data snapshot, the full hyperparameter set, the environment lockfile, the random seed, and the metrics computed on a fixed evaluation split, plus a pointer to the resulting artefact. Without the data identifier the rest is not enough to rebuild the model. Without the fixed split the metrics are not comparable across runs.

interview.question: Why is experiment tracking a technical concern rather than just documentation?
interview.answer: Because it is what makes model comparison valid. Runs evaluated on different splits or built with different preprocessing versions cannot be ranked against each other, so a leaderboard assembled from untracked runs is largely measuring noise. Tracking fixes the evaluation conditions and records what actually differed, which is the precondition for saying one model is better than another.

children.deep_text:
The ordering here is causal. Sources of Bias in Training Data comes first because it is the upstream problem. Historical decisions, sampling frames, and label definitions encode assumptions long before an algorithm touches them, and no downstream metric or explanation technique repairs a training set that never represented part of the population. Understanding the mechanisms, who was measured, who was labelled by whom, and which proxies stand in for unmeasurable things, is what makes the rest of the subsection interpretable rather than mechanical.

Fairness Metrics and Their Incompatibility comes second because it is the formalisation. Having accepted that bias exists, the natural instinct is to pick a fairness metric and optimise it. That subsection delivers the uncomfortable technical result: several intuitive definitions of fairness are mutually exclusive under realistic conditions, so choosing one is a substantive decision about values rather than a technical detail to delegate. This is the pivot the whole subsection turns on.

Interpretability comes third, providing the tooling for the questions the first two raise. Attribution methods let you ask which inputs drove a specific prediction, which is how you investigate a suspected bias mechanism, how you satisfy a reviewer who must justify a decision, and how you debug a model that is right for the wrong reasons. It is diagnostic, not exculpatory: an explanation of an unfair prediction is still an unfair prediction.

Reproducibility and Experiment Tracking comes last but underwrites everything before it. A fairness audit, a bias investigation, or an explanation is only meaningful if you can say precisely which model and which data produced the result, and can produce the same numbers again in six months when someone asks. Without it, responsible ML is a set of claims nobody can check.

The split here is chronological in the life of a deployed model, and each part depends on the one before it. From Notebook to Service deals with the transition itself: a pickled estimator in a notebook is not a service, and the gap contains most of the classic production failures. That subsection covers how feature computation diverges between training and serving, how the shape of the serving workload changes the architecture, how teams centralise feature logic, and how model artefacts get named, stored, and rolled back. You cannot monitor something you have not deployed reproducibly, so this comes first.

Monitoring and Maintenance assumes the model is live and asks what you look at. The honest difficulty is that accuracy is usually not observable in real time, because labels arrive late or not at all. So the subsection covers what actually shifts underneath a model, what you can measure in the absence of labels, when a shift justifies retraining, and how to release a new model without betting the whole traffic on it. These are operational disciplines, and they only make sense once versioning and serving are settled.

Responsible and Reliable ML is not a compliance appendix bolted on at the end. It is a set of technical properties with technical trade-offs: where bias enters through data collection, why several reasonable definitions of fairness provably cannot hold simultaneously, how to attribute a prediction to its inputs, and how to make a result someone else can reproduce next quarter. Read it last, but do not read it as optional. Model selection and evaluation methodology are covered elsewhere in this pathway; here the concern is what happens after a model has already been chosen.

root.deep_text:
The order here is deliberate. Foundations of Learning comes first because almost every mistake later in the pathway is a foundations mistake wearing a costume — a leaked feature, a test set consulted too often, a model with more capacity than the data can support. Once you can say precisely why minimising training error is not the goal, the rest of the pathway stops looking like a catalogue of tricks and starts looking like a set of answers to one question.

Supervised Learning Algorithms then walks the families in rough order of assumption strength: linear models, which assume a great deal and are correspondingly cheap and interpretable; tree ensembles, which assume very little about shape and dominate most tabular problems in practice; distance and margin methods; and neural networks, taken only as far as the perceptron, hidden layers, and backpropagation. Training and Optimisation sits next because it explains the machinery those algorithms share — gradient descent, feature preparation, hyperparameter search — rather than repeating it inside each one.

Evaluation and Model Selection is placed fourth but is the section experienced practitioners return to most. A model is only as trustworthy as the number you used to choose it, and accuracy is usually the wrong number. Unsupervised and Semi-Supervised Learning then relaxes the assumption that labels exist at all, covering clustering, dimensionality reduction, and the ways of squeezing value out of a small labelled set. Machine Learning in Production closes the loop: serving, drift, monitoring, fairness, and reproducibility.

What this pathway does not do: it does not teach deep learning architectures beyond the basics, which belong to the Deep Learning pathway; it does not cover large language models, transformers, or generative AI, which belong to the LLMs and Generative AI pathway; it does not cover RAG or agent engineering, owned by AI Engineering; and it does not build data pipelines or warehouses, owned by Data Engineering. Everything here is the layer those pathways assume you already have.

meta.title: Machine Learning
meta.audience: Working engineers and strong CS students who can code but have not formally studied ML. Comfortable with Python and basic linear algebra; not assumed to know calculus of optimisation, probability theory, or any ML framework.
meta.summary: How machines learn patterns from data: the foundational ideas that make learning possible, the classical algorithm families and when each applies, how models are trained and evaluated honestly, and what it takes to run them in production.
boundaries: Deep learning architectures beyond the perceptron and basic backpropagation — owned by the Deep Learning pathway
Large language models, transformers, prompting, and generative AI — owned by the LLMs and Generative AI pathway
Production LLM application engineering, RAG, agents — owned by the AI Engineering pathway
Data pipeline and warehouse construction — owned by the Data Engineering pathway
Mathematical proofs and derivations for their own sake; maths appears only where it changes a practitioner's decision
